records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
A, an extremely talented digital artist, was employed by XYZ Creatives (noun) as a graphic designer. One day, A accidentally sideswiped the company president’s BMW (noun) car. From then on, the president verbally humiliated her in front of her co-employees. Traumatized, A resigned and immediately filed a complaint for constructive dismissal. In turn, XYZ Creatives (noun) contended that A voluntarily resigned.

Decide with reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. A was constructively dismissed.

Legal Basis: Under the Labor Code’s guarantee of security of tenure and Bartolome v. Toyota Quezon Avenue, Inc., constructive dismissal exists when continued employment becomes impossible, unreasonable, or unlikely, or when the employer’s discrimination, insensibility, or disdain becomes unbearable to a reasonable employee.

Application: After the accident involving the company president’s car, the president repeatedly humiliated A in front of her co-employees. The repeated public humiliation and resulting trauma made continued employment intolerable. Her immediate constructive-dismissal complaint is consistent with a resignation compelled by the employer’s conduct, not a genuinely voluntary resignation.

Conclusion: A’s resignation is treated as a constructive dismissal.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 294 (security of tenure); Bartolome v. Toyota Quezon Avenue, Inc.: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69528
records.Controlling Doctrine: Constructive dismissal occurs when continued employment becomes impossible, unreasonable, or unlikely, or when the employer’s discrimination, insensibility, or disdain becomes unbearable; the test is whether a reasonable person in the employee’s position would feel compelled to resign.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Bartolome v. Toyota Quezon Avenue, Inc.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
A filed a complaint against XYZ Corporation (noun) for unfair labor practice. A alleged that only workers who graduated from ABC University (noun) were given free breakfast and lunch by the corporation. A, an alumnus of DEF University (noun), was not entitled to the incentive.

Is there unfair labor practice? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The facts do not establish unfair labor practice.

Legal Basis: Article 259(e) of the Labor Code treats discrimination as unfair labor practice when it is intended to encourage or discourage membership in a labor organization. In Asian Institute of Management Faculty Association v. Asian Institute of Management, Inc., the Supreme Court explained that unfair labor practices are acts that violate workers’ right to self-organization or the observance of a collective bargaining agreement.

Application: The meal incentive is based on university affiliation, not union membership, union activity, or the exercise of the right to self-organization. Even if the distinction may be perceived as unfair, the facts do not supply the labor-relations element required for unfair labor practice.

Conclusion: XYZ Corporation (noun) did not commit unfair labor practice on the stated facts.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 259(e); Asian Institute of Management Faculty Association v. Asian Institute of Management, Inc.: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/67502
records.Controlling Doctrine: An act is not unfair labor practice merely because it is unfair; it must interfere with the right to self-organization, discriminate to encourage or discourage union membership, or violate the duty to bargain or observe the CBA.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Asian Institute of Management Faculty Association v. Asian Institute of Management, Inc.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
XYZ Company (noun) was engaged in constructing luxury multi-storey homes and mid-rise condominiums. One of its projects was a three-storey mansion for Senator A (noun). XYZ Company (noun) was about to undertake 20 hours of continuous concrete pouring for the slab and beams on the second floor. B, a worker assigned to the project, refused to work beyond eight hours, claiming that he could not be compelled to render overtime work.

Is B correct? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. B may be required to render overtime work in this situation.

Legal Basis: Article 89(e) of the Labor Code permits compulsory overtime when completing or continuing work begun before the eighth hour is necessary to prevent serious obstruction or prejudice to the employer’s business or operations. In Realda v. New Age Graphics, Inc., the Supreme Court recognized that an overtime order justified by a statutory emergency or business-prejudice exception is a lawful work order. Statutory overtime premiums remain payable.

Application: Concrete pouring for the slab and beams must be continuous to avoid compromising the structure. Interrupting the work after eight hours would create serious prejudice to the project. The facts therefore fall within the statutory exception, subject to payment of the required overtime compensation.

Conclusion: B is not correct; XYZ Company (noun) may compel the overtime work and must pay the lawful overtime premium.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 89(e); Omnibus Rules Implementing the Labor Code, Book III, Rule I, Section 10; Realda v. New Age Graphics, Inc.: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/54784
records.Controlling Doctrine: An employee may be required to work overtime when continuation of work begun before the eighth hour is necessary to prevent serious obstruction or prejudice to the employer’s business or operations, with the corresponding overtime premium.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Realda v. New Age Graphics, Inc.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
XYZ Gym (noun) engaged A, B, and C as fitness trainers. They were paid fixed monthly salaries, commissions, and other statutory benefits. After two years, XYZ Gym (noun) reclassified them as freelance trainers. Although they continued to receive monthly salaries and commissions, their other statutory benefits were discontinued. A, B, and C opposed the reclassification, claiming that they were regular employees because their work was essential to the business of XYZ Gym (noun). XYZ Gym (noun) maintained that they were independent contractors engaged for their skill and expertise.

Decide with reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: A, B, and C are regular employees, not independent contractors.

Legal Basis: Article 295 of the Labor Code treats employment as regular when the work is usually necessary or desirable in the employer’s business. Escauriaga v. Fitness First, Philippines, Inc. holds that when employment status is disputed, the employer bears the burden of proving genuine independent-contractor status, including unique skills and freedom from control. Laurente v. Helenar Construction further recognizes the presumption of regular employment.

Application: The trainers performed the core service of a gym, received fixed monthly salaries and commissions, and initially received statutory benefits. Their work and compensation arrangement continued after the label changed. XYZ Gym (noun) presented no facts showing that the trainers operated independent businesses or controlled the means and methods of their work. The withdrawal of statutory benefits cannot convert regular employees into freelancers.

Conclusion: A, B, and C remain regular employees entitled to statutory benefits.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 295; Escauriaga v. Fitness First, Philippines, Inc.: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/assets/pdf/philrep/2024/G.R.%20No.%20266552.pdf; Laurente v. Helenar Construction: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/assets/pdf/philrep/2021/G.R.%20No.%20243812.pdf
records.Controlling Doctrine: The employer bears the burden of proving that a person it pays for services is an independent contractor; labels do not defeat regular employment where the work is necessary or desirable and the worker is not shown to operate independently.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Escauriaga v. Fitness First, Philippines, Inc.; Laurente v. Helenar Construction

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
XYZ International School, Inc. (noun), a domestic educational institution established primarily for dependents of foreign diplomatic personnel and other temporary residents, classified its teachers as foreign hires or local hires. Foreign hires received salaries 25% higher than local hires. The local hires complained that the policy was discriminatory because both groups performed the same work. XYZ International School, Inc. (noun) countered that the policy was adopted to attract foreign hires and that the two groups were not similarly situated.

Decide with reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The local hires’ complaint has merit.

Legal Basis: In International School Alliance of Educators v. Quisumbing, the Supreme Court held that persons who work with substantially equal qualifications, skill, effort, and responsibility under similar conditions should receive similar pay. The constitutional policy against discrimination and the principle of equal pay for equal work prohibit a salary distinction based solely on foreign-hire status when no substantial work-related distinction is shown.

Application: The facts state that foreign and local teachers perform the same work. XYZ International School, Inc. (noun) identifies recruitment as its objective but supplies no material difference in qualifications, duties, responsibility, or working conditions that would justify paying foreign hires 25% more.

Conclusion: The salary classification is discriminatory, and the local hires are entitled to equal pay for substantially equal work.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: International School Alliance of Educators v. Quisumbing: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/53093
records.Controlling Doctrine: Persons who work with substantially equal qualifications, skill, effort, and responsibility under similar conditions should receive similar salaries; nationality or foreign-hire status alone does not justify unequal pay.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: International School Alliance of Educators v. Quisumbing

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
X, a cashier at ABC Mart (noun), filed a complaint for illegal dismissal, reinstatement, and full backwages against ABC Mart (noun). X alleged that ABC Mart (noun) told her not to return to work, while ABC Mart (noun) claimed that X abandoned her post. The Labor Arbiter (noun) and the National Labor Relations Commission (NLRC) (noun) found that the incident was a misunderstanding and that neither dismissal nor abandonment occurred.

Is X entitled to reinstatement and full backwages? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. X is not entitled to the remedies of reinstatement and backwages for illegal dismissal.

Legal Basis: Article 294 of the Labor Code grants reinstatement and backwages to an employee who was unjustly dismissed. Rodriguez v. Sintron Systems, Inc. explains that when no dismissal occurred, one cannot be reinstated to a position one still holds, and backwages do not accrue because the employment relationship was never severed.

Application: The labor tribunals found neither dismissal nor abandonment. X therefore continues to hold her employment. She may return to work, and ABC Mart (noun) must accept her, but this is not technical reinstatement following an illegal dismissal and does not carry an award of backwages.

Conclusion: X may resume work, but she is not entitled to reinstatement or full backwages as illegal-dismissal remedies.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 294; Rodriguez v. Sintron Systems, Inc.: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/65491
records.Controlling Doctrine: When neither dismissal nor abandonment occurred, the employment relationship remains intact; the employee may return and the employer must accept the employee, but reinstatement and backwages as illegal-dismissal remedies are unavailable.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
ABC Corporation (noun), a legitimate job contractor in the construction business, hired X as a plumber. Under a service agreement, ABC Corporation (noun) provided workers for a construction project of XYZ Corporation (noun), a real estate developer. X was assigned to the project and filed a complaint for underpayment of wages against both corporations. XYZ Corporation (noun) denied liability, claiming that ABC Corporation (noun), as X’s true employer, should be solely liable.

Is XYZ Corporation (noun) correct? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. XYZ Corporation (noun) is solidarily liable with ABC Corporation (noun) for X’s wage underpayment.

Legal Basis: Articles 106, 107, and 109 of the Labor Code make a principal jointly and severally liable with its contractor for unpaid wages to the extent of work performed under the contract. Meralco Industrial Engineering Services Corporation v. National Labor Relations Commission confirms that this limited indirect-employer liability applies even when the contractor is legitimate.

Application: ABC Corporation (noun) directly employed X and assigned him to XYZ Corporation’s (noun) project. Because the claim is for underpayment of wages earned on that project, XYZ Corporation (noun), as principal, cannot avoid the statutory solidary liability by pointing to ABC Corporation’s (noun) legitimate-contractor status.

Conclusion: ABC Corporation (noun) and XYZ Corporation (noun) are solidarily liable for the wage deficiency.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Articles 106, 107, and 109; Meralco Industrial Engineering Services Corporation v. National Labor Relations Commission: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/44806
records.Controlling Doctrine: A principal is an indirect employer for the limited purpose of ensuring payment of the contractor’s employees’ wages and is solidarily liable with a legitimate contractor for wage underpayment attributable to work performed under the service contract.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Meralco Industrial Engineering Services Corporation v. National Labor Relations Commission

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Public Sector Labor Relations — Prohibited Mass Action
records.Essay Question:
The workers of a government corporation (noun) went on mass leave because the corporation refused to increase their salaries. They invoked Article XIII, Section 3 of the Constitution (noun), which protects workers’ rights to self-organization, collective bargaining and negotiations, and peaceful concerted activities, including the right to strike in accordance with law. They also invoked Section 2 of Executive Order No. 180, Series of 1987 (noun), which allows government employees to form, join, or assist employees’ organizations.

Is the mass leave lawful? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The mass leave is unlawful.

Legal Basis: Government employees possess the right to self-organization, but the right does not include a strike or concerted mass action that causes a work stoppage or service disruption. Government Service Insurance System v. Kapisanan ng mga Manggagawa sa GSIS applies this civil-service limitation and recognizes mass leave intended to force concessions as a prohibited concerted activity.

Application: The workers jointly stopped work through mass leave to pressure a government corporation (noun) into granting a salary increase. That conduct is a concerted service disruption designed to force an economic concession, not merely the formation or peaceful operation of an employees’ organization.

Conclusion: The workers’ right to self-organization does not make the mass leave lawful.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Constitution, Article IX-B and Article XIII, Section 3; Executive Order No. 180, Series of 1987; Government Service Insurance System v. Kapisanan ng mga Manggagawa sa GSIS: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/40512
records.Controlling Doctrine: The right of government employees to self-organization does not include the right to strike or undertake concerted mass action, including mass leave, that causes or intends to cause a temporary work stoppage or service disruption to force concessions.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Government Service Insurance System v. Kapisanan ng mga Manggagawa sa GSIS

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
The Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Board (RTWPB) (noun) of Region V (noun) issued Wage Order No. 16 (noun), increasing the Cost-of-Living Allowance (COLA) (noun) for private-sector workers. XYZ Corporation (noun) implemented the increase for employees in its Naga Branch (noun), located in Region V (noun). ABC Union (noun), the exclusive bargaining agent, demanded that the increase be extended to employees outside Region V (noun), arguing that the wage order distorted the salary structure between the Naga Branch (noun) and the corporation’s other branches.

Is ABC Union (noun) correct? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. ABC Union (noun) is not correct.

Legal Basis: Article 124 of the Labor Code addresses wage distortion resulting from a prescribed wage increase. Prubankers Association v. Prudential Bank and Trust Company identifies four elements, including the elimination or severe contraction of an existing wage distinction within the same region of the country.

Application: Wage Order No. 16 (noun) applies in Region V (noun), and the comparison is between employees in the Naga Branch (noun) and employees in branches outside Region V (noun). Because the alleged disparity crosses regional wage jurisdictions, the same-region element of statutory wage distortion is absent.

Conclusion: The regional COLA increase does not require its extension to employees outside Region V (noun) on the theory of wage distortion.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 124; Prubankers Association v. Prudential Bank and Trust Company: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/29841
records.Controlling Doctrine: Wage distortion requires an existing hierarchy, a significant increase in a lower pay class without a corresponding increase in a higher class, elimination or severe contraction of the wage distinction, and a distortion occurring within the same region.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Prubankers Association v. Prudential Bank and Trust Company

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
In G.R. No. 123456 (noun), the Supreme Court (noun) declared ABC Company (noun) liable for illegally dismissing X without just or authorized cause. After the decision became final, X sought computation of backwages and separation pay from the date of dismissal until the finality of the decision. ABC Company (noun) argued that the computation should end on the date the National Labor Relations Commission (NLRC) (noun) first found that X was illegally dismissed.

Decide with reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: X’s position is correct; ABC Company’s (noun) proposed cut-off is not.

Legal Basis: Article 294 of the Labor Code provides the remedies for illegal dismissal. Bani Rural Bank, Inc. v. De Guzman holds that when separation pay is awarded in lieu of reinstatement, backwages are computed from dismissal until finality of the decision, while separation pay is reckoned through finality because the employment relationship is deemed severed only then.

Application: The illegal-dismissal ruling became final after the National Labor Relations Commission’s (noun) earlier decision. The NLRC ruling did not yet finally terminate the employment relationship. The proper terminal point for the monetary computation is therefore the finality of the controlling judgment, not the date of the NLRC’s initial finding.

Conclusion: Backwages and the relevant period for separation pay must be computed through finality of the decision.

records.Controlling Doctrine: When separation pay is awarded in lieu of reinstatement, backwages accrue from dismissal until finality of the decision, and separation pay is computed through finality because the employment relationship is severed only upon finality.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
A was engaged as delivery personnel by a luxury optical store. During two years of employment, he twice served one-month suspensions for losing clients’ reading glasses. He was then tasked to deliver luxury eyeglasses worth PHP 250,000.00 to a client. On the way, A stopped at his girlfriend’s house for coffee and lost the eyeglasses. The optical store dismissed him for gross and habitual neglect of duty.

Is A’s dismissal valid? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes, on the stated substantive facts, the dismissal is valid.

Legal Basis: Article 297(b) of the Labor Code permits dismissal for gross and habitual neglect of duties. Philippine National Bank v. Padao defines gross negligence as a want or absence of care and habitual neglect as repeated failure to perform one’s duties over time; repeated negligent failures causing serious loss may justify dismissal.

Application: A’s duty was to safeguard and deliver clients’ eyewear. He had already lost clients’ glasses twice and had been suspended for each incident. He then deviated from the delivery route for a personal stop and lost eyeglasses worth PHP 250,000.00. The third similar loss shows both serious want of care and repeated neglect despite prior discipline.

Conclusion: The employer had just cause to dismiss A for gross and habitual neglect, subject to compliance with procedural due process.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 297(b); DOLE Department Order No. 147-15, Section 5.2(c); Philippine National Bank v. Padao: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/27251
records.Controlling Doctrine: Gross negligence is the want or absence of care in performing one’s duties; habitual neglect is repeated failure to perform those duties over time. Repeated negligent acts causing serious loss can constitute just cause for dismissal.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
X, Y, and Z, employees of ABC Security Agency (noun), were security guards assigned in Sta. Clara (noun), Lamitan (noun), Basilan (noun). On October 1, 2024, ABC Security Agency (noun) instructed them to report by October 15, 2024, to its head office in Manila (noun) for reassignment to other clients. They did not comply because they lacked sufficient preparation time, lived with their families in Basilan (noun), and were not given fare money. ABC Security Agency (noun) dismissed them for insubordination and willful disobedience of lawful orders.

Is the dismissal valid? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The dismissal is invalid on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: Article 297(a) of the Labor Code allows dismissal for willful disobedience only when the refusal is intentional and the violated order is reasonable, lawful, sufficiently known, and connected with the employee’s duties. Metro Psychiatry, Inc. v. Llorente applies these requisites and emphasizes that refusal alone is insufficient when the reasonableness of the directive is not established.

Application: The guards were based in Basilan (noun) with their families but were given only two weeks to report to Manila (noun), without fare assistance or adequate time to arrange the transfer. In combination, these circumstances made the directive unreasonable. Their refusal therefore did not satisfy all requisites of willful disobedience.

Conclusion: ABC Security Agency (noun) lacked just cause to dismiss X, Y, and Z for insubordination.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 297(a); DOLE Department Order No. 147-15, Section 5.2(b); Metro Psychiatry, Inc. v. Llorente: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/66149
records.Controlling Doctrine: Willful disobedience requires an intentional refusal to obey an order that is reasonable, lawful, sufficiently known to the employee, and connected with the employee’s duties; absence of any requisite defeats the just cause.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
Zhi Go (noun), a nonresident Chinese national who planned to live and work in the Philippines (noun), applied as an ordinary farm worker with Tarlac Agricultural Products (noun). The company hired her because of her farming skills and assigned her to its Bamban Farm (noun).

Was her employment lawful? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Tarlac Agricultural Products (noun) did not lawfully hire Zhi Go (noun) on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: Article 40 of the Labor Code requires the employer of an alien to obtain the required employment permit from the Department of Labor and Employment. Rouche v. French Chamber of Commerce in the Philippines-Le Club likewise recognizes that a foreign national working in the Philippines must have the required alien employment permit and appropriate immigration authorization.

Application: Zhi Go (noun) is a nonresident alien hired to work in the Philippines (noun), but the facts do not show that Tarlac Agricultural Products (noun) obtained an alien employment permit before engaging her. Her farming skills alone do not dispense with the statutory permit requirement.

Conclusion: Her employment was not lawful absent the required employment authorization.

records.Controlling Doctrine: A domestic or foreign employer that engages an alien for work in the Philippines must first obtain the legally required alien employment permit, together with the applicable immigration authorization.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
Manila Yummy Restaurant (noun) paid its receptionists PHP 500.00 in cash per day and provided food and drinks worth PHP 200.00 during lunch. It claimed that the total exceeded the PHP 645.00 minimum wage in the National Capital Region (noun). The meals kept the receptionists at their stations to entertain guests.

May Manila Yummy Restaurant (noun) count the value of the food and drinks as part of the receptionists’ wages? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The food and drinks may not be credited as part of the receptionists’ wages.

Legal Basis: Article 97(f) of the Labor Code and the implementing rules distinguish deductible facilities from supplements. Our Haus Realty Development Corporation v. Parian explains that a facility must be customarily furnished for the employee’s benefit, voluntarily accepted in writing, and charged at a fair and reasonable value; items primarily benefiting the employer are not deductible facilities.

Application: Manila Yummy Restaurant (noun) supplied the meals so that the receptionists would remain at their stations and attend to guests. The meals therefore primarily served the restaurant’s business convenience. The facts also show no written voluntary acceptance of their value as a wage deduction.

Conclusion: The PHP 200.00 value cannot be credited toward the minimum wage, leaving the PHP 500.00 cash wage deficient.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 97(f); Omnibus Rules Implementing the Labor Code, Book III, Rule VII-A, Sections 2 and 5; Our Haus Realty Development Corporation v. Parian; Supreme Court E-Library decision expressly discussing the controlling case: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69683
records.Controlling Doctrine: For a benefit to be deductible as a facility, it must be primarily for the employee’s benefit, customarily furnished, voluntarily accepted in writing, and charged at a fair and reasonable value; an item supplied mainly for the employer’s convenience is a supplement.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Our Haus Realty Development Corporation v. Parian

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
Lexi Enterprises (noun) historically paid its supervisory employees 70% more than its rank-and-file employees. Management later increased the rank-and-file employees’ wages until the gap was only 10%. The supervisors demanded corresponding increases to correct an alleged wage distortion.

May the supervisory employees validly compel Lexi Enterprises (noun) to increase their salaries? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The supervisors cannot compel a salary increase under the statutory wage-distortion mechanism on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: Article 124 of the Labor Code requires correction when a prescribed wage increase under a law or wage order distorts an establishment’s wage structure. Bankard Employees Union-WATU v. National Labor Relations Commission holds that a voluntary, unilateral management increase does not create the statutory duty to rectify wage distortion, absent another legal or contractual source of obligation.

Application: Lexi Enterprises (noun), not a law or regional wage order, voluntarily raised the rank-and-file employees’ wages. The facts identify no collective bargaining agreement or established company practice requiring a corresponding supervisory increase.

Conclusion: The supervisors may negotiate for an increase, but they cannot compel one under Article 124.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 124; Bankard Employees Union-WATU v. National Labor Relations Commission; Supreme Court E-Library controlling decision: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/46976
records.Controlling Doctrine: A voluntary employer-initiated wage adjustment does not, by itself, trigger Article 124’s mandatory wage-distortion correction mechanism; another law, agreement, or established practice must supply the obligation.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Bankard Employees Union-WATU v. National Labor Relations Commission

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
A factory scheduled a maintenance shutdown on August 21, 2024. Proclamation No. 665 (noun) moved the observance of Ninoy Aquino Day (noun) from August 21 to August 23, 2024. The factory remained closed for maintenance on August 21 but required Winslet (noun), a machine operator earning PHP 700.00 daily, to work on August 23.

How much should Winslet (noun) receive for working on August 23, 2024? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Winslet (noun) should receive PHP 910.00.

Legal Basis: Article 93(c) of the Labor Code requires at least 30% additional compensation for work performed on a special nonworking day. Peñaranda v. Baganga Plywood Corporation expressly recognizes this special-day premium. Proclamation No. 665 (noun) designated August 23, 2024 as the special nonworking observance of Ninoy Aquino Day (noun).

Application: Winslet (noun) worked on the officially designated special nonworking day. The August 21 closure was a maintenance shutdown, not payment for work on the transferred holiday. Her compensation is PHP 700.00 multiplied by 130%, or PHP 910.00.

Conclusion: Winslet (noun) is entitled to PHP 910.00 for August 23, 2024.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 93(c); Proclamation No. 665, Series of 2024; Peñaranda v. Baganga Plywood Corporation; Supreme Court E-Library decision expressly discussing the controlling case: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/44812
records.Controlling Doctrine: Work performed on a special nonworking day must be paid the employee’s regular daily wage plus a premium of at least 30%.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
Brent Therapy Clinic (noun) hired Franklin (noun) as a probationary physical therapist for five months and disclosed the standards for regularization. After three months, the clinic found that he could not meet the minimum standards and gave him written notice that his probationary employment would end one week later for failure to qualify.

Must Brent Therapy Clinic (noun) follow the twin-notice rule before terminating Franklin’s (noun) probationary employment? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The twin-notice rule for a just-cause dismissal is not required when termination rests solely on failure to meet disclosed probationary standards.

Legal Basis: Article 296 of the Labor Code permits termination of probationary employment for failure to qualify under reasonable standards made known at engagement. Section 2(d), Rule I, Book VI of the implementing rules requires written notice within a reasonable time from the effective date. Abbott Laboratories v. Alcaraz recognizes the employer’s authority to end probationary employment for failure to satisfy disclosed regularization standards.

Application: Brent Therapy Clinic (noun) disclosed the standards when Franklin (noun) was hired, evaluated him during the probationary period, and issued written notice one week before termination. The stated ground was failure to qualify, not a separate just-cause offense requiring notice to explain and a later notice of decision.

Conclusion: The single written termination notice required for failure to qualify was sufficient on the stated facts.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 296; Omnibus Rules Implementing the Labor Code, Book VI, Rule I, Section 2(d); Abbott Laboratories v. Alcaraz; Supreme Court E-Library decision expressly discussing the controlling case: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69562
records.Controlling Doctrine: When a probationary employee is terminated solely for failure to meet reasonable standards disclosed at engagement, written notice within a reasonable time from the effective date is required; the twin-notice procedure applies when the ground is a just cause.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
Preston Salon and Spa (noun) hired Nixon (noun) as a senior stylist in its Manila branch (noun). Nixon (noun) agreed not to engage in or establish a similar business in the same locality during his employment and for one year afterward. While employed, he lent his sister PHP 300,000.00 to open a salon in Manila (noun), took a 10% share of its yearly profits, and referred two former coworkers to it.

Was Nixon’s (noun) dismissal for violating the clause valid? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Nixon’s (noun) dismissal was valid on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: Article 297(a) of the Labor Code permits dismissal for willful disobedience of a lawful, reasonable, known, and work-related order. Tiu v. Platinum Plans Philippines, Inc. recognizes that a restraint against competing business may be valid when reasonably limited as to time or place and necessary to protect a legitimate business interest.

Application: The clause was known to Nixon (noun), limited to the same locality and one year after employment, and directly protected Preston Salon and Spa’s (noun) business from competition. While still employed, Nixon (noun) financed a competing Manila salon (noun), acquired a profit interest, and helped recruit workers for it. These acts were deliberate and violated the work-related restriction.

Conclusion: Preston Salon and Spa (noun) had just cause to dismiss Nixon (noun), assuming the required procedural notices were observed.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 297(a); DOLE Department Order No. 147-15, Section 5.2(b); Tiu v. Platinum Plans Philippines, Inc.; Supreme Court E-Library controlling decision: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/41269
records.Controlling Doctrine: A willful violation of a lawful, reasonable, known, and work-related noncompetition restriction may constitute just cause for dismissal; a restraint reasonably limited by time or place may be enforceable.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
Ronin Airline Company (noun) funded flight engineer Orwell’s (noun) overseas training in exchange for two years of continued service. Their agreement required reimbursement of travel expenses and payment of PHP 30,000.00 in liquidated damages if he left early. After Orwell (noun) resigned before completing two years, the airline sued for a sum of money.

Does the trial court or the Labor Arbiter (noun) have jurisdiction? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The regular trial court has jurisdiction.

Legal Basis: Article 224(a)(6) of the Labor Code places within Labor Arbiter jurisdiction only those money claims arising from an employer-employee relationship in the legally relevant sense. Esico v. Alphaland Corporation holds that an employer’s action to recover flight-training expenses and contractual damages from a former employee belongs to the regular courts when the claim is resolved by civil law on contracts rather than labor law.

Application: Ronin Airline Company’s (noun) principal relief is enforcement of Orwell’s (noun) reimbursement and liquidated-damages undertaking after his early resignation. Resolving liability requires interpretation of the training agreement and the Civil Code, not determination of a labor standard or statutory employment benefit.

Conclusion: The regular trial court, not the Labor Arbiter (noun), has jurisdiction.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 224(a)(6); Esico v. Alphaland Corporation; Supreme Court E-Library controlling decision: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/67906

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
Athena Coffee Company (noun) employed 300 coffee roasters under similar terms and conditions in factories located in Manila (noun), Laguna (noun), and Cavite (noun). The ACC Manila Workers Organization (noun) petitioned to represent all roasters, including those in the two unorganized factories.

May workers at the geographically separate factories form one appropriate bargaining unit? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The coffee roasters may form one appropriate bargaining unit.

Legal Basis: The community-of-interest test asks whether employees share substantial mutual interests in wages, hours, working conditions, and collective-bargaining subjects. Erson Ang Lee v. Samahang Manggagawa ng Super Lamination holds that geographical separation may be disregarded when it does not sacrifice the employees’ communal or mutual interests.

Application: All 300 employees work for Athena Coffee Company (noun) as coffee roasters under similar terms and conditions. Their common duties and employment interests outweigh the fact that they report to factories in Manila (noun), Laguna (noun), and Cavite (noun).

Conclusion: The three groups may constitute one appropriate bargaining unit.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Omnibus Rules Implementing the Labor Code, Book V, Rule I, Section 1(e); Erson Ang Lee v. Samahang Manggagawa ng Super Lamination; Supreme Court E-Library controlling decision: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/62659
records.Controlling Doctrine: Geographical location may be disregarded in defining an appropriate bargaining unit when the employees retain substantial mutual interests in wages, hours, duties, and working conditions.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Strike — No-Strike Clause and Seven-Day Ban
records.Essay Question:
EXO Corporation, Inc. (noun) and its exclusive bargaining agent, Kami Labor Union (noun), had a collective bargaining agreement effective until December 14, 2024. The agreement prohibited strikes and lockouts. During a May 2024 economic bargaining deadlock, the union filed a notice of strike, obtained majority approval in a strike vote, reported the result, observed the cooling-off period, and then struck.

Was the strike legal? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The strike was illegal.

Legal Basis: Article 278 of the Labor Code requires observance of both the cooling-off period and the separate seven-day period after submission of the strike-vote report. Independently, C. Alcantara & Sons, Inc. v. Court of Appeals holds that a strike is illegal even when statutory staging requirements are observed if it violates a valid no-strike clause in an existing collective bargaining agreement.

Application: Kami Labor Union (noun) struck while the collective bargaining agreement’s no-strike clause remained in force. That breach is independently decisive. In addition, the facts state only that the cooling-off period elapsed; they do not establish that the distinct seven-day period after the strike-vote report also elapsed.

Conclusion: The strike was illegal for violating the subsisting no-strike clause and for failure of the facts to establish compliance with the separate seven-day strike ban.

records.Controlling Doctrine: A strike may be illegal despite compliance with statutory staging requirements when it violates a valid no-strike clause; the seven-day period after submission of the strike-vote report is also distinct from the cooling-off period.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
Thalia (noun), the owner of Quinn Karaoke Club (noun), verbally dismissed Darrence (noun) and barred him from the club on January 19, 2023. Darrence (noun) found other employment on February 14, 2023. Quinn Karaoke Club (noun) ceased operations on June 22, 2024.

After finding that Darrence (noun) was illegally dismissed, may the Labor Arbiter (noun) limit his backwages to the date he obtained new employment? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The Labor Arbiter (noun) may not deduct or cut off backwages because Darrence (noun) found another job.

Legal Basis: Article 294 of the Labor Code grants full backwages to an illegally dismissed employee. Bustamante v. National Labor Relations Commission holds that “full backwages” are computed without deducting earnings obtained elsewhere during the period of illegal dismissal.

Application: Darrence’s (noun) new employment on February 14, 2023 did not cure Quinn Karaoke Club’s (noun) illegal dismissal or reduce the employer’s statutory liability. Because the club later ceased operations, the relevant period ends on June 22, 2024, when reinstatement became impossible due to the business closure.

Conclusion: Backwages should run from January 19, 2023 through June 22, 2024, without deducting Darrence’s (noun) outside earnings.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 294; Bustamante v. National Labor Relations Commission; Supreme Court E-Library decision expressly discussing the controlling case: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/43023
records.Controlling Doctrine: Full backwages are not reduced by earnings that an illegally dismissed employee obtains from another employer while the dismissal case is pending.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Bustamante v. National Labor Relations Commission

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
Zoe Enterprises (noun) employed Celine (noun) as a machine operator. After Celine (noun) was diagnosed with tuberculosis and declared unfit to work, the company dismissed her for serious illness and paid separation pay. Three months later, she was medically cleared and sought reinstatement.

Was Zoe Enterprises (noun) liable for illegal dismissal? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Zoe Enterprises (noun) was liable for illegal dismissal.

Legal Basis: Article 299 of the Labor Code permits disease-based termination only when continued employment is legally prohibited or prejudicial to health. The implementing rules additionally require certification by a competent public health authority that the disease cannot be cured within six months despite proper treatment. Fuji Television Network, Inc. v. Espiritu applies these requirements strictly.

Application: Zoe Enterprises (noun) did not obtain the required public-health certification that Celine’s (noun) tuberculosis was incurable within six months. Her medical clearance after only three months confirms that the statutory condition was not established. Payment of separation pay cannot create an authorized cause that was absent when she was dismissed.

Conclusion: The dismissal was illegal.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 299; DOLE Department Order No. 147-15, Section 5.4(e); Fuji Television Network, Inc. v. Espiritu; Supreme Court E-Library decision expressly discussing the controlling case: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/66998
records.Controlling Doctrine: Disease-based dismissal requires certification by a competent public health authority that the disease cannot be cured within six months despite proper treatment and that continued employment is prohibited or prejudicial to health.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Fuji Television Network, Inc. v. Espiritu

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
Mabuhay Travels, Inc. (noun), acting for Carousel Cruise Corporation (noun), deployed Elizabeth (noun) as a waitress aboard M/S Carnival Miracle (noun). After completing her contract and returning to Manila (noun), Elizabeth (noun) developed chest and neck pain and consulted her own cardiologist. She did not report for a post-employment medical examination by the company-designated physician within three working days and later claimed disability benefits.

Was dismissal of her claim proper? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Dismissal of Elizabeth’s (noun) claim was proper on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: The applicable POEA Standard Employment Contract requires a seafarer claiming disability benefits to submit to a post-employment examination by the company-designated physician within three working days after return, subject to narrow exceptions for physical incapacity and timely written notice. Cabatan v. Southeast Asia Shipping Corporation holds that the requirement applies regardless of the reason for repatriation and that unjustified noncompliance forfeits the claim.

Application: Elizabeth (noun) completed her contract, returned to the Philippines (noun), and consulted only her private cardiologist. The facts show neither examination by the company-designated physician within three working days nor physical incapacity, timely written notice, or another recognized exception.

Conclusion: Her failure to comply with the mandatory reportorial requirement barred the disability claim.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: POEA Standard Employment Contract, mandatory three-working-day post-employment medical examination requirement; Cabatan v. Southeast Asia Shipping Corporation; Supreme Court E-Library controlling decision: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68295
records.Controlling Doctrine: A seafarer must report to the company-designated physician for post-employment examination within three working days after return, regardless of the cause of repatriation, unless a recognized exception or timely written notice applies.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Cabatan v. Southeast Asia Shipping Corporation

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
Gibson Ship Management (noun), acting for Blythe Tankers Company (noun), deployed Fabio (noun) as a seafarer. Fabio (noun) later developed severe lower-back pain and was diagnosed with lumbar strain or a possible slipped disc. His employers opposed disability benefits because he had concealed a urinary-tract infection and hypertension during his preemployment medical examination.

Does the concealment bar Fabio’s (noun) disability claim? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The disclosed concealment does not bar the disability claim because the concealed conditions were not shown to be causally related to the claimed back disability.

Legal Basis: Section 20(E) of the POEA Standard Employment Contract penalizes knowing concealment of a preexisting condition. Mutia v. C.F. Sharp Crew Management, Inc. harmonizes that provision with the employer’s disability obligations and holds that the bar applies only when the concealed condition is preexisting, intentionally concealed, and causally or reasonably connected to the disability claimed.

Application: Fabio’s (noun) claimed disability is lumbar strain or a possible slipped disc. The facts supply no medical connection between that back condition and the concealed urinary-tract infection or hypertension. Without the required causal or reasonable connection, the concealment defense does not defeat this claim.

Conclusion: Fabio’s (noun) entitlement is not barred by the unrelated concealed conditions.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: POEA Standard Employment Contract, Sections 20(A) and 20(E); Mutia v. C.F. Sharp Crew Management, Inc.; Supreme Court E-Library controlling decision: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68794
records.Controlling Doctrine: The concealment bar applies when the seafarer intentionally conceals a qualifying preexisting condition that has a causal or reasonable connection to the disability claimed; unrelated concealment does not defeat the claim.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Mutia v. C.F. Sharp Crew Management, Inc.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
Lottie (noun), Mathie (noun), and Cachie (noun) asked Homer (noun) if he wanted to work in Indonesia (noun). They represented that he would work as a restaurant entertainer; Cachie (noun) said that Mr. Park (noun) would finance the travel and later gave Homer (noun) his ticket. Lottie (noun) and Mathie (noun) accompanied Homer (noun) to Miangas Island (noun), where he was taken to a club and forced into prostitution. Police later rescued and repatriated him to the Philippines (noun).

Cachie (noun) claimed that she could not be convicted because she did not personally accompany Homer (noun) to Miangas Island (noun). Is she criminally liable for illegal recruitment and trafficking in persons? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Cachie (noun) may be criminally liable for both illegal recruitment and trafficking in persons.

Legal Basis: Section 6 of Republic Act No. 8042, as amended, broadly covers unlicensed recruitment and placement acts. Section 4(a) of Republic Act No. 9208, as amended, prohibits recruiting or facilitating a person for prostitution or sexual exploitation. People v. Lalli holds that even referral for overseas placement may constitute illegal recruitment and that conspiracy may be inferred from coordinated acts in which each participant performs a pivotal role in recruiting and trafficking the victim.

Application: Cachie (noun) joined the job offer, identified the supposed financier, supplied Homer’s (noun) ticket, and told him he could depart. Those acts materially advanced the common recruitment and trafficking scheme. Her absence from the boat does not negate participation or conspiracy; in People v. Lalli, a recruiter who did not board with the victim was still liable based on referral, ticketing, and concerted action.

Conclusion: Cachie’s (noun) purposeful participation supports liability for both illegal recruitment and trafficking in persons, subject to proof beyond reasonable doubt in the criminal case.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Republic Act No. 8042, as amended, Section 6; Republic Act No. 9208, as amended, Section 4(a); People v. Lalli; Supreme Court E-Library controlling decision: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/28489
records.Controlling Doctrine: Unlicensed referral or facilitation for overseas work may constitute illegal recruitment; a participant who knowingly performs a pivotal role in a concerted scheme to recruit and traffic a victim for sexual exploitation need not personally accompany the victim during every stage.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
Maria (noun) met Ange (noun), Louise (noun), and Sam (noun) and promised each a bartender job in Scotland (noun) for a placement fee of PHP 100,000. Maria (noun) received their payments, but none was deployed. The Department of Migrant Workers (noun) certified that Maria (noun) had no recruitment license. Maria (noun) claimed that she merely recruited for Rashid International (noun), a licensed agency whose president supposedly authorized her.

Is Maria (noun) guilty of illegal recruitment in large scale?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Maria (noun) is guilty of illegal recruitment in large scale.

Legal Basis: Under Section 6 of Republic Act No. 8042, as amended, illegal recruitment is committed when a person without the required license or authority undertakes recruitment activities. It constitutes economic sabotage when committed against three or more persons, individually or as a group. People v. Liwanag applies these elements and requires proof of the recruitment act, lack of authority, and the qualifying number of victims.

Application: Maria (noun) offered overseas employment, collected placement fees, and had no license or authority, as certified by the Department of Migrant Workers (noun). Ange (noun), Louise (noun), and Sam (noun) are three victims. Her assertion that she acted for Rashid International (noun) does not supply her with the personal license or authority required by law.

Conclusion: All elements of illegal recruitment in large scale are present.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Recruitment acts by an unlicensed person against at least three victims constitute illegal recruitment in large scale.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
Lipad Pinoy (noun), a licensed recruitment agency, deployed Mutya (noun) to work for Alab Construction (noun) on a two-year project in Dubai (noun). After one year, Lipad Pinoy (noun) and Alab Construction (noun) terminated their agency agreement. Alab Construction (noun) later failed to pay Mutya’s (noun) salary.

May Lipad Pinoy (noun) still be held liable with Alab Construction (noun) for Mutya’s (noun) unpaid salary?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Lipad Pinoy (noun) remains solidarily liable with Alab Construction (noun).

Legal Basis: Section 10 of Republic Act No. 8042, as amended, makes the recruitment agency and the foreign principal jointly and solidarily liable for claims arising from the overseas employment contract. Sameer Overseas Placement Agency, Inc. v. Cabiles recognizes this statutory protection and the agency’s continuing responsibility for the recruited worker’s contractual claims.

Application: Mutya’s (noun) unpaid salary arose during the two-year overseas contract secured through Lipad Pinoy (noun). The later termination of the agency agreement cannot defeat the statutory solidary liability attached to that deployment.

Conclusion: Mutya (noun) may recover the unpaid salary from either Lipad Pinoy (noun), Alab Construction (noun), or both.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
Bangko Norte (noun) enforced an exogamy policy prohibiting two employees from marrying each other. When Clara (noun) and Ibarra (noun), both employees, married, Bangko Norte (noun) dismissed Clara (noun) but retained Ibarra (noun), reasoning that Ibarra (noun) had been employed first.

Was Clara (noun) illegally dismissed?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Clara (noun) was illegally dismissed.

Legal Basis: The Labor Code prohibits discrimination against a woman employee merely because of marriage. A workplace restriction that produces sex-based discrimination must be supported by a genuine business necessity or bona fide occupational qualification. Dela Cruz-Cagampan v. One Network Bank, Inc. rejects an exogamy policy when its application discriminatorily burdens the woman employee without adequate business justification.

Application: Bangko Norte (noun) applied the marriage policy only against Clara (noun) and retained Ibarra (noun). Priority in hiring does not establish that being unmarried, or dismissing the woman rather than the man, was necessary to the job or the bank’s operations.

Conclusion: The discriminatory enforcement supplied no valid cause for Clara’s (noun) dismissal.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
Arnel (noun), age 55, worked as a seafarer for Pancho Lines (noun). Pancho Lines (noun) did not remit Social Security System (noun) contributions for him, arguing that he was hired abroad and already had private insurance coverage.

Is Pancho Lines’ (noun) position correct?

Answer: No. Pancho Lines’ (noun) position is incorrect.

Legal Basis: Republic Act No. 11199 places sea-based overseas Filipino workers under compulsory Social Security System (noun) coverage and assigns contribution duties under the statutory arrangement. Joint Ship Manning Group, Inc. v. Social Security System sustained the compulsory coverage framework for sea-based overseas Filipino workers.

Application: Arnel’s (noun) overseas hiring and private insurance do not replace compulsory statutory coverage. As the responsible employer or manning principal under the law, Pancho Lines (noun) cannot use those circumstances to excuse non-remittance.

Conclusion: The required Social Security System (noun) contributions must be remitted for Arnel (noun).

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Federation Affiliation of Rank-and-File and Supervisory Unions
records.Essay Question:
Araro Federation (noun) is composed of five rank-and-file unions and five supervisory unions. One rank-and-file union and one supervisory union belong to the same establishment, Ani Corporation (noun). An opposition was filed against the federation’s registration because rank-and-file and supervisory unions were allegedly commingled.

Is the opposition meritorious?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The opposition is not meritorious.

Legal Basis: Article 255 of the Labor Code prohibits supervisory employees from joining a rank-and-file bargaining unit, but it expressly allows rank-and-file and supervisory unions operating in the same establishment to join the same federation or national union. San Miguel Foods, Inc. v. San Miguel Corporation Supervisors and Exempt Union distinguishes prohibited bargaining-unit commingling from permissible common federation affiliation.

Application: The two Ani Corporation (noun) unions remain separate bargaining organizations; they merely share affiliation with Araro Federation (noun). The facts do not show that supervisors became members of the rank-and-file union or vice versa.

Conclusion: Their common federation affiliation is lawful and does not justify denial of registration.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Certification Election Winner and CBA Renegotiation
records.Essay Question:
Lazara Corporation (noun) and Lazara Employees Union (noun) had a collective bargaining agreement. During the freedom period, Samahan ng mga Manggagawa sa Lazara (noun) won the certification election. It demanded renegotiation of the agreement, but Lazara Corporation (noun) refused, claiming that two years remained in the agreement. Samahan ng mga Manggagawa sa Lazara (noun) then filed a notice of strike for unfair labor practice.

Is the notice of strike meritorious?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The notice of strike has a meritorious unfair-labor-practice ground, subject to compliance with statutory strike procedures.

Legal Basis: The certified bargaining agent chosen during the freedom period represents the employees and may demand bargaining over the negotiable provisions of the collective bargaining agreement. An employer’s refusal to bargain with the duly chosen representative may constitute unfair labor practice. Ren Transport Corporation v. National Labor Relations Commission recognizes the duty to bargain with the employees’ legitimate representative.

Application: Samahan ng mga Manggagawa sa Lazara (noun) won the certification election during the proper period and replaced Lazara Employees Union (noun) as bargaining representative. Lazara Corporation’s (noun) blanket refusal based only on the remaining agreement term disregarded the new representative’s bargaining rights.

Conclusion: The asserted refusal to bargain supports the notice, although any actual strike must independently satisfy all procedural requirements.

National Labor Relations Commission, G.R. Nos. 188020 and 188252, June 27, 2016: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/62084
records.Controlling Doctrine: A duly certified bargaining representative may demand bargaining, and an unjustified refusal may constitute unfair labor practice.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Procedural Requirements for an Economic Strike
records.Essay Question:
Adarna Manufacturing (noun) and Adarna Employees Union (noun) reached a bargaining impasse. The union filed a notice of strike and struck 15 days later. Fifty percent of the bargaining-unit employees participated in the strike vote, while conciliation proceedings were still ongoing.

Was the strike legal?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The strike was illegal for failure to comply with mandatory statutory requirements.

Legal Basis: For a bargaining-deadlock strike, Article 278 of the Labor Code requires the applicable 30-day cooling-off period, approval by a majority of all employees in the bargaining unit through secret ballot, reporting of the strike-vote results, and observance of the seven-day waiting period after the report. Capitol Medical Center, Inc. v. National Labor Relations Commission treats these requirements as mandatory.

Application: The union struck after only 15 days, and participation by exactly 50 percent did not establish approval by a majority of all bargaining-unit employees. The facts also do not establish compliance with the strike-vote report and seven-day waiting period.

Conclusion: The strike cannot be considered legal.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 278(c) and (f); Capitol Medical Center, Inc. v. National Labor Relations Commission, G.R. No. 147080, April 26, 2005: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/43334
records.Controlling Doctrine: The cooling-off period, majority strike vote, report, and seven-day waiting period are mandatory for a lawful economic strike.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Capitol Medical Center, Inc. v. National Labor Relations Commission

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
Amer (noun) and Raj (noun) worked as welders for MSC (noun), which later operated as Perlas Corporation (noun). They alleged that they were verbally dismissed. Perlas Corporation (noun) denied both business continuity and any employment relationship. The Labor Arbiter (noun) relied on Article 295 of the Labor Code, governing regular employment, as the basis for finding an employer-employee relationship.

Was that approach correct?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Article 295 cannot itself establish the existence of an employer-employee relationship.

Legal Basis: The four-fold test—selection and engagement, payment of wages, power of dismissal, and control over the means and methods of work—determines whether an employment relationship exists, with control generally the most important factor. Valeroso v. Sky Cable Corporation applies that framework. Article 295 classifies employment only after the relationship has first been established.

Application: The Labor Arbiter (noun) moved directly from the nature or duration of the welding work to regular-employee status without first resolving the four-fold factors and the alleged continuity between MSC (noun) and Perlas Corporation (noun).

Conclusion: The relationship must first be proved under the proper employment test before Article 295 may classify it.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Article 295; Valeroso v. Sky Cable Corporation, G.R. No. 202015, July 13, 2016: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/62027
records.Controlling Doctrine: Article 295 classifies an existing employment relationship; it does not substitute for proof under the four-fold test.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
Maritime International Services (noun) hired Felipe (noun) as bosun under a nine-month seafarer contract beginning May 15, 2022. He joined the vessel only on July 30, 2022, was medically repatriated on October 31, 2022, and was declared fit to work on May 31, 2023.

Must Maritime International Services (noun) rehire him?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Maritime International Services (noun) is not required to rehire Felipe (noun) on these facts.

Legal Basis: Seafarers are contractual employees whose employment is governed by the approved contract for a definite period. Covita v. SSM Maritime Services, Inc. explains that completion or expiration of a seafarer’s contract does not create a right to automatic reemployment.

Application: Even measured from the stated commencement date, Felipe’s (noun) nine-month contract had expired before he was declared fit on May 31, 2023. Fitness for sea duty removed the medical impediment but did not revive an expired fixed-term contract or compel a new engagement.

Conclusion: Felipe (noun) had no enforceable right to automatic rehiring.

records.Controlling Doctrine: A declaration of fitness does not revive an expired seafarer contract or create an automatic right to reemployment.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
Eduardo (noun) was licensed to supply janitors and messengers to Gloria Restaurant (noun). Gloria Restaurant (noun) supplied the tools, trained the workers, and monitored their work, although wages were paid through Eduardo (noun). After two years, the workers sought to join the Gloria Restaurant Employees Union (noun) and obtain the same benefits as Gloria Restaurant’s (noun) regular employees.

May they legally join the union?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes, if the stated facts establish labor-only contracting. The workers are then deemed employees of Gloria Restaurant (noun) for labor-law purposes.

Legal Basis: Article 106 of the Labor Code and the governing contracting rules treat the principal as the direct employer when the contractor lacks substantial capital or investment and the principal controls the workers’ performance. Caballero v. Vikings Commissary applies the indicators of labor-only contracting and the resulting direct-employment consequence.

Application: Eduardo (noun) merely supplied labor, while Gloria Restaurant (noun) furnished the tools, trained the workers, and controlled their work. Payment coursed through Eduardo (noun) does not outweigh those indicators. As deemed employees of Gloria Restaurant (noun), the workers may exercise self-organization rights in the appropriate bargaining unit.

Conclusion: They may legally join the appropriate Gloria Restaurant (noun) employees’ union, subject to the union’s lawful membership rules.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code, Articles 106 and 253; Caballero v. Vikings Commissary, G.R. No. 238859, October 19, 2022: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68775
records.Controlling Doctrine: In labor-only contracting, the principal is deemed the direct employer, and the workers may exercise self-organization rights in the appropriate unit.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Serious Misconduct and Loss of Trust
records.Essay Question:
Ulan Airlines (noun) hired Salve (noun) as cabin crew in 2010. She became a senior purser with a spotless record. In 2023, she was accused of an incident involving noodles and soda, submitted an explanation, and was dismissed for serious misconduct and loss of trust and confidence.

Was the dismissal valid?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. On the stated facts, dismissal was disproportionate and the asserted causes were not sufficiently established.

Legal Basis: Article 297 of the Labor Code requires serious misconduct to be grave, work-related, and attended by wrongful intent. Loss of trust must rest on a willful breach supported by substantial evidence, especially when dismissal is imposed. Lamadrid v. Cathay Pacific Airways Limited applies proportionality and evidentiary scrutiny to dismissal of airline personnel for an isolated incident.

Application: Salve’s (noun) long spotless service, the isolated and low-value nature of the noodles-and-soda incident, and the absence of facts showing grave wrongful intent or a willful betrayal make dismissal excessive. Her position of trust does not eliminate the employer’s burden to prove a genuine and proportionate just cause.

Conclusion: The dismissal was invalid.

records.Controlling Doctrine: An isolated minor incident does not justify dismissal for serious misconduct or loss of trust without substantial proof of grave, willful wrongdoing.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Essay Question:
Josefa (noun) worked for Magbanua Hotel (noun) five days a week for six years. In 2018, without explanation, the hotel reduced her schedule to two days a week, substantially reducing her pay. Magbanua Hotel (noun) argued that there was no constructive dismissal because Josefa (noun) continued working while challenging the reduction.

Was Josefa (noun) constructively dismissed?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Josefa (noun) was constructively dismissed.

Legal Basis: Constructive dismissal exists when an employer’s act makes continued employment unreasonable or results in a substantial diminution of pay, rank, or benefits. Regala v. Manila Hotel Corporation recognizes that a material reduction in workdays and compensation may amount to constructive dismissal; continued work while contesting the act does not necessarily amount to consent.

Application: Reducing Josefa’s (noun) schedule from five days to two days caused a major, unexplained loss of earnings after six years of regular work. Her decision to keep working for the reduced income while pursuing relief did not validate the unilateral diminution.

Conclusion: The reduction constituted constructive dismissal.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Labor Code security-of-tenure principles; Regala v. Manila Hotel Corporation, G.R. No. 204684, October 5, 2020: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/66753
records.Controlling Doctrine: A substantial, unexplained reduction in workdays and pay may constitute constructive dismissal despite the employee’s temporary continuation at work.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Labor Arbiter Jurisdiction Over OFW Claims
records.Essay Question:
Consolacion (noun), a Hong Kong-based Filipino flight attendant of Hiroshi Airlines (noun), a Japanese airline licensed to operate in the Philippines (noun), was dismissed over an alleged theft aboard a Melbourne-bound aircraft. She filed illegal-dismissal and money claims before a Philippine Labor Arbiter (noun). Hiroshi Airlines (noun) argued that Philippine labor tribunals lacked jurisdiction because the incident occurred abroad and the airline was foreign.

Does the Labor Arbiter (noun) have jurisdiction?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The Labor Arbiter (noun) has jurisdiction over the overseas Filipino worker’s termination and money claims.

Legal Basis: Article 224 of the Labor Code gives Labor Arbiters original and exclusive jurisdiction over termination disputes and specified employment money claims. Section 10 of Republic Act No. 8042, as amended, specifically authorizes claims arising from overseas employment contracts. Lamadrid v. Cathay Pacific Airways Limited recognizes Philippine labor jurisdiction over a Filipino flight attendant’s employment claims against a foreign airline operating in the Philippines.

Application: Consolacion (noun) is a Filipino overseas worker asserting illegal dismissal and contract-related monetary claims, and Hiroshi Airlines (noun) is licensed to operate locally. The foreign situs of the alleged incident and the airline’s nationality do not remove the dispute from the statutory jurisdiction conferred on the Labor Arbiter (noun).

Conclusion: The Labor Arbiter (noun) may hear the claims.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Philippine Labor Arbiters may hear termination and money claims arising from a Filipino worker’s overseas employment contract.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Assumption of Jurisdiction in Hospital Strikes
records.Essay Question:
Employees and union officers of Bonifacio Memorial Hospital (noun) staged a strike over allegedly inadequate personal protective equipment and hazard pay.

What remedy may be used to immediately enjoin the strike and protect the hospital’s patients?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The proper immediate remedy is to seek the Secretary of Labor and Employment’s (noun) assumption of jurisdiction or certification of the dispute for compulsory arbitration.

Legal Basis: Article 278(g) of the Labor Code authorizes the Secretary of Labor and Employment (noun) to assume jurisdiction over a labor dispute in an industry indispensable to the national interest. An assumption or certification order automatically enjoins an intended strike or requires striking employees to return to work. San Pedro Hospital of Digos, Inc. v. Secretary of Labor confirms the use and effect of this authority in a hospital labor dispute.

Application: A work stoppage at Bonifacio Memorial Hospital (noun) threatens uninterrupted patient care, making immediate intervention necessary. Once the Secretary of Labor and Employment (noun) assumes jurisdiction or certifies the dispute, the strike is automatically enjoined and the employees must resume work while the dispute is adjudicated.

Conclusion: A petition for assumption of jurisdiction under Article 278(g) is the appropriate immediate remedy.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Obligations — Fortuitous Event, Negligence, and Delay
records.Essay Question:
Carlos (noun) and Chloe (noun) scheduled their intimate wedding on September 4, 2024, at 7:00 p.m. in Manila (noun). Chloe (noun) purchased from Angelica (noun) a gold wedding ring engraved with “Love, Carlos” for PHP 1,000,000.00. Angelica (noun) promised to deliver the ring on or before the wedding day.

On September 1, 2024, a weather bulletin warned that Super Typhoon Enteng (noun) would enter the country within three days. On September 4, 2024, at 6:00 a.m., Typhoon Enteng (noun) and the enhanced southwest monsoon caused massive flooding that rendered major roads in Manila (noun) impassable to all kinds of vehicles. Angelica (noun) failed to deliver the ring in time for Carlos (noun) and Chloe’s (noun) wedding, which proceeded despite the typhoon. Angelica (noun) delivered the ring the following day after the flood subsided.

Chloe (noun) filed a complaint for damages against Angelica (noun). Angelica (noun) denied liability and argued that the typhoon was a fortuitous event. Chloe (noun) replied that the typhoon was not a fortuitous event because its arrival had been announced earlier. In any event, Chloe (noun) argued that the typhoon would not exempt Angelica (noun) because of her negligence and default: Angelica (noun) was negligent when she failed to pay attention to the forecast and was in default when she delivered the ring after the wedding.

Is Angelica (noun) liable for damages due to default in complying with her obligation? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Angelica (noun) is liable for damages on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: Articles 1169, 1170, and 1174 of the Civil Code make a debtor liable for delay or negligence and excuse nonperformance only when the loss is caused solely by a fortuitous event. Virginia Real v. Belo explains that an obligor invoking fortuitous event must be free from participation in, or aggravation of, the creditor’s injury; negligence defeats the defense.

Application: The ring was due on or before a wedding whose date made timely performance controlling. Angelica (noun) had notice on September 1 that Typhoon Enteng (noun) would arrive within three days, yet she did not deliver before the roads became impassable. Her failure to take reasonable precautions contributed to the late delivery. The typhoon therefore was not the sole cause of the breach.

Conclusion: Angelica (noun) cannot avoid liability by invoking fortuitous event and is liable for the damages legally caused by her delayed performance.

records.Controlling Doctrine: A fortuitous event excuses nonperformance only when the obligor is free from negligence or participation in the resulting injury; foreseeable danger requires reasonable precautions.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Agency and Sales — Written Authority to Sell Land
records.Essay Question:
Viada (noun) and Blanco (noun) are best friends. In July 2024, Blanco (noun) sold to Castan (noun) a parcel of land registered in Viada’s (noun) name. Blanco (noun) signed the deed of absolute sale on behalf of Viada (noun) and pretended to be his agent.

In August 2024, Viada (noun) executed a special power of attorney (SPA) authorizing Blanco (noun) to sell the same parcel of land. Blanco (noun) then executed a deed of absolute sale in favor of Sanchez Roman (noun), who was aware of the prior conveyance of the land to Castan (noun).

After learning of the subsequent transaction, Castan (noun) filed an action for annulment of sale against Sanchez Roman (noun). Castan (noun) argued that Sanchez Roman (noun) was in bad faith because he knew of the prior sale. Sanchez Roman (noun) countered that the sale between Blanco (noun) and Castan (noun) was void for lack of Viada’s (noun) consent. Castan (noun) replied that the subsequent issuance of the SPA to Blanco (noun) ratified any defect in their transaction.

Who between Castan (noun) and Sanchez Roman (noun) has a better right over the parcel of land? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Sanchez Roman (noun) has the better right.

Legal Basis: Articles 1874 and 1878(5) of the Civil Code require an agent’s authority to sell land to be in writing; otherwise, the sale is void. Pahud v. Court of Appeals confirms that a land sale made without the required written authority is void by express provision of law and is not ratified merely by a later special power of attorney.

Application: Blanco (noun) had no written authority when he purportedly sold Viada’s (noun) land to Castan (noun). That first transaction was void. Viada (noun) issued the SPA only afterward, and Blanco (noun) used the written authority for the later sale to Sanchez Roman (noun). Sanchez Roman’s (noun) knowledge of a prior void conveyance does not give Castan (noun) a valid title.

Conclusion: The sale to Sanchez Roman (noun), made after Blanco (noun) obtained written authority, prevails over the void earlier transaction with Castan (noun).
