records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Property and Succession — Reconveyance, Co-ownership, and Implied Trust
records.Essay Question:
Alice (noun) and Sheila (noun) occupied a parcel of land that they inherited from their parents. In 2003, Alice (noun) executed an affidavit of self-adjudication over the property and obtained a certificate of title solely in her name.

In August 2024, Sheila (noun) discovered that she had been excluded from the certificate of title. Sheila (noun) filed an action against Alice (noun) to reconvey the land based on implied trust. Sheila (noun) alleged continuous actual possession of the property and deprivation of her share as a compulsory heir.

Alice (noun) countered that the prescriptive period to reconvey real property based on an implied trust is 10 years, reckoned from her repudiation of the trust in 2003 when the certificate of title was issued in her name. Thus, according to Alice (noun), Sheila’s (noun) action for reconveyance filed only in 2024 had already prescribed.

Has Sheila’s (noun) cause of action to recover her share in the property from Alice (noun) prescribed? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Sheila’s (noun) action has not prescribed.

Legal Basis: Articles 494, 1144(2), and 1456 of the Civil Code govern co-ownership and implied trusts. Rivera v. Villanueva holds that an extrajudicial adjudication does not bind excluded heirs who had no knowledge of or participation in it; an action that is effectively one for partition remains available while co-ownership is recognized. An owner in actual possession may also seek to quiet title without prescription running against that possession.

Application: Sheila (noun) continuously possessed the inherited property and learned only in August 2024 that Alice (noun) had titled it solely in her own name. The 2003 affidavit, executed without Sheila’s (noun) knowledge or participation, did not by itself communicate a clear and unequivocal repudiation of the co-ownership to her. Her possession independently prevents the title from becoming secure against her merely by lapse of time.

Conclusion: Sheila’s (noun) 2024 action to recover or partition her inherited share is not barred by prescription.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Civil Code, Articles 494, 1144(2), and 1456; Rivera v. Villanueva: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/67810
records.Controlling Doctrine: An excluded co-heir who remains in actual possession is not bound by an unknown unilateral adjudication, and prescription does not run without a clear repudiation of co-ownership communicated to that co-heir.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Obligations — Novation by Substitution of Debtor
records.Essay Question:
In 2017, Maloi (noun) leased her real property to Sheena (noun) for 10 years under a rental-escalation clause that read: “For the first five years, the rental rate shall be PHP 10,000.00 per month, subject to a 10% increase for the succeeding years.”

In 2020, Sheena (noun) assigned to Colet (noun) her rights and obligations under the lease. Colet (noun) then paid the agreed rentals to Maloi (noun). In 2023, Colet (noun) paid the PHP 10,000.00 monthly rent through postdated checks, but the checks were dishonored because they were drawn against a closed account. Maloi (noun) charged Colet (noun) with estafa.

Maloi (noun) separately demanded from Sheena (noun) the unpaid rentals and stipulated rent increases, but Sheena (noun) refused. Sheena (noun) denied liability and argued that her obligation had been extinguished when Colet (noun) substituted her as lessee. Sheena (noun) added that Maloi (noun) had accepted rental payments from Colet (noun).

Did novation extinguish Sheena’s (noun) obligation under the lease? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Sheena’s (noun) obligation was not extinguished by novation.

Legal Basis: Articles 1292 and 1293 of the Civil Code require an express declaration or complete incompatibility between the old and new obligations, as well as the creditor’s consent to a substitution of debtor. Food Fest Land, Inc. v. Siapno holds that a creditor’s acceptance of payments from a third person, without an agreement releasing the original debtor, does not establish novation.

Application: The facts show that Maloi (noun) accepted rent from Colet (noun), but they do not show that Maloi (noun) unequivocally agreed to release Sheena (noun) from the original lease. The assignment and third-party payments were compatible with Sheena’s (noun) continuing liability.

Conclusion: No subjective novation occurred, and Sheena (noun) remains liable under the original lease.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Civil Code, Articles 1292 and 1293; Food Fest Land, Inc. v. Siapno: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/64913
records.Controlling Doctrine: Acceptance of payment from a third person does not substitute the debtor or release the original debtor unless the creditor’s consent to novation and release is clear and unequivocal.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Succession — Conflict of Laws and Holographic Will
records.Essay Question:
Primo (noun), a French national and permanent resident of Canada (noun), executed in the Philippines (noun) a holographic will that he entirely wrote, dated, and signed. Primo (noun) listed in the will various real and personal properties situated in the Philippines (noun), France (noun), and Canada (noun). He bequeathed the properties in the Philippines (noun) to his parents, the properties in France (noun) to his siblings, and the properties in Canada (noun) to his wife and children.

In 2024, Primo (noun) suffered a heart attack and died in Australia (noun) while attending a conference. He was survived by his wife, two children, parents, and three siblings.

What laws govern the formalities of Primo’s (noun) holographic will, the distribution of his estate, and the qualifications of his heirs? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Philippine law governs the will’s formalities; French law governs the estate’s distribution and the heirs’ capacity to succeed.

Legal Basis: Articles 16(2), 17, 810, 816, and 1039 of the Civil Code apply. Llorente v. Court of Appeals confirms that the decedent’s national law governs the order of succession, the amount of successional rights, and the intrinsic validity of testamentary provisions. Palaganas v. Palaganas likewise recognizes the conflict-of-laws rules for wills made by aliens and the need to prove the applicable foreign law.

Application: Primo (noun) executed the holographic will in the Philippines (noun), and its stated execution—entirely written, dated, and signed by him—complies with the Philippine formal rule. Because Primo (noun) remained a French national, French law governs distribution and heir qualifications regardless of his residence in Canada (noun), his death in Australia (noun), or the location of the property. The relevant French law must be pleaded and proved in the probate proceeding.

Conclusion: Apply Philippine law to form and duly proven French law to the intrinsic succession issues and heir qualifications.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Civil Code, Articles 16(2), 17, 810, 816, and 1039; Llorente v. Court of Appeals: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/38202; Palaganas v. Palaganas: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/33838
records.Controlling Doctrine: The law of the place of execution may govern testamentary form, while the decedent’s national law governs intrinsic validity, distribution, successional shares, and capacity to inherit; foreign law must be proved as fact.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Property Relations — Cohabitation and Recovery of Property
records.Essay Question:
In 2021, Jesse (noun) and Celeste (noun) married. After a year, Jesse (noun) took all their savings and abandoned Celeste (noun) for his paramour, Diana (noun). Jesse (noun) asked Diana (noun) to quit her job. Diana (noun) hesitated because she had no money and was drowning in debt, but Jesse (noun) promised to provide for all her needs. Jesse (noun) and Diana (noun) then lived together.

The following day, Jesse (noun) and Diana (noun) bought a brand-new car. The vehicle was registered exclusively in Diana’s (noun) name. Celeste (noun) learned of the purchase and filed an action to recover the vehicle from Diana (noun). Celeste (noun) claimed that Jesse (noun) was still her lawful husband and that the car formed part of their community property. Diana (noun) countered that she and Jesse (noun) were co-owners of the vehicle.

Can Celeste (noun) recover the vehicle from Diana (noun)? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Celeste (noun) may recover the vehicle from Diana (noun).

Legal Basis: Article 148 of the Family Code provides that parties who are incapacitated to marry each other co-own only property acquired through their actual joint contributions. If one party is validly married to another, that party’s share accrues to the absolute community or conjugal partnership in the valid marriage. Joaquino v. Reyes applies this rule to property acquired during an adulterous cohabitation.

Application: Jesse’s (noun) subsisting marriage to Celeste (noun) prevented him from marrying Diana (noun). The facts show that Diana (noun) had no money and made no actual contribution to the purchase. The funds came from Jesse (noun), who had taken the spouses’ savings. Registration in Diana’s (noun) name does not create a contribution or defeat the lawful marital property regime.

Conclusion: The vehicle belongs to the marital community of Jesse (noun) and Celeste (noun), and Celeste (noun) may recover it from Diana (noun).

records.Controlling Doctrine: In a cohabitation where the parties cannot marry each other, only proven actual contributions create co-ownership; the validly married party’s share accrues to the property regime of the subsisting marriage.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Persons and Family Relations — Impugning Legitimacy
records.Essay Question:
In 1990, Monica (noun) was born during the marriage of her parents, Anton (noun) and Steph (noun). In 2024, Monica (noun) discovered that Patrick (noun) had signed her birth certificate as her father. Monica (noun) looked for Patrick (noun) and learned that he had died a year earlier. She also learned that Patrick (noun) had been Steph’s (noun) last boyfriend before Steph (noun) married Anton (noun).

Monica (noun) then filed a complaint for partition of Patrick’s (noun) estate. She claimed that she was the nonmarital child of Patrick (noun) and Steph (noun) and submitted her birth certificate, on which Patrick (noun) had recognized her as his daughter.

Patrick’s (noun) heirs opposed the complaint. They argued that Monica (noun) was presumed to be the legitimate child of Anton (noun) and Steph (noun) under Article 164 of the Family Code, which states that “children conceived or born during the marriage of the parents are legitimate.” They also invoked the rule that only the husband may impugn the child’s legitimacy.

May Monica (noun) impugn her own legitimacy in an action for partition? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Monica (noun) may not impugn her own legitimacy in the partition case.

Legal Basis: Articles 164, 170, and 171 of the Family Code reserve an action to impugn legitimacy to the husband and, only in specified exceptional circumstances, his heirs. Ordoña v. Local Civil Registrar of Pasig City holds that a child born during a valid and subsisting marriage cannot choose her own filiation and that only the husband or his qualified heirs may attack legitimacy.

Application: Monica (noun) was born while Anton (noun) and Steph (noun) were married. Her attempt to establish a different filiation in Patrick’s (noun) estate partition is a collateral attack on her legitimacy. Monica (noun) is not among the persons whom the Family Code authorizes to bring that action, and Patrick’s (noun) signature on the birth certificate does not confer such standing.

Conclusion: Monica (noun) cannot impugn her legitimacy in the partition proceeding.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Legitimacy may be impugned only by the husband or, in the statutory exceptional cases, his heirs; the child cannot choose a different filiation through a collateral attack.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Sales — Maceda Law and Cash Surrender Value
records.Essay Question:
Zion (noun) purchased a condominium unit from Hammered Homes Realty (HHR) (noun) for PHP 10,000,000.00. He paid a PHP 2,000,000.00 down payment, while the PHP 8,000,000.00 balance was payable over 80 months in monthly installments of PHP 100,000.00.

Zion (noun) began paying the monthly installments on April 15, 2022. Due to financial difficulties, he began defaulting on June 15, 2024, after paying total monthly installments of PHP 1,800,000.00. On August 15, 2024, Zion (noun) received a notarized letter cancelling the contract to sell.

Zion (noun) then went to HHR’s (noun) office to claim the cash surrender value of his payments under Republic Act No. 6552 (noun), the Realty Installment Buyer Act (noun), or the Maceda Law (noun).

Is Zion (noun) entitled to a cash surrender value? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Zion (noun) is entitled to the statutory cash surrender value.

Legal Basis: Section 3 of Republic Act No. 6552 (Maceda Law) grants a defaulting buyer who has paid at least two years of installments a cash surrender value equal to 50% of total payments, subject to the statute’s cancellation procedure. Orbe v. Filinvest Land, Inc. explains that the two-year threshold refers to the total payments equivalent to 24 monthly installments and that down payments, deposits, and similar amounts are included.

Application: Zion (noun) paid PHP 2,000,000.00 as down payment plus PHP 1,800,000.00 in monthly installments, for total payments of PHP 3,800,000.00. At PHP 100,000.00 per monthly installment, that total is equivalent to 38 installments, exceeding the 24-installment threshold. His minimum cash surrender value is 50% of PHP 3,800,000.00, or PHP 1,900,000.00, and payment of that value is part of an effective statutory cancellation.

Conclusion: Zion (noun) is entitled to at least PHP 1,900,000.00 as cash surrender value, subject to compliance with the Maceda Law’s cancellation requirements.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Mortgage — Pactum Commissorium and Subsequent Sale
records.Essay Question:
Rico (noun) mortgaged a parcel of land to Maris (noun) as security for a loan. In the mortgage contract, Rico (noun) appointed Maris (noun) as attorney-in-fact to sell the land in case of default in payment of the loan.

Rico (noun) failed to pay his obligation. Maris (noun) then purchased the land from Rico (noun) through a deed of absolute sale. Rico (noun) later questioned the mortgage contract, arguing that it violated the prohibition against pactum commissorium and that the subsequent sale was therefore also void.

Is the sale between Rico (noun) and Maris (noun) valid? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The separate sale is valid on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: Article 2088 of the Civil Code prohibits a creditor’s automatic appropriation or disposal of mortgaged property upon the debtor’s default. Garcia v. Villar identifies the requisites of pactum commissorium: property is given as security, and the agreement stipulates the creditor’s automatic appropriation upon nonpayment.

Application: The mortgage did not provide that ownership would automatically pass to Maris (noun) upon Rico’s (noun) default. It authorized a sale, and the facts state that Rico (noun) and Maris (noun) later executed a separate deed of absolute sale. That later consensual conveyance, rather than automatic appropriation by operation of the mortgage clause, defeats the second requisite of pactum commissorium.

Conclusion: The subsequent deed of sale is not void as pactum commissorium.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Sales and Lease — Option and Right of First Refusal
records.Essay Question:
Kiko (noun) leased a parcel of land to Jackie (noun) from January to December 2024. In July 2024, Kiko (noun) sent Jackie (noun) a letter stating: “I am giving you the first opportunity to buy the leased property for PHP 1,000,000.00. You have until the expiration of the lease contract within which to decide.”

Jackie (noun) immediately informed Kiko (noun) that she would buy the leased property for PHP 800,000.00. Kiko (noun) did not reply. In August 2024, Jackie (noun) learned that Kiko (noun) had sold the leased property to Bogs (noun) for PHP 800,000.00.

Aggrieved, Jackie (noun) filed an action against Kiko (noun) and Bogs (noun) to rescind their contract of sale. She claimed that the transaction violated her right of first refusal and that she should be allowed to buy the property at the same price of PHP 800,000.00.

May Jackie (noun) rescind the sale between Kiko (noun) and Bogs (noun) for the alleged violation of her right of first refusal? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Jackie (noun) may not rescind the sale.

Legal Basis: Articles 1324 and 1479 of the Civil Code govern offers and options. Philippine National Oil Company v. Keppel Philippines Holdings, Inc. explains that an accepted unilateral promise to sell is binding as an option only when supported by consideration distinct from the price; without such consideration, the offer may be withdrawn before acceptance.

Application: Kiko’s (noun) letter was not a right-of-first-refusal clause in the lease but an offer to sell for PHP 1,000,000.00. Jackie’s (noun) reply proposing PHP 800,000.00 was a counteroffer and therefore a rejection of the original offer. Kiko (noun) never accepted the counteroffer, and Jackie (noun) gave no separate consideration to keep the original offer open.

Conclusion: No enforceable option or sale arose in Jackie’s (noun) favor, so she has no basis to rescind the later sale to Bogs (noun).

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Persons and Family Relations — Presumptive Death
records.Essay Question:
Sergio (noun) and Calista (noun) married in 2015. In 2019, Sergio (noun) began complaining of recurring, severe migraines and then left without telling Calista (noun) where he was going. Calista (noun) eventually fell in love with her best friend, Albert (noun).

In 2024, Calista (noun) filed a summary proceeding to have Sergio (noun) declared presumptively dead so that she could marry Albert (noun). Calista (noun) alleged that Sergio’s (noun) only known relative was his brother, Robert (noun), who lived in Cotabato City (noun). Calista (noun) wrote Robert (noun) and asked about Sergio (noun), but Robert (noun) replied that he did not know where Sergio (noun) was. Calista (noun) also asked Sergio’s (noun) friends, without success. She therefore honestly believed that Sergio (noun) was dead.

Is Calista’s (noun) petition for declaration of presumptive death meritorious? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Calista’s (noun) petition is not meritorious.

Legal Basis: Article 41 of the Family Code requires four consecutive years of absence and a well-founded belief that the absent spouse is already dead before the present spouse may remarry. Republic v. Tampus holds that well-founded belief must result from diligent and reasonable active efforts to locate the absent spouse; mere inquiries from relatives and friends, the passage of time, and an honest subjective belief are insufficient.

Application: Although Sergio (noun) had been absent for at least four years, Calista (noun) only wrote his brother, Robert (noun), and asked some friends. The facts show no inquiry with government agencies, hospitals, law-enforcement authorities, employers, or other reasonably available records and channels. Her efforts were passive and limited rather than the active search required by Article 41.

Conclusion: Calista (noun) failed to establish a well-founded belief based on diligent search, so the petition should be denied.

records.Controlling Doctrine: A well-founded belief in an absent spouse’s death requires diligent, reasonable, and active efforts to locate the spouse; limited inquiries from relatives and friends and the mere passage of time do not suffice.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Essay Question:
Ginny (noun) arrived at Star Viva Hotel (SVH) (noun) and entrusted her vehicle’s ignition key to Marco (noun), a parking attendant who issued her a valet-parking customer claim stub. After parking the vehicle, Marco (noun) placed the ignition key in a safety box. Ginny (noun) then proceeded to the hotel lobby to check in.

At midnight, the hotel security officer informed Ginny (noun) that her vehicle had been carnapped. Ginny (noun) filed an action for damages against SVH (noun) for the loss of the vehicle. In its answer, SVH (noun) denied responsibility for any loss or damage to vehicles in the parking area, claiming that valet parking was merely a special privilege provided for the convenience of hotel guests.

Is SVH (noun) liable for the loss of Ginny’s (noun) vehicle? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. SVH (noun) is liable for the loss of the vehicle.

Legal Basis: Articles 1962, 1998, 1999, and 2000 of the Civil Code impose on a depositary and hotelkeeper the duty to safeguard and return property delivered by a guest, including vehicles placed in hotel annexes. Durban Apartments Corporation v. Pioneer Insurance and Surety Corporation holds that a valet-parking arrangement is a deposit once the establishment receives the vehicle or its keys for safekeeping and issues a claim stub.

Application: Ginny (noun) surrendered the ignition key to SVH’s (noun) attendant, Marco (noun), who accepted custody, parked the vehicle, secured the key, and issued a claim stub. Those acts perfected a deposit and placed the vehicle under the hotel’s control. Calling valet parking a privilege does not remove the statutory duty of safekeeping.

Conclusion: SVH (noun) is liable for failing to return Ginny’s (noun) deposited vehicle.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Civil Code, Articles 1962 and 1998–2000; Durban Apartments Corporation v. Pioneer Insurance and Surety Corporation: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/33974
records.Controlling Doctrine: A valet service creates a deposit when the establishment receives the vehicle or its keys for safekeeping; the hotelkeeper must exercise the legally required care and return the deposited property.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Persons and Family Relations — Custody of Illegitimate Child
records.Essay Question:
In 2021, Kynan (noun) was born to live-in partners Popoy (noun) and Basha (noun). After a year, Popoy (noun) and Basha (noun) separated because of irreconcilable differences. Basha (noun) worked as a market vendor to support Kynan (noun) and often left him in the care of his maternal grandmother. Popoy (noun) occasionally sent money for Kynan’s (noun) needs.

Basha (noun) later had a discreet romantic relationship with her best friend, Helen (noun). In 2024, Popoy (noun) filed a case for sole custody of Kynan (noun), alleging that Basha (noun) was an unfit mother. Popoy (noun) argued that Basha’s (noun) lesbian relationship was not conducive to Kynan’s (noun) proper moral development. Basha (noun) countered that she could care for and provide for Kynan (noun) despite her modest income.

Are there compelling reasons to deprive Basha (noun) of Kynan’s (noun) custody? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The stated facts do not establish a compelling reason to deprive Basha (noun) of custody.

Legal Basis: Article 176 of the Family Code places an illegitimate child under the mother’s parental authority, while the child’s best interests remain paramount. Pablo-Gualberto v. Gualberto holds that a parent’s sexual preference or alleged moral lapse does not by itself prove unfitness; it must be shown to have an adverse effect on the child or to interfere with proper parental care.

Application: Kynan (noun) is an illegitimate child of tender age whom Basha (noun) supports through her work. Leaving him with his maternal grandmother while working is consistent with providing care, not abandonment. Her relationship with Helen (noun) is discreet, and no fact shows harm to Kynan (noun), neglect, or interference with Basha’s (noun) parental duties.

Conclusion: Popoy (noun) has not shown the compelling unfitness required to remove Kynan (noun) from Basha’s (noun) custody.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Family Code, Article 176; Pablo-Gualberto v. Gualberto: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/43331
records.Controlling Doctrine: A mother’s sexual orientation or relationship is not by itself a compelling ground to remove custody; the challenger must prove a concrete adverse effect on the child or parental neglect or incompetence.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Succession — Testamentary Dispositions for the Poor and the Soul
records.Essay Question:
Lennon (noun) made a last will and testament containing two simple dispositions:

“First, I am leaving one-half of my estate in favor of the poor. Second, I am leaving the other half of my estate in favor of my soul.”

Lennon (noun) named Atty. Manresa (noun) as executor and instructed him to carry out the will. In 2024, Lennon (noun) died single and childless. His will was then presented for probate.

Lennon’s (noun) siblings opposed probate and claimed his entire estate through intestate succession. They argued that the first disposition was void because it favored unknown persons and that the second was void because the beneficiary lacked civil personality.

Are the dispositions in Lennon’s (noun) will void? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The two dispositions are not void merely because the beneficiaries are described generally.

Legal Basis: Articles 1029 and 1030 of the Civil Code expressly authorize dispositions for prayers and pious works for the benefit of the testator’s soul and dispositions in favor of the poor in general. Villavicencio v. Quinio sustained testamentary provisions of this character against collateral relatives, while Baltazar v. Laxa recognizes the State’s duty to give effect to legally tenable testamentary wishes, including directions for masses for the repose of the testator’s soul.

Application: The disposition for Lennon’s (noun) soul is administered by the executor, with court approval, in the manner fixed by Article 1029. The gift to the poor is deemed limited to poor persons living in Lennon’s (noun) domicile at death unless the will shows a different intent, with Atty. Manresa (noun) making the designation and distribution subject to court approval. On the given facts, only siblings—collateral relatives, not compulsory heirs—oppose the will.

Conclusion: Both dispositions are valid, subject to the statutory method of administration and the rights of any compulsory heirs if later established.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Civil Code, Articles 1029 and 1030: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/2/53360; Villavicencio v. Quinio: https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri1939/apr1939/gr_l-45248_1939.html; Baltazar v. Laxa: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/54689
records.Controlling Doctrine: General testamentary gifts for the poor and for prayers or pious works benefiting the testator’s soul are valid and are administered according to Articles 1029 and 1030, subject to court approval and compulsory-heir rights.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Contracts — Reformation of Instrument and Simple Donation
records.Essay Question:
Sharon (noun) owned a parcel of land adjoining the sea, with flat terrain at the center and an elevated, rocky northern portion. She executed a written instrument donating the flat portion to Nicholas (noun), who accepted the donation in the same instrument.

After a survey, Nicholas (noun) discovered that the technical description in the deed of donation referred to the rocky northern portion. Sharon (noun), however, had died without correcting the mistake. Nicholas (noun) asked Sharon’s (noun) heirs to execute an amended deed of donation covering the flat terrain, but they refused.

Nicholas (noun) filed an action against Sharon’s (noun) heirs for reformation of the instrument to reflect the parties’ true intention.

May the trial court compel Sharon’s (noun) heirs to reform the instrument and execute an amended deed of donation? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The court may not reform this deed of donation.

Legal Basis: Articles 1359 and 1366 of the Civil Code govern reformation and expressly prohibit it for a simple donation inter vivos in which no condition is imposed. Banico v. Stager explains that reformation generally requires a prior meeting of minds, a written instrument that fails to express the parties’ true intent, and mistake, fraud, inequitable conduct, or accident; the statutory exclusions still control.

Application: Sharon (noun) made and Nicholas (noun) accepted a simple, unconditional donation inter vivos. Even if the technical description resulted from mistake and did not express the intended terrain, Article 1366 removes this type of instrument from the remedy of reformation. The court cannot compel the heirs to make a new donation of a different portion after Sharon’s (noun) death.

Conclusion: The requested reformation and amended deed cannot be ordered.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Although mistake may ordinarily justify reformation, Article 1366 bars reformation of a simple unconditional donation inter vivos.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Sales — Contract to Sell and Double Sale
records.Essay Question:
On July 5, 2024, Odrey (noun) and Jeboy (noun) executed a notarized agreement for the sale of real property. It stated: “Odrey agrees to sell Lot 0416 (noun) to Jeboy for a total consideration of PHP 1,000,000.00. Upon full payment of the purchase price, Odrey will execute a deed of absolute sale in favor of Jeboy.” The following day, Jeboy (noun) recorded the instrument with the Register of Deeds (noun).

On August 5, 2024, Odrey (noun) and Lorenz (noun) executed a notarized document over the same land. It stated: “For and in consideration of PHP 1,000,000.00, receipt of which is hereby acknowledged, Odrey hereby sells, transfers, and conveys, and by these presents has sold, transferred, and conveyed Lot 0416 to Lorenz.” The deed between Odrey (noun) and Lorenz (noun) was not registered.

After discovering the transaction, Jeboy (noun) invoked the rules on double sale and argued that he had the better right because he was the first registrant in good faith.

Do the rules on double sale apply? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Article 1544 on double sales does not apply.

Legal Basis: Article 1544 of the Civil Code presupposes two valid sales of the same property by the same seller to different buyers. Torrecampo v. Alindogan holds that the rule does not apply when the first agreement is merely a contract to sell, because ownership remains with the prospective seller until the suspensive condition—usually full payment—is fulfilled.

Application: Odrey’s (noun) July 5 agreement promised to execute a deed of absolute sale to Jeboy (noun) only after full payment. It was therefore a contract to sell, not a completed sale, and Jeboy’s (noun) registration of that instrument did not transfer ownership. The August 5 deed to Lorenz (noun) was the only stated sale.

Conclusion: There were not two sales within Article 1544, so Jeboy (noun) cannot claim priority under the double-sale rule.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Article 1544 does not apply when the first transaction is a contract to sell because the prospective seller retains ownership until fulfillment of the suspensive condition.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Quasi-delict — Employer Liability and Legal Interest
records.Essay Question:
Alan (noun), a mall security guard, negligently shot Kazuto (noun), a customer who died at the scene. Kazuto’s (noun) heirs filed an action for damages against Alan (noun), for his own negligence, and against his employer, Ryota Security Agency (RSA) (noun), for failing to exercise diligence in the selection and supervision of its employees.

The trial court found both Alan (noun) and RSA (noun) negligent and ruled:

“FOR THESE REASONS, the complaint for quasi-delict is GRANTED. Alan is civilly liable to pay the heirs of Kazuto PHP 1,000,000.00 in actual damages, PHP 500,000.00 in moral damages, and PHP 500,000.00 in exemplary damages. Ryota Security Agency, as employer, is subsidiarily liable to pay the damages in case of the employee’s insolvency.

“The award of damages shall earn interest at 12% from the filing of the complaint until finality of the decision.

“SO ORDERED.”

Did the trial court properly impose the civil liabilities of Alan (noun) and RSA (noun)? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The court correctly found a basis for liability but misstated RSA’s (noun) liability and the interest.

Legal Basis: Articles 2180 and 2194 of the Civil Code make an employer that fails to rebut the presumption of negligent selection or supervision directly and solidarily liable with the negligent employee. Metro Manila Transit Corporation v. Court of Appeals confirms that this liability is primary and solidary, not conditioned on the employee’s insolvency. Lara’s Gifts & Decors, Inc. v. Midtown Industrial Sales, Inc. clarifies that unliquidated damages generally earn 6% legal interest from finality of judgment until full satisfaction unless the amount was established with reasonable certainty at an earlier demand.

Application: The court found both Alan (noun) and RSA (noun) negligent. RSA’s (noun) liability therefore cannot be merely subsidiary; it is direct and solidary with Alan’s (noun) liability. The damages were unliquidated and had to be proved in court, so imposing 12% interest from filing was also erroneous. The applicable post-judgment rate is 6% per year from finality until payment.

Conclusion: Modify the judgment to make Alan (noun) and RSA (noun) solidarily liable and to impose 6% annual interest on the adjudged damages from finality of judgment until full payment.

Midtown Industrial Sales, Inc.: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68597
records.Controlling Doctrine: An employer found liable under Article 2180 is directly and solidarily liable with the negligent employee; unliquidated damages ordinarily earn 6% legal interest from finality of judgment until full payment.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Contracts - Relativity and Transmissibility to Heirs
records.Essay Question:
A (noun) leased out his penthouse condominium unit to B (noun).

Unfortunately, A figured in an accident and perished, leaving his son, C (noun), as his sole heir. Subsequently, C demanded that B vacate the premises by noon of the following day. B refused, showing C the duly executed lease agreement between her and A. B claimed that she had a right to remain in the unit because the term of the lease had yet to expire. C countered that he had nothing to do with the lease contract because it was executed between his father and B and, therefore, did not bind him.

Is C correct? Give your reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer:

No. C (noun) is not correct; as A’s (noun) heir, C is bound by A’s transmissible obligations under the unexpired lease.

Legal Basis:

Article 1311 of the Civil Code provides that contracts take effect between the parties, their assigns, and heirs, except when the rights and obligations are non-transmissible by their nature, stipulation, or law. The heir’s liability, however, does not extend beyond the value of the property received from the decedent. William Ong Genato v. Benjamin Bayhon applies this rule to contractual obligations transmitted to heirs.

Application:

The duty to honor the agreed lease term is patrimonial and is not shown to be personal or otherwise non-transmissible. C succeeded to A’s position as lessor and cannot terminate the lease merely because C did not personally sign it. Any monetary liability imposed on C as heir remains limited to the value of the inheritance.

Conclusion:

Therefore, C must respect B’s lease until it expires, subject to the contract’s lawful terms.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Civil Code, Art. 1311; William Ong Genato v. Benjamin Bayhon: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/49586
records.Controlling Doctrine: A decedent’s patrimonial contractual obligations pass to the heirs unless they are non-transmissible; an heir’s liability is limited to the inheritance received.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Property - Forest Land and Acquisitive Prescription
records.Essay Question:
The government owned a 12-hectare parcel of land in Cavite (noun), classified as forest land. Informal settlers built shanties on the land because it was flat and had no trees.

In 2023, the government decided to plant narra trees and demanded that the informal settlers vacate. A (noun), the owner of one shanty, refused, claiming ownership of the occupied portion through acquisitive prescription.

Is A’s claim meritorious? Decide with reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer:

No. A’s (noun) claim is not meritorious because forest land remains inalienable land of the public domain and cannot be acquired by prescription.

Legal Basis:

Article XII, Section 2 of the Constitution and Articles 420 and 1113 of the Civil Code reserve property of the public dominion from private prescription. Heirs of Mario Malabanan v. Republic explains that land of the public domain cannot be acquired by prescription unless it has first been expressly classified as alienable and disposable and, when prescription is invoked, declared patrimonial property of the State.

Application:

The land was expressly classified as forest land. Its flat condition, lack of trees, and use for shanties do not reclassify it. No government act declaring it alienable, disposable, and patrimonial is stated. A’s possession, regardless of length, therefore cannot ripen into private ownership.

Conclusion:

Accordingly, A acquired no title by prescription and must yield to the government’s demand to vacate.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Persons and Family Relations - Capacity to Marry Abroad
records.Essay Question:
A (noun), a member of a popular boy band in the Philippines (noun), got his girlfriend, B (noun), pregnant.

A and B married in Hong Kong (noun), where the legal age for marriage was at least 15. At the time, A and B were 17 and 16 years old, respectively, and both were Filipino citizens. A continued his career, while B concealed her pregnancy in the United States of America (noun). She returned to the Philippines only after giving birth to their son.

Tired of being A’s secret, B filed a petition to declare the marriage void.

Will the petition prosper? Give your reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer:

Yes. B’s (noun) petition should prosper because both Filipino parties lacked legal capacity to marry under their national law.

Legal Basis:

Article 15 of the Civil Code makes Philippine laws on status, condition, and legal capacity binding on Filipino citizens even abroad. Articles 5 and 35(1) of the Family Code require each contracting party to be at least 18 and declare a marriage by a party below 18 void. Article 26’s recognition of foreign marriages expressly retains the exceptions in Article 35(1). Ambrose v. Suque-Ambrose confirms the nationality principle governing a Filipino’s status and legal capacity.

Application:

Although Hong Kong (noun) law allegedly permitted marriage at their ages, A (noun) and B were Filipino citizens aged 17 and 16. Their national law withheld capacity from both. The place of celebration cannot cure that essential incapacity.

Conclusion:

Therefore, the marriage is void ab initio, and B’s petition should be granted.

records.Controlling Doctrine: A Filipino’s legal capacity follows Philippine national law even when the marriage is celebrated abroad; a party below 18 lacks capacity to marry.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Co-ownership - Legal Redemption and Excessive Price
records.Essay Question:
A (noun), B (noun), and C (noun) are co-owners of a three-hectare agricultural parcel with a fair market value of PHP 9 million, or PHP 3 million per hectare.

A offered to sell his share to B and C for PHP 10 million. B and C declined and asked A to reduce the price to PHP 3 million, the prevailing fair market value per hectare. A refused and sold his one-hectare share to X (noun) for PHP 10 million.

May B and C go to court to seek reduction of the purchase price so they can exercise legal redemption? Give your reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer:

Yes. B (noun) and C (noun) may seek judicial determination of a reasonable redemption price, but reduction is not automatic; they must prove that the stated PHP 10 million price is grossly excessive.

Legal Basis:

Article 1620 of the Civil Code allows a co-owner to redeem a share sold to a third person. If the price is grossly excessive, the redemptioner pays only a reasonable price. Article 1623 requires exercise within 30 days from written notice of the sale. Avila v. Spouses Barabat holds that the deed’s price is ordinarily respected, but the redemptioner may prove gross excessiveness and obtain a judicially fixed reasonable price.

Application:

A (noun) sold a one-hectare share to X (noun), a third person, for PHP 10 million, while the stated fair market value is PHP 3 million. That disparity permits B and C to ask the court to assess gross excessiveness. They must present competent proof and timely exercise redemption after proper written notice; fair market value is evidence, not an automatic substitute for the sale price.

Conclusion:

Thus, B and C may sue to redeem at a court-determined reasonable price if they prove gross excessiveness and comply with Article 1623.

records.Controlling Doctrine: A redeeming co-owner generally pays the actual sale price, but may prove that it is grossly excessive and obtain a judicially fixed reasonable price.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Essay Question:
A (noun) borrowed PHP 100,000.00 from B (noun).

C (noun), A’s good friend, issued a promissory note in favor of B, binding herself to pay A’s loan on its due date.

Was the loan agreement between A and B novated? Give your reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer:

No. The issuance of C’s (noun) promissory note did not, by itself, novate and extinguish A’s (noun) debt to B (noun).

Legal Basis:

Articles 1292 and 1293 of the Civil Code require a clear intent to extinguish the old obligation or incompatibility between the old and new obligations; substitution of a new debtor also requires the creditor’s consent. Spouses Reyes v. BPI Family Savings Bank holds that novation is never presumed and must be established by an express declaration or complete incompatibility.

Application:

C promised B that she would pay A’s debt, but the facts do not show that B accepted C as a substitute and released A. C’s undertaking can coexist with A’s original obligation. There is neither an express discharge nor objective incompatibility.

Conclusion:

Therefore, no novation occurred, and A remains liable unless B clearly agreed to substitute C and extinguish A’s obligation.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Novation is never presumed; substitution of a debtor requires the creditor’s consent and a clear extinguishment of the old obligation.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Essay Question:
At B’s (noun) request, A (noun) lent his white van to B so B could drive his wife, C (noun), from Tarlac (noun) to XYZ Medical Center (noun) in BGC (noun) for treatment.

On the return trip, after leaving C at the hospital, people flagged the van, believing it was a UV Express (noun) for hire. B allowed them to board and collected fares. While B was driving along a provincial road, a flash flood wrecked the van.

Is B liable to A for the loss? Give your reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer:

Yes. B (noun) is liable even if the flash flood was fortuitous because he used the van for a purpose different from the agreed commodatum.

Legal Basis:

Under Articles 1933 and 1942(2) of the Civil Code, commodatum is a gratuitous loan for use, and the bailee is liable for loss—even through a fortuitous event—when he devotes the thing to a purpose different from that for which it was loaned. Republic v. Bagtas applies the rule that a borrower cannot avoid liability for fortuitous loss when the law places the risk upon him because of his use or retention of the thing.

Application:

A (noun) lent the van solely to transport C (noun) for medical treatment. B converted it into a passenger vehicle for hire and collected fares. That commercial use materially departed from the agreed purpose before the van was destroyed.

Conclusion:

Therefore, Article 1942 makes B liable to A for the van’s loss despite the flash flood.

records.Controlling Doctrine: A bailee in commodatum bears even fortuitous loss when he uses the thing for a purpose different from that agreed upon.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Persons and Family Relations - Legitimacy After Annulment
records.Essay Question:
A (noun) and B (noun) were husband and wife. A was pregnant at their wedding, but, contrary to what she made B believe, C (noun), A’s former fiancé, was the child’s father.

Shortly after the wedding, A gave birth to D (noun). As D grew, B became suspicious and secretly obtained a DNA test, which showed that he was not D’s biological father. B then obtained a decree annulling the marriage.

In view of the annulment decree, is D legitimate, legitimated, or illegitimate? Give your reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer:

D (noun) remains legitimate. The annulment decree and the privately obtained DNA result do not, by themselves, convert D’s status to illegitimate.

Legal Basis:

Articles 164 and 167 of the Family Code presume a child conceived or born during the marriage to be legitimate, even if the mother declares otherwise. Article 54 preserves the legitimacy of children conceived or born before a judgment of annulment under Article 45 becomes final. Under Articles 170 and 171, legitimacy may be impugned only by the proper person, within the prescribed period and in the proper action. Ordoña v. Local Civil Registrar of Pasig City enforces these restrictions on attacks against legitimacy.

Application:

D was born during A’s (noun) and B’s (noun) subsisting marriage and before the annulment decree. The stated proceeding was for annulment of marriage, not a timely action to impugn D’s legitimacy. A secret DNA test does not itself alter civil status.

Conclusion:

Therefore, D remains legitimate unless and until legitimacy is successfully impugned in the manner and period fixed by law.

records.Controlling Doctrine: A child born during a subsisting marriage remains legitimate after annulment; legitimacy can be attacked only by the persons, action, grounds, and periods fixed by law.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Succession - Heir Liability Limited to Inheritance
records.Essay Question:
A (noun) was adopted by X (noun), the owner of a local chicken-and-beer restaurant.

For several years, X’s business struggled. To keep it afloat, X obtained bank loans totaling PHP 2.5 million. X later died in an accident, leaving A as sole heir. X’s estate was appraised at PHP 1 million and paid that entire amount to the banks. The banks then sued A for the unpaid PHP 1.5 million.

Will the action prosper? Decide with reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer:

No. The banks cannot recover the deficiency from A’s (noun) separate property because A’s liability as heir does not exceed the value inherited from X (noun).

Legal Basis:

Articles 774 and 776 of the Civil Code transmit a decedent’s property, rights, and obligations to the heirs only to the extent of the inheritance. Article 1311 similarly binds heirs to transmissible contracts but limits their liability to the property received. William Ong Genato v. Benjamin Bayhon reiterates that contractual obligations pass to heirs without creating unlimited personal liability.

Application:

X left PHP 1 million in estate assets against PHP 2.5 million in bank debt. The estate paid the full PHP 1 million. Because A received no value beyond that exhausted estate, the remaining PHP 1.5 million cannot be collected from A personally.

Conclusion:

Accordingly, the deficiency action against A must fail, absent an independent personal undertaking by A.

records.Controlling Doctrine: An heir answers for a decedent’s transmissible debts only up to the value of the inheritance received.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Essay Question:
Childhood friends A (noun), B (noun), and C (noun) borrowed PHP 3 million from XYZ Bank (noun) for a joint venture.

They signed a promissory note binding themselves jointly and severally to pay on December 1, 2024, without need of demand. On maturity, all three defaulted. XYZ Bank demanded the full amount only from A. A objected that the bank should have demanded payment from all three co-debtors.

Is A correct? Give your reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer:

No. A (noun) is not correct because XYZ Bank (noun) may demand the entire debt from any one solidary debtor.

Legal Basis:

Articles 1207 and 1216 of the Civil Code recognize solidary liability when the obligation expressly so provides and authorize the creditor to proceed against any one, some, or all solidary debtors simultaneously until the debt is fully collected. Living @ Sense, Inc. v. Malayan Insurance Co., Inc. applies Article 1216 and holds that the creditor need not implead every solidary debtor.

Application:

The note says A, B (noun), and C (noun) are jointly and severally liable, which is an express stipulation of solidarity. Upon default, the bank could demand the whole PHP 3 million from A alone. A’s remedy after payment is contribution from the co-debtors under Article 1217, not rejection of the bank’s demand.

Conclusion:

Therefore, the demand against A alone is valid.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Essay Question:
A (noun) had three children: X (noun), Y (noun), and Z (noun).

In her will, A instituted only X and Y as heirs to her entire estate. She disinherited Z because Z married a drug addict who was disrespectful.

Is Z’s disinheritance valid? Give your reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer:

No. Z’s (noun) disinheritance is invalid because the stated reason is not one of the exclusive statutory causes for disinheriting a child or descendant.

Legal Basis:

Articles 915 and 916 of the Civil Code require disinheritance to be made in a will and for a cause expressly specified by law. Article 919 exhaustively lists the causes for disinheriting children and descendants. Dy Yieng Seangio v. Reyes requires strict compliance: the cause must be legal, true, and expressly stated.

Application:

A (noun) disinherited Z because Z married a drug addict who was disrespectful. Neither parental disapproval of the marriage nor the spouse’s disrespect, without facts bringing Z’s own conduct within Article 919, is a statutory cause. The omission of Z from the institution of heirs cannot cure the defective disinheritance.

Conclusion:

Therefore, Z’s disinheritance is ineffective, and Z may demand the legitime and the remedies provided by Article 918.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Persons and Family Relations - Psychological Incapacity
records.Essay Question:
A (noun) and B (noun) married in 2018.

After the marriage, A discovered that B refused to seek gainful employment, depended entirely on A’s salary, and held daily drinking sprees for his friends in their home. On one occasion, B even asked A to dance for them while they drank.

A petitioned to declare the marriage void because of B’s psychological incapacity. B opposed, arguing that because he was mentally healthy, he could not be psychologically incapacitated.

Is B’s argument consistent with prevailing jurisprudence? Give your reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer:

No. B’s (noun) argument is inconsistent with prevailing jurisprudence because psychological incapacity is a legal concept and does not require mental illness or a medical diagnosis.

Legal Basis:

Article 36 of the Family Code voids a marriage when a spouse was psychologically incapacitated, at the time of celebration, to comply with essential marital obligations. Tan-Andal v. Andal holds that psychological incapacity is not a medical illness; it is shown by clear and convincing evidence of an enduring aspect of personality structure that manifests through grave, incurable-in-the-legal-sense inability, with juridical antecedence, to perform essential marital obligations.

Application:

B cannot defeat the petition merely by proving that he is mentally healthy. However, A (noun) must still prove more than laziness, drinking, or refusal to work as isolated acts. She must connect B’s conduct to a durable personality structure existing at the marriage’s inception and causing a genuine incapacity—not mere unwillingness—to perform essential obligations.

Conclusion:

Therefore, B’s stated defense is legally wrong, although A must still satisfy Tan-Andal’s evidentiary requirements before nullity may be decreed.

records.Topic: Persons and Family Relations - Apparent Authority to Solemnize Marriage
records.Essay Question:
On March 15, 2025, A (noun) and B (noun) married before Judge C (noun), the solemnizing officer, inside her chambers at the Regional Trial Court for Makati City (noun).

Unknown to A and B, the Supreme Court (noun) had dismissed Judge C from the service on March 14, 2025 for grave misconduct. Judge C had gained access to her chambers on the wedding day only to collect her belongings.

What is the status of A and B’s marriage? Give your reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer:

The marriage is valid, assuming both A (noun) and B (noun) honestly believed in good faith that Judge C (noun) still had authority to solemnize it.

Legal Basis:

Articles 3(1), 7, and 35(2) of the Family Code ordinarily require solemnization by an authorized officer and declare a marriage void when the officer lacks authority. Article 35(2), however, creates an exception when either or both contracting parties believed in good faith that the solemnizing officer had legal authority. Genio v. People states this general rule and statutory good-faith exception.

Application:

Judge C’s dismissal the day before removed her legal authority. Nevertheless, the ceremony occurred in her official chambers, and the facts expressly state that A and B did not know of the dismissal. Nothing indicates bad faith by either contracting party. Their reasonable good-faith belief brings the marriage within Article 35(2)’s exception; Judge C’s lack of authority does not by itself invalidate it.

Conclusion:

Therefore, A and B’s marriage is valid, without prejudice to any liability of Judge C for acting without authority.

records.Controlling Doctrine: A marriage solemnized by an unauthorized officer is valid when either or both contracting parties believed in good faith that the officer had legal authority.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Succession - Proximity of Degree in Intestacy
records.Essay Question:
A (noun) died intestate without ascendants, descendants, or a surviving spouse.

A was survived by B (noun), a cousin, and C (noun), a sister.

May B demand that C divide A’s estate equally with him? Give your reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer:

No. B (noun), a cousin in the fourth civil degree, is excluded by C (noun), A’s (noun) sister in the second civil degree.

Legal Basis:

Article 962 of the Civil Code provides that the relative nearest in degree excludes the more distant, except when representation properly applies. Articles 1003 and 1009 call brothers and sisters before other collateral relatives. Bagunu v. Piedad holds that, among collateral relatives, proximity is controlling except for the statutory representation of children of brothers or sisters.

Application:

C is A’s sister and a collateral relative in the second degree. B is A’s cousin in the fourth degree and does not represent a deceased brother or sister of A. Because a nearer collateral relative survives, B is not called to the intestate succession.

Conclusion:

Therefore, B cannot demand half of the estate; C excludes B and inherits the estate, subject to any other legally established heirs or obligations.

records.Controlling Doctrine: The nearest relative excludes a more distant collateral relative unless the statutory right of representation applies.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Property Relations - Conjugal Property and Forged Mortgage
records.Essay Question:
A (noun) and B (noun) married in 1991 without a prenuptial agreement.

In 1997, A forged B’s signature on the promissory note for a loan from Commercial Bank (PCB) (noun) for A’s printing business. A also forged B’s signature on a real estate mortgage over three parcels acquired during the marriage. After A defaulted, PCB foreclosed, bought the parcels as highest bidder, and obtained a certificate of sale.

Upon learning of the mortgage and sale, B sued to nullify the mortgage and cancel the certificate of sale because he had not consented.

Is B correct? Give your reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer:

Yes. B (noun) is correct because the real estate mortgage over the conjugal parcels was executed without his genuine written consent or prior court authority.

Legal Basis:

Articles 116 and 124 of the Family Code presume property acquired during marriage to be conjugal and make an unauthorized disposition or encumbrance void. The transaction is treated as a continuing offer that may become binding only if the non-consenting spouse accepts it, or a court authorizes it, before withdrawal. Commoner Lending Corp. v. Balandra applies Article 124 to a 1997 mortgage based on forged spousal authority and confirms both the initial nullity and the possibility of later acceptance.

Application:

The parcels were acquired during the marriage and are presumed conjugal. A’s (noun) forgery supplied no consent from B. The facts show that B challenged the mortgage upon discovery; they do not show later acceptance, partial payment, or court authorization. PCB’s foreclosure could convey no enforceable mortgage right against the conjugal parcels.

Conclusion:

Therefore, the mortgage and the foreclosure certificate should be annulled, without prejudice to any personal loan liability of A and to proof that B later accepted the continuing offer, which the stated facts do not show.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Family Code, Arts. 116 and 124; Commoner Lending Corp. v. Balandra: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68846
records.Controlling Doctrine: An encumbrance of conjugal property without the other spouse’s written consent or court authority is void but operates as a continuing offer capable of later acceptance before withdrawal.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Essay Question:
A (noun), a public school teacher at XYZ Elementary School (noun), obtained several Government Service Insurance System (GSIS) (noun) loans totaling PHP 147,000.00.

When A retired in 2020, GSIS deducted PHP 638,172.59 from her retirement benefits and treated the loans as settled. GSIS had imposed 12% annual interest on arrears compounded monthly and a 6% annual penalty compounded monthly, increasing the obligation by 432.135%.

After failing to obtain relief from GSIS, A asked the court to reduce the interest and penalties as unconscionable.

Is A’s argument meritorious? Give your reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer:

Yes. A’s (noun) challenge is meritorious because the combined compounded interest and penalties are prima facie iniquitous and unconscionable in the stated circumstances.

Legal Basis:

Articles 1229 and 2227 of the Civil Code authorize courts to equitably reduce iniquitous or unconscionable penalties and liquidated damages. Freedom of contract under Article 1306 remains subject to law, morals, good customs, public order, and public policy. Aclado v. GSIS held that the same 12% interest on arrears and 6% penalty, both compounded monthly and producing a 432.135% increase, were shocking, oppressive, and subject to judicial reduction.

Application:

A borrowed PHP 147,000.00, yet GSIS deducted PHP 638,172.59 because of the compounded charges. The figures and rates reproduce Aclado’s material circumstances. The escalation is not merely burdensome; it is disproportionate to the principal and calls for equitable moderation.

Conclusion:

Therefore, the court may reduce the interest and penalties to reasonable levels consistent with Aclado.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Courts may reduce stipulated interest and penalties when their combined application is iniquitous or unconscionable in the case’s context.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Sales - Form and Perfection of Contract
records.Essay Question:
A (noun) entered into a written contract selling a house and lot to B (noun).

To avoid thousands of pesos in notarization fees, A and B did not have the contract notarized. B asked her nephew, C (noun), a second-year law student, to review it. C told B that the sale was void because it was not in a public instrument and advised her to seek a judicial declaration of nullity.

Is C correct? Give your reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer:

No. C (noun) is not correct; the absence of notarization does not, by itself, invalidate a perfected written sale of real property between A (noun) and B (noun).

Legal Basis:

Articles 1356, 1357, and 1358 of the Civil Code distinguish the validity of a contract from the public form required for convenience, registration, and effect against third persons. Once a contract is perfected, either party may compel execution of the proper public instrument. Fil-Estate Properties, Inc. v. Hermana Realty, Inc. holds that a private written real-property agreement may remain valid despite being unnotarized under Article 1358.

Application:

The facts state that A and B entered into a contract of sale and deliberately omitted only notarization. No defect in consent, object, consideration, or written form is alleged. The document remains private and may require authentication in evidence; it cannot be registered as a public instrument until properly acknowledged, but those consequences do not make the sale void between the parties.

Conclusion:

Therefore, C’s advice is wrong. A or B may instead compel execution of a notarized public instrument for registration.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Notarization and public form under Article 1358 are generally for convenience and registration, not essential to the validity of a perfected written sale between the parties.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Donation - Adulterous Relationship and Public Policy
records.Essay Question:
A (noun) leased his condominium unit for 10 years at PHP 50,000.00 per month.

While his wife, B (noun), was in the United States of America (noun), A kept his mistress, X (noun), in his house. A later donated to X the right to receive all rentals from the condominium lessee.

B sued to declare the donation void because A and X were guilty of concubinage. A and X argued that the civil action must be dismissed until concubinage was first proved in a separate criminal case.

Decide with reason(s).
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer:

B’s (noun) action should not be dismissed. A separate criminal conviction for concubinage is not a prerequisite to nullifying the donation.

Legal Basis:

Article 739(1) of the Civil Code declares void donations between persons guilty of adultery or concubinage at the time of donation. The donor’s or donee’s spouse may bring the action, and guilt may be proved by a preponderance of evidence in that same civil proceeding. Arcaba v. Vda. de Batocael applies Article 739 and recognizes that the prohibited relationship may be established in the civil case without a prior criminal conviction.

Application:

B alleges that A (noun) harbored X (noun) as his mistress and then donated the rental right to her. B may prove those facts in the nullity action under the civil standard. A and X’s demand for a separate criminal prosecution improperly adds a requirement that Article 739 rejects.

Conclusion:

Therefore, the civil action may proceed, and the donation must be declared void if B proves the prohibited relationship by a preponderance of evidence.

records.Controlling Doctrine: A spouse may prove adultery or concubinage by a preponderance of evidence in the same civil action to annul a prohibited donation; no prior criminal conviction is required.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Persons and Family Relations — Void Marriages as a Defense to Bigamy
records.Essay Question:
In 1981, JR (noun) married then-16-year-old Inka (noun) in a civil ceremony solemnized by the mayor of their hometown. They lived together until 2007, when JR admitted having an affair with Elena (noun). Inka later discovered that JR and Elena had married in 1995, so she filed a criminal complaint against JR for bigamy.

JR argued that he could not be criminally liable because his marriage to Inka was void for lack of a valid marriage license and his marriage to Elena was void for lack of a marriage ceremony. Elena had also filed a petition for nullity in the Regional Trial Court of Quezon City (noun), which later declared her marriage to JR void for being bigamous; that judgment became final.

Does JR have a valid defense in the bigamy case? Decide with reasons.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes, conditionally. JR (noun) has a valid defense if he proves that the first marriage was void ab initio for lack of a valid marriage license, or that the second marriage was independently void ab initio for lack of a marriage ceremony. The judgment declaring the second marriage void merely because it was bigamous does not, standing alone, exculpate him.

Legal Basis: Article 349 of the Revised Penal Code requires a subsisting first marriage and a subsequent marriage possessing the essential requisites for validity. Under Articles 2, 3, 4, and 35 of the Family Code, absence of an essential or formal requisite—subject to statutory exceptions—renders a marriage void. In Pulido v. People, the Supreme Court held that an accused may prove in the bigamy case that the prior or subsequent marriage was void ab initio; a prior judicial declaration of nullity is not indispensable for that defense.

Application: If JR proves that no valid marriage license supported the first marriage and no license exception applied, the prosecution cannot establish a legally subsisting first marriage. Alternatively, if he proves that no marriage ceremony occurred for the second union, that union lacked an essential requisite of marriage. Either independently proven defect may defeat an element of bigamy. However, the later declaration that the second marriage was void because it was bigamous only follows from the alleged bigamy and cannot by itself erase criminal liability.

Conclusion: JR has a valid defense only upon proof of an independent void-ab-initio ground affecting the first or second marriage; the bigamy-based nullity judgment alone is insufficient.

records.Controlling Doctrine: An accused may establish in the bigamy prosecution that the first or second marriage was void ab initio without first obtaining a judicial declaration. A second marriage's nullity solely because it is bigamous is not, by itself, a defense.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Persons and Family Relations — Custody of an Illegitimate Child
records.Essay Question:
Anita (noun), an entertainer at Empyrea (noun), a men’s club and lounge, became pregnant by Billy (noun) and later gave birth to Marisol (noun). Despite Billy’s opposition, Anita returned to work to support Marisol and provided her with a house, a nanny, and other necessities.

Billy offered to support Anita and Marisol if they lived with him. When Anita refused, Billy petitioned for custody, alleging that Anita was unfit because of her occupation. Anita maintained that an illegitimate child is under the mother’s sole parental authority.

If you were the judge, how would you decide the petition? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The petition should be denied, and custody should remain with Anita (noun).

Legal Basis: Article 176 of the Family Code places an illegitimate child under the parental authority of the mother. Article 213 provides that a child below seven years of age should not be separated from the mother absent compelling reasons. Pablo-Gualberto v. Gualberto V teaches that the child’s best interests are paramount and that alleged moral lapses justify removing custody only when they adversely affect the child’s welfare or materially impair proper parental care.

Application: Marisol (noun) is an illegitimate young child, and Anita has supplied a home, care, and necessities. Billy (noun) relies on Anita’s work at a men’s club, but the occupation alone does not establish an imperative or compelling cause, nor does it show harm to Marisol or neglect of parental duties. On the stated facts, transferring custody would displace the statutory maternal authority without proof of unfitness.

Conclusion: Billy’s petition should be denied because Marisol’s best interests and the governing custody rules favor Anita.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Property and Succession — Sale of a Co-owner’s Undivided Share
records.Essay Question:
Lani (noun) and Rufino (noun) died, leaving four children, including Arturo (noun) and Bugoy (noun). The heirs sold one-half of their parents’ property to Honorato (noun). Of the remaining portions, one quarter was occupied by Arturo’s children, Ildefonso (noun) and Bienvenido (noun), while Bugoy sold the other quarter to the Spouses Cruz (noun) by deed of sale.

The Spouses Cruz filed an ejectment case involving the one-fourth portion they purchased. Bienvenido then sued them for recovery of ownership, quieting of title, and annulment of the deed, alleging that Bugoy was not the sole owner of property that originally belonged to Rufino’s estate. The Spouses Cruz argued that the heirs had already divided the property and that Bienvenido had chosen the wrong remedy.

Will Bienvenido’s complaint prosper? Discuss.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No, the complaint will not prosper insofar as it seeks to nullify the sale outright or recover the common property from the buyers. The conveyance is effective at least to the extent of Bugoy’s (noun) undivided share, subject to partition.

Legal Basis: Under the Civil Code rules on co-ownership, each co-owner has full ownership of his or her undivided share and may alienate it, but the effect of an alienation involving a specific physical portion is limited to the portion ultimately allotted to the seller upon partition. Reyes v. Spouses Garcia holds that the buyer is substituted as co-owner to the extent of the seller’s pro-indiviso interest and that partition, rather than annulment of the sale or recovery of the common property, is the proper remedy for determining specific portions.

Application: Upon Lani’s (noun) and Rufino’s (noun) deaths, their children became co-owners before partition. Bugoy could therefore transfer his hereditary, undivided interest to the Spouses Cruz (noun). Because the facts do not conclusively establish a binding partition, the sale does not necessarily give the buyers ownership of the exact physical quarter they claim; its effect is confined to whatever portion may be allotted to Bugoy. That uncertainty calls for partition, not total annulment of the deed.

Conclusion: Bienvenido’s action, as framed, should fail; the parties’ specific rights should be settled through partition, with the sale respected only within Bugoy’s lawful share.

records.Controlling Doctrine: A co-owner may alienate a pro-indiviso share. A purported sale of a definite physical portion is effective only within the portion later allotted to the seller, and partition is the proper remedy for fixing the parties' specific shares.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Essay Question:
Felicia (noun) and Rocky (noun) became lovers and had two children, Enrico (noun) and Euriz (noun). Rocky later died in a vehicular collision. A year afterward, Rocky’s father, Hilario (noun), died.

In settling Hilario’s estate, Enrico and Euriz claimed an interest as Rocky’s biological children, asserting a right to represent their predeceased father. Hilario’s legitimate heirs opposed the claim and invoked Article 992 of the Civil Code, arguing that Enrico and Euriz were barred from inheriting from Rocky’s ascendants.

Are Hilario’s legitimate heirs correct? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. On the stated facts, Enrico (noun) and Euriz (noun) may represent Rocky (noun) in Hilario’s (noun) estate, subject to proof of filiation and the ordinary requirements of intestate succession.

Legal Basis: Article 992 of the Civil Code contains the so-called iron-curtain rule, while the Code’s provisions on representation permit descendants to step into the place of a predeceased heir in the direct descending line. In Aquino v. Aquino, the Supreme Court reexamined Article 992 and held that nonmarital grandchildren are not barred from inheriting from their grandparents and other direct ascendants by right of representation solely because of their parents’ marital status.

Application: Rocky predeceased his father, Hilario. Enrico and Euriz are stated to be Rocky’s biological, nonmarital children. Their claim runs vertically through Rocky to their grandfather, not collaterally between the legitimate and nonmarital family lines that Article 992 was historically read to separate. Accordingly, once filiation and the other succession facts are established, they may occupy Rocky’s place by representation.

Conclusion: The legitimate heirs are incorrect; Article 992 does not, by itself, defeat Enrico’s and Euriz’s right to represent Rocky in Hilario’s estate.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Nonmarital grandchildren may inherit from grandparents and other direct ascendants by right of representation; Article 992 does not impose an iron curtain in the direct descending line solely because of marital status.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Damages — Temperate Damages for Unproved Funeral Expenses
records.Essay Question:
Rene (noun) and Sebastian (noun), who were bitter enemies, engaged in a gunfight. Rene killed Sebastian with a shot to the head.

In the murder case against Rene, Sebastian’s heirs failed to establish the amount of funeral expenses because their evidence was inadequate. The trial court nevertheless awarded temperate damages, reasoning that it could not ignore that the heirs necessarily incurred funeral expenses.

Is the award proper? Discuss.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. An award of temperate damages is proper because the pecuniary loss is certain even though its exact amount was not adequately proved.

Legal Basis: Article 2224 of the Civil Code allows temperate or moderate damages when some pecuniary loss has been suffered but its amount cannot, from the nature of the case, be proved with certainty. Applying People v. Jugueta, the Supreme Court in People v. Badillo expressly recognized funeral and burial expenses as pecuniary losses supporting temperate damages when their exact amount was not proven.

Application: Sebastian’s (noun) death necessarily required disposition of his remains and caused his heirs to incur funeral or burial expenses. Their inadequate proof prevents an award of actual damages in an unverified amount, but it does not erase the established fact of pecuniary loss. Article 2224 therefore authorizes a reasonable temperate award.

Conclusion: The trial court properly awarded temperate damages despite the heirs’ failure to prove the exact funeral expenses.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Temperate damages may replace unproved actual funeral or burial expenses when death makes the pecuniary loss certain but the exact amount cannot be established.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question:
Taylor (noun) received Harry (noun) in her house and told him to feel at home. Inside the house, Harry (noun) planned to steal money from Taylor (noun) and covertly took her cellphone. After several attempts, he opened Taylor’s (noun) electronic-wallet account, but it had a zero balance. Harry (noun) returned the cellphone and left disappointed. He was charged with and convicted of the impossible crime of theft.

Is Harry (noun) liable for the impossible crime of theft?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Harry (noun) is liable for an impossible crime involving cybertheft.

Legal Basis: Article 4(2) of the Revised Penal Code imposes liability when an act would be an offense against persons or property were it not for the inherent impossibility of accomplishment or the use of inadequate or ineffectual means. Laurel v. Abrogar holds that intangible property capable of appropriation may be the subject of theft. Section 6 of Republic Act No. 10175 increases the penalty when a Revised Penal Code crime is committed through information and communications technology.

Application: Harry (noun) intended to take money belonging to Taylor (noun), obtained her phone, and accessed the electronic wallet. The intended taking failed only because the account unexpectedly contained no funds, a circumstance beyond his control. His acts would have constituted theft had the electronic funds existed, and he used information technology in executing them.

Conclusion: The inherent factual impossibility of taking money from the empty account makes him liable for the impossible crime, with the cybercrime qualifying circumstance.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Article 4(2); Republic Act No. 10175, Section 6; Laurel v. Abrogar, G.R. No. 155076, January 13, 2009: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/48437
records.Controlling Doctrine: An intended offense against property may constitute an impossible crime when completion is prevented by an unknown factual impossibility; intangible property can be the object of theft.
