records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Murder by Inducement; Reward and Treachery
records.Essay Question:
Andy (noun) paid Billie (noun) PHP 50,000 to kill Charlie (noun). Billie (noun) found Charlie (noun) asleep and stabbed him to death. The trial court convicted Andy (noun) and Billie (noun) of murder, appreciating reward and treachery, and imposed reclusion perpetua without benefit of parole in lieu of the death penalty. Only Andy (noun) appealed, arguing that he should be liable only for homicide because neither reward nor treachery could be appreciated against him.

What crime did Andy (noun) commit, and what is the proper penalty?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Andy (noun) is guilty of murder as a principal by inducement, with reclusion perpetua as the proper penalty.

Legal Basis: Article 17 of the Revised Penal Code treats one who directly induces another to commit a crime as a principal. Under Article 248, a killing committed in consideration of a price, reward, or promise is murder. People v. Cañete holds that price or reward affects both the person who offers it and the person who accepts it. Under Article 62, a circumstance concerning the material execution, such as treachery, affects only a participant who knew of it.

Application: Andy’s (noun) payment was the determining inducement for Billie’s (noun) killing of Charlie (noun), and the agreed reward itself qualified the killing as murder as to Andy (noun). Nothing shows that Andy (noun) knew Billie (noun) would attack Charlie (noun) while asleep, so treachery cannot additionally aggravate Andy’s (noun) liability.

Conclusion: Andy (noun) is liable for murder by inducement, qualified by reward, and should be sentenced to reclusion perpetua.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Articles 17, 62, and 248; People v. Cañete, G.R. No. L-37945, May 28, 1984: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/assets/dtSearch/dtSearch_system_files/dtisapi6.dll?DocId=28275%26Index=%2A4aeb4dbdcceeda9b59b85ae3fb22cec0%26cmd=getdoc ; People v. Cabillan, G.R. No. 131808, February 6, 2002: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/50181
records.Controlling Doctrine: Price or reward qualifies the killing for both offeror and acceptor, while treachery affects an inducer only if the inducer knew the treacherous means would be used.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: People v. Cañete; People v. Cabillan

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question:
Adele (noun), a grocery cashier, was charged under an information alleging that, with intent to gain and abuse of confidence, she stole grocery items worth PHP 1,500 without her employer’s consent. The trial court convicted her of qualified theft, reasoning that her cashier position entailed a high degree of confidence because she handled the employer’s property.

Was Adele (noun) properly convicted of qualified theft?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Adele (noun) should be liable only for simple theft on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: Article 308 of the Revised Penal Code defines theft. Under Article 310, theft is qualified by grave abuse of confidence only when the confidence reposed in the offender is substantial and the taking is facilitated by a serious breach of that trust. Batislaon v. People distinguishes mere employee access from the grave confidence required for qualified theft.

Application: Adele’s (noun) work gave her access to grocery items, but the facts do not show that those goods were specially entrusted to her custody or that a high fiduciary confidence, beyond ordinary employment access, enabled the taking.

Conclusion: The taking constitutes simple theft, not qualified theft.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Articles 308 and 310; Batislaon v. People, G.R. No. 256624, July 26, 2023: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69203
records.Controlling Doctrine: Ordinary employee access does not by itself amount to the grave abuse of confidence required for qualified theft.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question:
Police received information that Larry (noun) sold illegal drugs and organized an entrapment operation with PO1 Miguel (noun) as poseur-buyer. After the informant introduced them, Larry (noun) demanded payment for PHP 1,000 worth of shabu, while PO1 Miguel (noun) insisted on seeing the item first. Larry (noun) took a sachet from his pocket, whereupon the officers arrested him and seized it. The sachet tested positive for shabu.

Is Larry (noun) criminally liable under Republic Act No. 9165 even though the sale was not consummated?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Larry (noun) is liable for attempted sale of dangerous drugs, which carries the same penalty prescribed for the consummated act under Republic Act No. 9165.

Legal Basis: Article 6 of the Revised Penal Code defines an attempt as commencement by overt acts without completion because of a cause other than spontaneous desistance. Section 26(b) of Republic Act No. 9165 punishes an attempt to sell dangerous drugs with the same penalty as the completed offense. People v. Tumulak applies these provisions where intent to sell and overt acts are proved but the sale is interrupted.

Application: Larry (noun) appeared for the transaction, demanded payment, possessed the shabu, and produced the sachet for the buyer. Police intervention prevented delivery and payment, not Larry’s (noun) voluntary desistance.

Conclusion: The facts establish attempted sale punishable under Sections 5 and 26(b) of Republic Act No. 9165.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Article 6; Republic Act No. 9165, Sections 5 and 26(b); People v. Tumulak, G.R. No. 206054, July 25, 2016: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/62182
records.Controlling Doctrine: An overt, interrupted offer to sell dangerous drugs is an attempted sale punished as the consummated offense under Section 26(b).

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Private Conspirator After Public Officer’s Death
records.Essay Question:
The Ombudsman (noun) found probable cause against Governor Rocky (noun) and Quentin (noun), a private individual, for allegedly conspiring to violate Section 3(e) of Republic Act No. 3019. Governor Rocky (noun) was later killed in an ambush, but the Ombudsman (noun) filed the information against Quentin (noun) before the Sandiganbayan (noun). Quentin (noun) moved to quash, arguing that the death of the public officer extinguished the private conspirator’s criminal liability.

Was Quentin’s (noun) criminal liability extinguished?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Governor Rocky’s (noun) death did not extinguish Quentin’s (noun) own potential criminal liability.

Legal Basis: Article 89 of the Revised Penal Code extinguishes only the deceased accused’s personal criminal liability. A private person may be prosecuted under Republic Act No. 3019 when alleged to have conspired with a public officer. People v. Go holds that the law requires the private person’s conspiracy with a public officer but does not invariably require both to remain jointly indicted when the public officer can no longer be charged because of death.

Application: The information alleges that Quentin (noun) conspired with Governor Rocky (noun) while the latter was a public officer. Governor Rocky’s (noun) death bars prosecution of him personally, but it neither erases the alleged conspiracy nor transfers that personal extinguishment to Quentin (noun).

Conclusion: The prosecution against Quentin (noun) may proceed, subject to proof of every element beyond reasonable doubt.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Article 89; Republic Act No. 3019, Section 3(e); People v. Go, G.R. No. 168539, March 25, 2014: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/56694
records.Controlling Doctrine: The death of a public officer extinguishes only that officer’s liability; a private alleged conspirator may be prosecuted alone.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Conspiracy and Multiple Counts of Rape
records.Essay Question:
Alvin (noun), Dennis (noun), and an unidentified John Doe (noun) were charged with rape through force, violence, and intimidation, conspiring and mutually helping one another, and taking turns raping AAA (noun). The prosecution proved that Alvin (noun) raped AAA (noun) first, Dennis (noun) second, John Doe (noun) third, and Alvin (noun) again fourth. The trial court convicted Alvin (noun) and Dennis (noun) of only three counts, excluding the rape personally committed by John Doe (noun).

Was the number of convictions correct?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Alvin (noun) and Dennis (noun) are each liable for four counts of rape if the charged conspiracy was proved.

Legal Basis: In conspiracy, the act of one conspirator in furtherance of the common design is the act of all. People v. Diega holds that a rapist is responsible not only for the rape personally committed but also for the rapes committed by co-conspirators, even when a co-conspirator is unidentified or at large.

Application: The four penetrations were separately consummated pursuant to the alleged joint design. Alvin (noun) and Dennis (noun) are therefore answerable for John Doe’s (noun) rape as well as the rapes each participant personally committed.

Conclusion: The proper number is four counts of rape for each proved conspirator.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Robbery With Homicide Versus Homicide and Theft
records.Essay Question:
Levi (noun) engaged Leo’s (noun) escort services for PHP 50,000. After they had sex, Levi (noun) paid only PHP 10,000. Feeling shortchanged, Leo (noun) repeatedly stabbed Levi (noun). Leo (noun) then rummaged through Levi’s (noun) belongings and took his wallet, cellphone, and watch. Leo (noun) was convicted of robbery with homicide because the killing allegedly occurred by reason of or on occasion of robbery.

Was the conviction for that special complex crime correct?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Leo (noun) is liable for separate crimes of homicide and theft on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: Robbery with homicide requires that the original criminal design be robbery and that the homicide occur by reason of or on occasion of that robbery. Catacutan v. People holds that when the intent to rob arises only after the killing, the taking is an afterthought and the acts constitute separate crimes.

Application: Leo (noun) stabbed Levi (noun) out of anger over the underpayment. Nothing indicates an intent to steal before or during the attack. Only after the killing did he search the victim’s belongings and take property.

Conclusion: Because robbery was an afterthought, the proper offenses are homicide and theft, not robbery with homicide.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Robbery with homicide does not arise when the intent to take property is formed only after the killing.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question:
Domeng (noun), in conspiracy with Dado (noun) and Dario (noun), kidnapped and detained nine-year-old Rosanna (noun).

They demanded PHP 2 million as ransom from Rosanna’s (noun) family in exchange for her life and liberty, and the family agreed to pay. While Rosanna (noun) remained in captivity, Domeng (noun), Dado (noun), and Dario (noun) killed her.

What crime, if any, did they commit? Discuss.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Domeng (noun), Dado (noun), and Dario (noun) committed kidnapping for ransom with homicide.

Legal Basis: Article 267 of the Revised Penal Code, as amended, treats the killing of a kidnapped victim during detention as part of the special complex crime. People v. Bernardo explains that the classification applies whether the killing was originally intended or arose only during the detention.

Application: The conspirators deprived nine-year-old Rosanna (noun) of liberty to extort PHP 2 million from her family, then killed her while she remained captive. The ransom purpose and the death during detention are both present.

Conclusion: They are liable for the special complex crime of kidnapping for ransom with homicide.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Principal by Inducement and Irresistible Force
records.Essay Question:
Mark (noun) was charged with rape as a principal by direct participation, while his employer, Ado (noun), was charged as a principal by inducement for forcing Mark (noun) to commit rape at gunpoint.

The trial court acquitted Mark (noun) because he acted under the compulsion of irresistible force, but convicted Ado (noun) of rape. Ado (noun) appealed, arguing that he could not be liable because there was no punishable principal by direct participation.

Is Ado’s (noun) argument tenable? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Ado’s (noun) argument is not tenable.

Legal Basis: Under Articles 12(5) and 17(2) of the Revised Penal Code, one who directly forces another to commit a crime is a principal by inducement, while irresistible force is a personal exempting circumstance of the person compelled. People v. Pantoja explains that a person acting under an exempting circumstance commits the act but is not punishable because intelligence or free will is absent.

Application: Ado (noun) used a gun to compel Mark (noun) to perform the rape. Mark’s (noun) exemption concerns his own lack of free will; it does not erase the criminal act or transfer the exemption to Ado (noun), whose coercion caused the act.

Conclusion: Mark’s (noun) acquittal does not relieve Ado (noun), who remains liable as a principal by inducement.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Reclusion Perpetua and the Three-Fold Rule
records.Essay Question:
Miguel (noun) was convicted of murdering his neighbor, Nikkolas (noun), with treachery and evident premeditation, and was sentenced to reclusion perpetua.

After serving 30 years, Miguel (noun) petitioned for habeas corpus. He claimed that the three-fold rule meant he had served the maximum of his sentence and that continued imprisonment violated his liberty.

Will Miguel’s (noun) petition prosper? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Miguel’s (noun) habeas corpus petition will not prosper.

Legal Basis: Article 70 of the Revised Penal Code governs the successive service of multiple penalties. Miguel v. Director of the Bureau of Prisons holds that the 30-year computation assigned to a perpetual penalty for Article 70 purposes does not cap reclusion perpetua at 30 years or create an automatic right to release.

Application: Miguel (noun) is serving one indivisible penalty, not multiple penalties requiring successive service. His reliance on the three-fold rule is therefore misplaced, and the lapse of 30 years alone does not make his continued detention illegal.

Conclusion: The petition should be denied.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question:
Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System (MWSS) (noun) employee Japar (noun) regularly signed disbursement vouchers for field-work expenses and later liquidated them with receipts.

Another MWSS (noun) employee, Jonas (noun), needed PHP 230,000. Jonas (noun) completed one of the vouchers ordinarily used by Japar (noun), forged Japar’s (noun) signature, and presented it to cashier Filomena (noun), who released the money. The forgery was later discovered, and Jonas (noun) admitted what he had done.

Jonas (noun) was convicted of malversation. Was the conviction proper? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Jonas’s (noun) conviction for malversation was improper.

Legal Basis: Article 217 of the Revised Penal Code requires that the public officer have custody or control of the public funds by reason of office and be accountable for them. Sarion v. People and Fajardo v. People treat official accountability as an indispensable element; employment in government alone is insufficient.

Application: Jonas (noun) obtained the PHP 230,000 only by forging Japar’s (noun) voucher. The facts do not show that Jonas (noun) was authorized by his office to receive, keep, or account for those funds. His conduct may support another offense, including the panel’s formulation of estafa through falsification of a public document, but it does not satisfy malversation’s accountability element.

Conclusion: The malversation conviction was not proper.

People, G.R. No. 239823, September 25, 2019: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/65695
records.Controlling Doctrine: A public employee cannot be convicted of malversation unless the funds were under that employee’s official custody or control and the employee was accountable for them.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Theft of Lost Property and Finder in Law
records.Essay Question:
Milet (noun) accidentally dropped a bundle of US$4,000 on a sidewalk after returning from the public market. Thirteen-year-old Henri (noun) found and secretly picked up the money.

Henri (noun) later encountered gardener Junie (noun). After learning where Henri (noun) had obtained the money, Junie (noun) grabbed it, kept US$2,000 as his “balato,” exchanged it into Philippine currency, and bought luxury goods.

Charged with theft, Junie (noun) argued that he could not be liable because he was not the person who originally found the money. Is Junie (noun) correct? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Junie (noun) is liable for theft.

Legal Basis: Article 308 of the Revised Penal Code covers the appropriation of lost property instead of returning it to the owner or local authorities. Pante v. People holds that liability is not confined to the first physical finder; a person who knowingly receives and appropriates lost property may be a “finder in law.”

Application: Junie (noun) knew from Henri (noun) that the US dollars belonged to someone else. Rather than return the money, he took half, converted it, and spent it for personal benefit, demonstrating intent to gain.

Conclusion: Junie’s (noun) claim that he was not the original finder does not defeat his liability for theft.

records.Controlling Doctrine: A person who knowingly receives and appropriates lost property can be a finder in law and liable for theft even if another person physically found the property first.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question:
Police officer John (noun) ran after Randy (noun), who had just killed Willy (noun) in John’s (noun) presence. John (noun) fired at Randy (noun) in an attempt to stop him.

Randy (noun) fired back and seriously wounded John (noun), who survived because of timely medical assistance. Charged with frustrated homicide, Randy (noun) claimed self-defense.

Is Randy’s (noun) claim of self-defense tenable? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Randy’s (noun) claim of self-defense is not tenable.

Legal Basis: Article 11(1) of the Revised Penal Code makes unlawful aggression an indispensable element of self-defense. Galang v. Court of Appeals explains that without unlawful aggression, there can be no complete or incomplete self-defense. A police officer’s necessary act to arrest or stop a person who has just committed a killing is an act in the performance of duty, not unlawful aggression.

Application: John (noun) personally witnessed Randy (noun) kill Willy (noun), pursued him, and fired to stop his escape. On the stated facts, John’s (noun) conduct was connected with the lawful performance of police duty. Randy’s (noun) return fire therefore did not repel unlawful aggression.

Conclusion: Because the indispensable element of unlawful aggression is absent, Randy (noun) cannot successfully invoke self-defense.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Self-defense fails when the supposed aggression is a police officer’s lawful performance of duty, because unlawful aggression is indispensable.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question:
Moe (noun), Curly (noun), and Larry (noun) were drinking and singing inside a karaoke bar when Buboy (noun) suddenly entered and, without warning, shot all three with a .45-caliber pistol.

Buboy (noun) fled. Moe (noun), Curly (noun), and Larry (noun) died from gunshot wounds to their heads and bodies. After Buboy’s (noun) arrest, the prosecutor charged him with three counts of homicide.

Do you agree with the homicide charges? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. On the stated facts, Buboy (noun) should be charged with three counts of murder qualified by treachery.

Legal Basis: Article 248 of the Revised Penal Code classifies a killing attended by treachery as murder. People v. Agsalog explains that treachery exists when the means of attack gives the victim no opportunity to defend or retaliate and is consciously adopted to ensure execution without risk to the attacker.

Application: Buboy (noun) entered without warning and immediately shot the three victims while they were drinking and singing. The sudden gun attack left them defenseless, and each death is a distinct killing.

Conclusion: The proper charges are three counts of murder, not homicide.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Articles 14(16) and 248; People v. Agsalog, G.R. No. 141087, March 31, 2004: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/46047
records.Controlling Doctrine: A sudden, consciously adopted attack that leaves victims no opportunity to defend themselves constitutes treachery and qualifies each killing as murder.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question:
Michael (noun) made a prohibited U-turn while driving on a highway. Police officer Dyords (noun) accosted him, and they argued. Dyords (noun) drew his service firearm, ordered Michael (noun) out of the car, handcuffed him, and pinned his head and body against the pavement until he could no longer breathe. Michael (noun) died.

Charged with homicide, Dyords (noun) invoked the exempting circumstance of accident.

If you were the judge, how would you resolve Dyords’s (noun) defense? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: I would reject Dyords’s (noun) defense of accident.

Legal Basis: Article 12(4) of the Revised Penal Code requires a person invoking accident to have been performing a lawful act with due care. Article 4 makes a person criminally liable for the natural consequences of a felony. People v. Cristobal, applying Luz v. People, explains that a traffic violation ordinarily calls for confiscation of the driver’s license rather than a custodial arrest.

Application: Dyords (noun) did not merely enforce the traffic rule. He drew a firearm, handcuffed Michael (noun), and pinned him to the pavement until he suffocated. Those acts were neither a lawful, careful performance of duty nor a mere accident. The fatal consequence flowed from Dyords’s (noun) unlawful restraint and force.

Conclusion: The accident exemption does not apply, and Dyords (noun) remains criminally liable for the resulting homicide.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Articles 4 and 12(4); People v. Cristobal, G.R. No. 234207, June 10, 2019: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/65317; Picardal v. People, G.R. No. 235749, June 19, 2019: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/65319
records.Controlling Doctrine: Accident is unavailable when the accused was not performing a lawful act with due care; a fatal consequence naturally flowing from unlawful restraint remains attributable under Article 4.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question:
A police officer responded to a disturbance call at an apartment in Quezon City (noun) and saw Sisa (noun) stabbing her one-year-old child with a kitchen knife.

The officer grabbed Sisa (noun), who then dropped the knife. The child survived multiple stab wounds. At trial, Sisa (noun) argued that she voluntarily desisted and could therefore be liable only for attempted parricide.

Is Sisa’s (noun) contention tenable? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Sisa’s (noun) reliance on voluntary desistance is not tenable.

Legal Basis: Article 6 of the Revised Penal Code recognizes spontaneous desistance only when the offender stops by a free and spontaneous act before performing all acts of execution. People v. Lizada explains that desistance prompted by an external constraint is not spontaneous and does not erase liability for an attempted felony.

Application: Sisa (noun) dropped the knife only after the police officer physically grabbed her. Her cessation was caused by an external intervention, not by an unprompted decision to abandon the attack.

Conclusion: Sisa (noun) cannot invoke spontaneous desistance to avoid liability; the proper stage of parricide must be determined from the acts of execution and injuries proved.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Articles 6 and 246; People v. Lizada, G.R. Nos. 143468-71, January 24, 2003: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/44312
records.Controlling Doctrine: Desistance caused by police intervention is not spontaneous and does not exempt an offender from liability for the attempted felony already begun.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Robbery With Homicide and Integrated Offenses
records.Essay Question:
Anna (noun) and Barbara (noun) saw Javier (noun) and Jorge (noun) rob an elderly woman of her purse and beat her to death. When Anna (noun) and Barbara (noun) tried to help, Javier (noun) and Jorge (noun) stabbed both of them before fleeing with the purse.

Anna (noun) survived a stab wound that punctured her lung, but Barbara (noun) died from nine stab wounds.

What charge or charges should be filed for the elderly woman’s death, Barbara’s (noun) death, and Anna’s (noun) injuries? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Javier (noun) and Jorge (noun) should be charged with one special complex crime of robbery with homicide.

Legal Basis: Article 294(1) of the Revised Penal Code treats homicide committed by reason of or on occasion of robbery as a special complex crime. People v. Daguman holds that all homicides and physical injuries committed on the occasion of the robbery are integrated into the single, indivisible offense, regardless of the number or identity of the victims.

Application: The elderly woman was killed during the taking of her purse. Barbara (noun) was killed and Anna (noun) was wounded when they intervened while the robbers were completing and escaping from the robbery. Those violent acts occurred on the occasion of the same robbery.

Conclusion: The two deaths and Anna’s (noun) injuries are absorbed in one charge of robbery with homicide.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Article 294(1); People v. Daguman, G.R. No. 219116, August 26, 2020: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/67068
records.Controlling Doctrine: All killings and physical injuries committed by reason of or on occasion of one robbery are integrated into the single special complex crime of robbery with homicide.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question:
Jenny (noun) obtained fire insurance from YG Insurance Co. (noun). She issued a postdated check payable to cash for PHP 15,000 and handed it to Lisa (noun), YG’s (noun) sales agent.

Lisa (noun) did not remit the check. She deposited it in her husband’s bank account, but the check was dishonored because it was drawn against a closed account.

What crime, if any, did Lisa (noun) commit, and what is the prescribed penalty? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Lisa (noun) committed an impossible crime of theft.

Legal Basis: Article 4(2) of the Revised Penal Code punishes an act that would be an offense against persons or property were its accomplishment not inherently impossible or the means inadequate or ineffectual. Jacinto v. People applies this rule when an accused appropriates a check that turns out to have no value. Article 59 prescribes arresto mayor or prisión correccional, depending on the social danger and degree of criminality shown.

Application: Lisa (noun), with intent to gain, appropriated YG’s (noun) check by depositing it into her husband’s account instead of remitting it. Theft could not be consummated because the closed-account check had no realizable value, a fact unknown to her.

Conclusion: Lisa (noun) is liable for an impossible crime of theft, punishable within Article 59’s stated range as judicially determined.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Articles 4(2) and 59; Jacinto v. People, G.R. No. 162540, July 13, 2009: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/40577
records.Controlling Doctrine: Appropriating a check with intent to gain may constitute an impossible crime of theft when the check is valueless for a reason unknown to the offender.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question:
At about 3:00 a.m. on May 15, 2013, Lucy (noun), Mary (noun), and Raphael (noun) were in a passenger jeepney driven by Raphael (noun). Kiko (noun), driving a Virgen Bus (noun) at high speed in the opposite direction, overtook another vehicle and entered the jeepney’s lane.

The collision killed Raphael (noun), seriously injured Lucy (noun) and Mary (noun), and caused PHP 500,000 in damage to the jeepney. The prosecutor filed one information for reckless imprudence resulting in serious physical injuries and another for reckless imprudence resulting in homicide and damage to property.

Was the prosecutor correct? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The prosecutor should file one information covering the single quasi-offense and all its consequences.

Legal Basis: Article 365 of the Revised Penal Code punishes the negligent act itself, not each resulting injury as a separate intentional felony. Ivler v. Modesto-San Pedro holds that a single negligent act producing death, physical injuries, and property damage constitutes one quasi-offense of reckless imprudence.

Application: Kiko’s (noun) single act of recklessly overtaking caused one collision and all the resulting death, injuries, and property damage. Splitting those consequences into two informations treats the effects as separate offenses despite their single negligent source.

Conclusion: One information should charge reckless imprudence resulting in homicide, serious physical injuries, and damage to property.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question:
During a foot patrol prompted by reports of illegal activity, police officer Pepe (noun) saw Raul (noun) inside a small shanty holding a disposable syringe. Pepe (noun) entered through the open door, arrested Raul (noun), and seized 23 more syringes and empty ampoules.

Pepe (noun) marked, photographed, and inventoried the items in the presence of Raul (noun), a barangay kagawad (noun), a Department of Justice (DOJ) (noun) representative, and a media practitioner. The items were kept in a sealed container, but the prosecution presented only Pepe (noun) as its witness and no forensic-examination result.

Should Raul (noun) be convicted of illegal possession of drug paraphernalia? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Raul (noun) should be acquitted because the prosecution did not prove beyond reasonable doubt that the ordinary items were drug paraphernalia.

Legal Basis: Sections 12 and 21 of Republic Act No. 9165 require proof that the seized equipment was fit or intended for introducing dangerous drugs into the body and require submission to the PDEA (noun) forensic laboratory. Cuico v. People holds that ordinary items such as syringes cannot be treated as drug paraphernalia from appearance or police opinion alone; forensic testing is material to identity and chain of custody.

Application: The prosecution produced syringes and empty ampoules but no laboratory result showing traces of a dangerous drug or their prohibited intended use. Pepe’s (noun) experience and sole testimony cannot cure that evidentiary gap.

Conclusion: Reasonable doubt remains as to an essential element, so Raul (noun) must be acquitted.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Child Abuse and Intent to Debase
records.Essay Question:
Joben (noun), a school principal, summoned 15-year-old students Paula (noun) and Gina (noun) to the faculty room about a sexual text message referring to Joben’s (noun) daughter.

In front of teachers and students, Joben (noun) angrily questioned and insulted them, threatened to sue, raised a middle finger, and called them “burikat” or “whores.” Paula (noun) and Gina (noun) later told their parents they were ashamed to return to school.

Is Joben (noun) guilty of other acts of child abuse under Section 10(a) of Republic Act No. 7610? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No, on the stated facts and controlling case analogy, the required intent to debase, degrade, or demean was not proved beyond reasonable doubt.

Legal Basis: Section 10(a) of Republic Act No. 7610 punishes other acts of child abuse. Brinas v. People holds that, where the alleged act is inherently non-abusive in the statutory sense, the prosecution must establish the specific intent to debase, degrade, or demean the child’s intrinsic worth and dignity.

Application: Joben’s (noun) words and gesture were offensive and humiliating, but the episode arose in the heat of anger over a message involving her daughter. Those circumstances do not, without more, prove the specific statutory intent beyond reasonable doubt.

Conclusion: Joben (noun) should be acquitted of the Section 10(a) charge, without implying that her conduct was proper or free from other consequences.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question:
In 2003, the Province of Davao del Sur (noun) directly purchased a Ford Ranger XLT (noun) and a Toyota Hilux (noun) for the governor and vice-governor without competitive public bidding. Governor Luis (noun) signed the purchase requests, and the Bids and Awards Committee (BAC) (noun) approved direct purchase. The vehicles were delivered, inspected, accepted, and paid for.

After the Ombudsman-Mindanao (noun) found noncompliance with procurement procedure, it charged Luis (noun) and the BAC (noun) members under Section 3(e) of Republic Act No. 3019. The Sandiganbayan (noun) convicted them solely because violating procurement law supposedly established evident bad faith and manifest partiality.

Was the Sandiganbayan (noun) correct? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. A procurement-law violation alone does not establish every element of Section 3(e) of Republic Act No. 3019.

Legal Basis: Section 3(e) requires, among other elements, manifest partiality, evident bad faith, or gross inexcusable negligence, plus undue injury to a party or an unwarranted benefit, advantage, or preference. Martel v. People holds that breach of procurement rules does not automatically prove those separate statutory elements.

Application: The conviction rested solely on the absence of competitive bidding. The facts, as stated, do not independently identify the required culpable mode or show undue injury or an unwarranted private benefit.

Conclusion: The Sandiganbayan’s (noun) reasoning was insufficient, and conviction under Section 3(e) cannot rest on the procurement irregularity alone.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Republic Act No. 3019, Section 3(e); Martel v. People, G.R. Nos. 224720-23 and 224765-68, February 2, 2021: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/67194
records.Controlling Doctrine: A procurement-law violation is not automatically a Section 3(e) graft offense; the prosecution must separately prove culpable conduct and undue injury or unwarranted benefit.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Robbery by Intimidation and Abuse of Public Position
records.Essay Question:
One Sunday afternoon, at the corner of C.P. Garcia Avenue (noun) and Katipunan Avenue (noun), an off-duty police officer accosted a motorcycle rider and inspected the motorcycle’s compartment box.

Pretending to find a sachet of shabu, the officer demanded PHP 1,000 to prevent the rider’s arrest. Afraid of life imprisonment for a crime not committed, the rider paid. A surveillance camera recorded the incident.

Will a robbery charge prosper against the off-duty police officer? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The officer committed robbery by intimidation.

Legal Basis: Articles 293 and 294(5) of the Revised Penal Code require an unlawful taking of another’s personal property, with intent to gain, by violence or intimidation. Sosas v. People holds that law-enforcement officers who abuse their authority to intimidate a person into paying money commit robbery by extortion.

Application: The officer falsely claimed to have found shabu and used the threat of arrest and severe punishment to compel payment. The rider’s apparent consent was produced by fear, while intent to gain is shown by the officer’s demand and receipt of the money. His police position supplied the intimidation even though he was off duty.

Conclusion: A charge of robbery by intimidation will prosper, with abuse of public position considered when legally proper.

records.Controlling Doctrine: A police officer who exploits apparent authority and threatens arrest to obtain money commits robbery by intimidation.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question:
To motivate their eight-year-old daughter to study and have a better future, her parents made her kneel on rice spread on the floor, spanked her with a bamboo stick, or required her to stand in the rain for hours whenever any grade fell below 80.

Did the parents commit a crime? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The parents’ excessive punishments constitute child cruelty punishable under Section 10(a) of Republic Act No. 7610.

Legal Basis: Section 10(a) of Republic Act No. 7610 punishes other acts of child abuse. Fernandez v. People recognizes that parental discipline is excluded from cruelty only when it is reasonable in manner and moderate in degree and does not cause physical or psychological injury.

Application: Prolonged standing in the rain, kneeling on rice, and striking an eight-year-old with a bamboo stick are disproportionate to the educational purpose asserted. The repeated methods inflict degrading physical and psychological punishment beyond reasonable parental correction.

Conclusion: The parents may be held liable for child cruelty under Section 10(a), subject to proof of the statutory elements beyond reasonable doubt.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Republic Act No. 7610, Section 10(a); Fernandez v. People, G.R. No. 217542, November 21, 2018: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/64751
records.Controlling Doctrine: Parental discipline loses statutory protection when its manner is unreasonable, excessive, and injurious or degrading to the child.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Economic Abuse Through Denial of Support
records.Essay Question:
An estranged married couple agreed to let their 14-year-old child choose the parent with whom to live. The child chose the mother.

Displeased, the husband stopped paying the child’s tuition and stopped supporting the wife, although he was vice-president of a highly profitable company.

Did the husband commit a crime? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes, if the deliberate deprivation was used to control or punish the wife or child as the facts indicate, the husband committed economic abuse under Republic Act No. 9262.

Legal Basis: Section 5(e)(2) of Republic Act No. 9262 penalizes deprivation or denial of financial support legally due to a woman or her child when committed in the statutory context. Melgar v. People confirms that deliberate denial of support to a child may constitute violence against women and children, while Acharon v. People requires proof of the legally due support and the prohibited purpose or effect.

Application: The husband had financial capacity but stopped support immediately because the child chose the mother. The timing and stated displeasure show that support was withheld to pressure or retaliate against the wife and child.

Conclusion: The facts support prosecution for economic abuse, subject to proof of every element beyond reasonable doubt.

No. 223477, February 14, 2018: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/63887; Acharon v. People, G.R. No. 224946, November 9, 2021: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68085
records.Controlling Doctrine: Deliberately withholding legally due support to control or punish a woman or her child may constitute economic abuse under Republic Act No. 9262.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question:
The head of a large company’s human-resources division copied an employee’s physical address, email address, birthdate, civil status, and photographs, then shared them with a friend who found the employee attractive.

Did the human-resources head commit a crime? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The unauthorized sharing may constitute unauthorized disclosure under the Data Privacy Act of 2012.

Legal Basis: Republic Act No. 10173 protects personal and sensitive personal information and limits processing and disclosure to lawful grounds. Section 32 penalizes a personal information controller or processor, or its responsible officers, employees, or agents, who discloses personal information to a third party without consent. Zoleta v. Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas explains that sensitive and privileged information receive a special regime of protection under Philippine privacy law.

Application: The human-resources head obtained the data through the employment relationship and disclosed it for a friend’s private interest, without the employee’s consent or any stated lawful basis.

Conclusion: The facts support liability for unauthorized disclosure, subject to proof of the accused’s covered role and the other statutory elements.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Republic Act No. 10173, Sections 3, 12, 13, and 32; Zoleta v. Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, G.R. No. 258888, August 29, 2023: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69447
records.Controlling Doctrine: Employment access to personal data does not authorize disclosure to a third party for a private purpose without consent or another lawful basis.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Zoleta v. Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question:
While a person passed a construction site for a new Hall of Justice (noun), construction workers shouted: “Hoy bakla, halika rito at haplusin mo ’ko!” “Hoy bakla, ang pangit mo!” and “Bakla, mukha ka pa ring lalaki kahit ano’ng gawin mo!”

Did the workers commit a crime? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The statements constitute gender-based sexual harassment in a public space under the Safe Spaces Act.

Legal Basis: Sections 4 and 11 of Republic Act No. 11313 cover unwanted sexual remarks and transphobic, homophobic, or sexist slurs made in streets and other public spaces. Falcis v. Civil Registrar General recognizes that the Safe Spaces Act specifically addresses and penalizes transphobic, homophobic, and sexist slurs.

Application: The workers directed unwanted sexual invitations and repeated homophobic ridicule at a passerby because of perceived sex, gender, sexual orientation, identity, or expression. A construction site along a passage open to the public falls within the law’s public-space protection.

Conclusion: The workers may be prosecuted for gender-based street and public-spaces sexual harassment.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Homophobic or transphobic slurs and unwanted sexual invitations directed at a person in a public space are punishable under the Safe Spaces Act.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question:
During an intense operational meeting, the campaign manager of a presidential candidate said: “Dapat ipapatay na lang natin ang mga bumabatikos sa kandidato natin.”

The campaign manager was later charged with proposal to commit murder.

Can the campaign manager be convicted of that offense? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Proposal to commit murder is not independently punishable under the Revised Penal Code.

Legal Basis: Article 8 of the Revised Penal Code provides that conspiracy and proposal to commit a felony are punishable only when the law specifically prescribes a penalty. Pascual v. People reiterates this limiting rule. The Code specifically punishes proposals for certain offenses, but it does not create an offense of proposal to commit murder.

Application: Even assuming that the statement was a proposal rather than rhetoric or a mere suggestion, no penal provision specifically punishes proposal to commit murder. Penal statutes cannot be extended by analogy.

Conclusion: The campaign manager cannot be convicted of the offense charged.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Article 8; Pascual v. People, G.R. Nos. 241248 and 241257-59, June 16, 2021: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/67750
records.Controlling Doctrine: Proposal to commit a felony is punishable only when a statute specifically provides a penalty; proposal to commit murder is not such an offense.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Theft Through Temporary Taking and Use
records.Essay Question:
During a Senate (noun) hearing in aid of legislation, a senator’s staff member secretly took a resource person’s mobile phone, read its messages, and hurriedly wrote notes for the senator.

The staff member then secretly returned the phone. The resource person learned of the taking only because a journalist’s TikTok (noun) video captured the act and went viral.

Can the staff member be liable for theft of the phone? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The temporary taking and unauthorized use can constitute consummated theft.

Legal Basis: Article 308 of the Revised Penal Code requires taking another’s personal property, without consent, with intent to gain, and without violence, intimidation, or force. People v. Bustinera holds that the mere unauthorized use of property unlawfully taken constitutes gain, and Valenzuela v. People holds that theft is consummated upon completed taking with intent to gain.

Application: The staff member secretly obtained control of the phone, used its contents for the hearing, and acted without the owner’s knowledge or consent. Returning the device after obtaining that unauthorized benefit does not undo the completed taking.

Conclusion: The staff member may be held liable for consummated theft.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Article 308; People v. Bustinera, G.R. No. 148233, June 8, 2004: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/46991; Valenzuela v. People, G.R. No. 160188, June 21, 2007: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/41676
records.Controlling Doctrine: Unauthorized temporary use supplies intent to gain, and later return does not erase a theft already consummated by completed taking.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: People v. Bustinera; Valenzuela v. People

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Accessory by Concealing the Body of the Crime
records.Essay Question:
In a rage during a golf game, a high-ranking public official struck a caddy with a golf club, killing the caddy immediately.

The official then called a loyal security guard who had not witnessed the killing and ordered the guard to place the body in a golf cart and dump it in a nearby lake to make the death appear to be drowning. The body was discovered, and both were charged as co-conspirators in homicide.

Can the security guard be convicted as a principal in homicide? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The security guard is not a principal in the homicide but may be liable as an accessory.

Legal Basis: Articles 17 and 19 of the Revised Penal Code distinguish principals from accessories. An accessory, with knowledge of the crime and without prior participation as principal or accomplice, acts afterward by concealing or destroying the body of the crime to prevent discovery. People v. Lamsen applies Article 19(2) to post-crime concealment.

Application: The guard neither participated in nor agreed to the killing before it occurred. His conduct began only after the caddy was dead, when he concealed and dumped the body to mislead investigators.

Conclusion: He cannot be convicted as a principal or co-conspirator in homicide on these facts, but he may be convicted as an accessory under Article 19(2).
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Articles 17 and 19(2); People v. Lamsen, G.R. Nos. 133527-28, September 20, 2001: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/37083
records.Controlling Doctrine: A person who joins only after a killing and conceals the corpse to prevent discovery is an accessory, not a principal in the homicide.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question:
A crime defined in the Revised Penal Code is punishable by arresto menor. After finding the accused guilty beyond reasonable doubt, should the judge apply the Indeterminate Sentence Law?

Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The Indeterminate Sentence Law does not apply.

Legal Basis: Section 2 of Act No. 4103 excludes persons whose maximum term of imprisonment does not exceed one year. People v. Hamoy expressly applies that exception. Under Article 27 of the Revised Penal Code, arresto menor runs from one day to 30 days.

Application: The statutory maximum for arresto menor is only 30 days, far below the one-year threshold. The sentence therefore falls within the express statutory exception.

Conclusion: The judge should impose the proper straight penalty and should not fix minimum and maximum indeterminate terms.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Act No. 4103, Section 2; Revised Penal Code, Article 27; People v. Hamoy, G.R. No. 227505, October 2, 2017: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/63708
records.Controlling Doctrine: The Indeterminate Sentence Law does not apply when the maximum imprisonment does not exceed one year, including arresto menor.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question:
A prisoner who had been convicted but whose appeal remained pending died from complications caused by COVID-19 (noun).

Should the pending appeal be dismissed as a consequence? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The criminal case and appeal should be dismissed and terminated because death occurred before final judgment.

Legal Basis: Article 89(1) of the Revised Penal Code extinguishes criminal liability by death. People v. Brillantes, applying People v. Bayotas, holds that an accused’s death pending appeal extinguishes criminal liability and civil liability based solely on the offense, while civil claims based on other sources of obligation may survive in a proper separate action.

Application: Because the conviction was still under appeal, it was not final when the prisoner died. There is no longer an accused upon whom the criminal penalty may be imposed.

Conclusion: The appeal should be dismissed, criminal liability and civil liability ex delicto are extinguished, without prejudice to independently sourced civil claims allowed by law.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Death before final judgment extinguishes criminal liability and civil liability ex delicto, while independently sourced civil claims may survive.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question:
A person arrested for playing cara y cruz was charged under Presidential Decree No. 1602. Counsel argued for dismissal because the accused was poor, the coin game was the accused’s only entertainment, casino gamblers wager far larger sums, and foreign gamblers were welcomed in the Philippines (noun).

Is counsel’s argument legally tenable? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Poverty and the stated comparisons are not exempting circumstances and do not legalize the prohibited gambling act.

Legal Basis: Presidential Decree No. 1602 penalizes unauthorized gambling, while Article 12 of the Revised Penal Code exhaustively identifies exempting circumstances. Yun Kwan Byung v. Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation states the general rule that gambling is illegal unless affirmatively authorized by law.

Application: Playing cara y cruz is not made lawful by the accused’s poverty, motive, or comparison with licensed gambling. None of those considerations appears among Article 12’s exemptions, and lawful casino gaming rests on specific statutory authorization.

Conclusion: The defense does not justify dismissal of the illegal-gambling charge.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Presidential Decree No. 1602; Revised Penal Code, Article 12; Yun Kwan Byung v. Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation, G.R. No. 163553, December 11, 2009: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/51152
records.Controlling Doctrine: Unauthorized gambling remains punishable despite poverty or benign motive; licensed gambling is different because it rests on affirmative legal authorization.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question:
At an Enhanced Community Quarantine (ECQ) (noun) barangay checkpoint, a barangay tanod (noun) confronted a resident over non-essential travel.

Angered by the tanod’s (noun) tone, the resident punched the tanod’s (noun) head. The tanod (noun) fell, suffered a brain hemorrhage, and died. Charged with homicide, the resident argued that there could be no conviction because there was no intent to cause death.

Is the defense tenable? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The lack of intent to kill does not relieve the resident of liability for the death, although praeter intentionem may mitigate the penalty if proved.

Legal Basis: Article 4(1) of the Revised Penal Code makes a person committing a felony liable although the wrongful act differs from that intended. Article 13(3) recognizes the mitigating circumstance that the offender did not intend to commit so grave a wrong. Urbano v. People applies liability for the resulting death while appreciating that mitigating circumstance when the means used and surrounding facts show a lesser intended harm.

Application: The intentional punch was a felony, and the tanod’s (noun) fatal fall and brain hemorrhage directly followed it. The resident is answerable for that natural consequence even if only physical injury was intended.

Conclusion: The homicide defense fails, but lack of intent to cause so grave a wrong may mitigate liability.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Articles 4(1) and 13(3); Urbano v. People, G.R. No. 182750, January 20, 2009: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/48637
records.Controlling Doctrine: An offender is liable for a death naturally caused by an intentional assault even without intent to kill, though praeter intentionem may mitigate the penalty.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Aggravating Circumstances — Chief Executive and Nighttime
records.Essay Question:
During a nighttime concert at the Cultural Center of the Philippines (CCP) (noun), Chito (noun) physically assaulted another attendee, Butch (noun). Chito (noun) slapped Butch (noun) several times in front of the President of the Philippines (noun), who was also present.

Are there any modifying circumstances affecting Chito’s (noun) criminal liability? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The offense is aggravated because it was committed in the presence of the Chief Executive; nighttime is not appreciable on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: Article 14(5) of the Revised Penal Code lists commission of a crime in the presence of the Chief Executive as an aggravating circumstance. Article 14(6) treats nighttime as aggravating only when it facilitates the offense. People v. Abrazaldo explains that nighttime, by itself, is not aggravating and must have been purposely sought or used to facilitate the crime.

Application: Chito (noun) repeatedly slapped Butch (noun) in front of the President of the Philippines (noun), satisfying the circumstance identified in Article 14(5). The concert’s occurrence at night, without proof that Chito (noun) sought or exploited darkness, does not establish nocturnity.

Conclusion: Presence of the Chief Executive aggravates the offense, but nighttime does not.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Article 14(5) and (6); People v. Abrazaldo, G.R. No. 124392, February 7, 2003: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/47695
records.Controlling Doctrine: Commission of a crime in the known presence of the Chief Executive is aggravating; nighttime is not aggravating unless deliberately sought or used to facilitate the crime or ensure impunity.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question:
Pido (noun), a private contractor, was convicted of plunder in conspiracy with government officials and sentenced by the Sandiganbayan (noun) to reclusion perpetua. Years later, Pido’s (noun) childhood friend, Benjamin (noun), became Secretary of Justice (noun) and convinced the President of the Philippines (noun) to pardon him.

Both the judgment and the pardon were silent as to accessory penalties. After his release, Pido (noun) decided to run for mayor of his hometown in Bulacan (noun). The incumbent mayor asked whether Pido’s (noun) candidacy could be challenged.

On what ground or grounds may the candidacy be challenged? Discuss.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The candidacy may be challenged because Pido (noun) remains perpetually disqualified from public office.

Legal Basis: Articles 36, 41, and 73 of the Revised Penal Code provide that reclusion perpetua carries perpetual absolute disqualification, that accessory penalties are deemed imposed with the principal penalty, and that a pardon does not restore the right to hold public office unless the pardon expressly does so. Risos-Vidal v. Commission on Elections recognizes that the wording of the pardon controls whether political rights were expressly restored.

Application: Pido’s (noun) judgment need not separately state the accessory penalty because it follows reclusion perpetua by operation of law. His pardon was silent: it neither expressly remitted perpetual absolute disqualification nor restored his right to hold public office.

Conclusion: The incumbent mayor may challenge Pido’s (noun) candidacy on the ground of continuing perpetual absolute disqualification and non-restoration of the right to hold public office.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Articles 36, 41, and 73; Risos-Vidal v. Commission on Elections, G.R. No. 206666, January 21, 2015: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/58837
records.Controlling Doctrine: An accessory disqualification follows the principal penalty by operation of law and survives a pardon unless the pardon expressly remits the disqualification or restores the right to hold public office.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question:
Samuel (noun), a Filipino citizen of Chinese descent, assisted the Chinese Government (noun) in surveying and identifying secure shores in the Philippines (noun). Samuel (noun) believed that he was helping the Philippines (noun) because the geodetic maps would allegedly be transmitted to the Philippine Government (noun) for future use.

Before the survey was completed, Chinese military vessels entered the Scarborough shores (noun), established a station secured by two warships, and populated two islets claimed by the Chinese Government (noun), using Samuel’s (noun) maps.

Therese (noun), Samuel’s (noun) helper, saw his meetings with Chinese officials but did not understand the conversations. Rolando (noun), his gardener, understood Chinese but had poor eyesight; he attended the meetings and glimpsed maps signed by Samuel (noun).

Is Samuel (noun) liable for treason? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Samuel (noun) is not liable for treason on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: Article 114 of the Revised Penal Code makes treason a wartime offense and requires either two witnesses to the same overt act or a confession in open court. Estrada v. Sandiganbayan describes treason and conspiracy to commit treason as offenses committed in time of war. Adherence also requires an intent to betray and must be accompanied by aid or comfort to an enemy.

Application: The facts do not establish a state of war between the Philippines (noun) and China (noun). Samuel (noun) also believed the maps would benefit the Philippine Government (noun), negating an intent to betray. Finally, Therese (noun) and Rolando (noun) did not both competently perceive the same overt act of giving the maps to an enemy.

Conclusion: The wartime, adherence, and two-witness requirements are not established; Samuel (noun) cannot be convicted of treason.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Article 114; Estrada v. Sandiganbayan, G.R. No. 148965, February 26, 2002: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/50350
records.Controlling Doctrine: Treason requires a wartime enemy, intent to adhere to that enemy coupled with aid or comfort, and proof by two witnesses to the same overt act or confession in open court.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question:
Rita (noun) asked 14-year-old Belen (noun) to meet her at DuoMart Supermarket (noun) for an errand. Rita (noun) instead brought Belen (noun) to a nearby hotel and introduced her to Elmer (noun). Rita (noun) left them in a room, where Elmer (noun) had sexual intercourse with Belen (noun).

When Rita (noun) returned, Elmer (noun) paid her PHP 2,200, of which PHP 700 was given to Belen (noun). Rita (noun) warned Belen (noun) not to tell anyone. Before they left, police officers entered the room and arrested Elmer (noun) and Rita (noun).

Rita (noun) argued that she did not force Belen (noun), who admitted consenting to the intercourse for a fee. What crime, if any, is Rita (noun) liable for? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Rita (noun) is liable for qualified trafficking in persons involving a child.

Legal Basis: Sections 3, 4, and 6 of Republic Act No. 9208, as amended, punish recruiting, transporting, providing, or obtaining a person for prostitution or sexual exploitation and qualify the offense when the trafficked person is a child. People v. Leocadio holds that a child’s recruitment or transport for exploitation is trafficking even without proof of coercive means, and consent does not negate the offense.

Application: Rita (noun) deceived 14-year-old Belen (noun) about an errand, transported her to a hotel, provided her to Elmer (noun) for paid sexual intercourse, accepted payment, and demanded secrecy. Belen’s (noun) minority qualifies the trafficking, and her purported consent is immaterial.

Conclusion: Rita (noun) is liable for qualified trafficking in persons.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Republic Act No. 9208, as amended, Sections 3, 4, and 6; People v. Leocadio, G.R. No. 237697, July 15, 2020: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/66293
records.Controlling Doctrine: Recruiting, transporting, providing, or obtaining a child for prostitution or sexual exploitation constitutes qualified trafficking; the child’s consent and the absence of coercive means do not defeat liability.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question:
Jon (noun) and Pilar (noun) had been in a dating relationship for one year. Because of Jon’s (noun) abusive behavior, Pilar (noun) ended the relationship and refused to reconcile.

Jon (noun) then uploaded to his social-media account a video of their sexual intercourse and nude pictures of Pilar (noun), all of which he had recorded on his cellphone without her knowledge. Distraught, Pilar (noun) filed a complaint with the Office of the Prosecutor (noun) and submitted the posted video and photographs as evidence.

What offense or offenses, if any, did Jon (noun) commit? Discuss.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Jon (noun) may be held liable for psychological violence under Republic Act No. 9262 and for violations of Republic Act No. 9995.

Legal Basis: Section 5(i) of Republic Act No. 9262 punishes conduct that causes mental or emotional anguish, public ridicule, or humiliation to a woman with whom the offender has or had a dating relationship. Acharon v. People explains that the prohibited act, the resulting anguish, and the statutory mental element must be proved. Sections 4(a) and 4(d) of Republic Act No. 9995 separately prohibit secretly recording a sexual act or private area where privacy is reasonably expected and publishing that material online. XXX261049 v. People identifies the elements of unauthorized recording under Section 4(a).

Application: Jon (noun) secretly recorded Pilar (noun) during sexual activity, then uploaded the intimate material after she refused reconciliation. The recording and publication satisfy the conduct prohibited by Republic Act No. 9995. The retaliatory disclosure to humiliate a former dating partner, together with Pilar’s (noun) distress, supports psychological violence under Republic Act No. 9262.

Conclusion: Jon (noun) may be prosecuted for the applicable acts of photo and video voyeurism and for psychological violence, subject to proof of each offense’s distinct elements.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Republic Act No. 9262, Sections 3 and 5(i); Republic Act No. 9995, Sections 4(a) and 4(d); Acharon v. People, G.R. No. 224946, November 9, 2021: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68085; XXX261049 v. People, G.R. No. 261049, June 26, 2023: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69510
records.Controlling Doctrine: Secretly recording and publishing intimate material may create separate liability under the Anti-Photo and Video Voyeurism Act; retaliatory publication that causes a former dating partner mental or emotional anguish may also constitute psychological violence when its distinct elements are proved.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Acharon v. People; XXX261049 v. People

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Essay Question:
Socorro (noun) owned and leased an apartment building where Rami (noun) was a tenant under a two-year lease. After losing his job following the pandemic, Rami (noun) stopped paying rent during the second year. Socorro (noun) repeatedly demanded payment and eventually filed an ejectment case.

After Rami (noun) received the summons, he locked himself inside the unit. When he later left briefly for the supermarket, Socorro (noun) padlocked the apartment and cut off its utilities.

What crime, if any, did Socorro (noun) commit? Discuss.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Socorro (noun) committed unjust vexation.

Legal Basis: Article 287 of the Revised Penal Code, as amended, covers conduct that unjustifiably annoys, irritates, torments, or disturbs another when no more specific offense applies. Maderazo v. People holds that a lessor who takes the law into his own hands by padlocking leased premises may commit unjust vexation. Alejandro v. Bernas further explains that padlocking premises and cutting utilities without violence, threats, or intimidation does not establish grave coercion but may establish unjust vexation.

Application: Socorro (noun) had already invoked the lawful ejectment process but nevertheless excluded Rami (noun) from his dwelling and disconnected utilities without a court order. The acts foreseeably annoyed and disturbed Rami (noun), while the facts do not show violence, threats, or intimidation required for grave coercion.

Conclusion: Socorro (noun) is liable for unjust vexation.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Article 287, as amended; Maderazo v. People, G.R. No. 165065, September 26, 2006: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/43100; Alejandro v. Bernas, G.R. No. 179243, September 7, 2011: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/27939
records.Controlling Doctrine: A lessor who bypasses pending ejectment proceedings by padlocking leased premises and cutting utilities may commit unjust vexation; without violence, threats, or intimidation, grave coercion is not established.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Maderazo v. People; Alejandro v. Bernas
G.R. No. 165065, September 26, 2006; G.R. No. 179243, September 7, 2011

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Topic: Legislative Inquiries — Contempt and Due Process
records.Essay Question:
The Senate (noun) conducted investigations on strengthening government efforts against fugitives from justice. Winston (noun), a notorious drug dealer who had avoided warrants of arrest and hold-departure orders, was invited as a resource person.

Asked about the modus operandi and the immigration officers who helped him escape, Winston (noun) replied, “I will leave it to the Senate (noun) to find out.” The senators immediately cited him in contempt and ordered his detention until he answered.

Did the Senate (noun) lawfully cite Winston (noun) in contempt? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The immediate contempt citation was unlawful.

Legal Basis: Article VI, Section 21 of the 1987 Constitution requires Congress to respect the rights of persons appearing in legislative inquiries. Ong v. Senate recognizes that a witness must be given a meaningful opportunity to explain before contempt is imposed.

Application: Winston (noun) was cited in contempt immediately after an unresponsive answer. The Senate (noun) did not first allow him to explain or otherwise accord the process required before detention.

Conclusion: The contempt citation and detention violated due process.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article VI, Section 21; Ong v. Senate, G.R. No. 257401, March 28, 2023: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69108
records.Controlling Doctrine: Congress has inherent contempt power in aid of legislation, but it must respect the witness’s rights and afford an opportunity to be heard before punitive detention.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
Rocco (noun), a lawyer, filed a petition for mandamus to compel the President of the Philippines (noun) to defend the West Philippine Sea (noun) against Chinese incursions. He alleged that the President (noun) had a ministerial duty to protect national territory.

Rocco (noun) also sought to compel the President (noun) to bring the territorial dispute before the United Nations Security Council (noun) after diplomatic protests failed.

Will the petition prosper? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Mandamus will not lie.

Legal Basis: Mandamus compels only a clear ministerial duty, not an act involving judgment or discretion. Esmero v. Duterte treats decisions concerning the West Philippine Sea and recourse through foreign relations as matters entrusted to executive discretion.

Application: The choice of military, diplomatic, or multilateral measures requires policy judgment by the President (noun) as chief architect of foreign policy. Rocco (noun) has no clear legal right to one particular course.

Conclusion: The Court cannot compel the requested foreign-affairs actions by mandamus.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Rule 65, Rules of Court; 1987 Constitution, Article VII; Esmero v. Duterte, G.R. No. 256288, July 29, 2021: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/67553
records.Controlling Doctrine: Mandamus reaches only ministerial duties; courts cannot dictate discretionary presidential choices in foreign relations and national defense.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
Omar (noun), an Iranian national admitted to the Philippines (noun) as a refugee, petitioned for naturalization after more than ten years in the country. The trial court found that he possessed all qualifications and none of the disqualifications.

The Office of the Solicitor General (noun) objected because Iranian law does not grant Filipinos reciprocal naturalization rights.

Will the absence of reciprocity bar Omar’s (noun) naturalization? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Reciprocity does not bar the petition of a recognized refugee.

Legal Basis: The 1951 Refugee Convention and the Rule on Facilitated Naturalization of Refugees and Stateless Persons remove reciprocity as an obstacle for qualified refugees. Republic v. Karbasi applied the refugee framework in naturalization.

Application: Omar (noun) was admitted as a refugee and was found qualified. Requiring protection from, or reciprocity by, the country from which he fled would defeat the protective rule.

Conclusion: Lack of Iranian reciprocity does not bar Omar’s (noun) naturalization.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Commonwealth Act No. 473; 1951 Refugee Convention, Article 34; A.M. No. 21-07-22-SC, Section 5(a); Republic v. Karbasi, G.R. No. 210412, July 29, 2015: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/60816
records.Controlling Doctrine: A recognized refugee who otherwise qualifies may use facilitated naturalization without satisfying the ordinary reciprocity disqualification.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
Andrew (noun), a long-time advocate of women’s rights, is a bona fide member of BINI-bini Party (noun), which represents the women sector under the party-list system.

After the party won a seat in 2022, Andrew (noun), its first nominee, assumed office. An electoral protest alleged that he was unqualified because he is male.

Is Andrew (noun) qualified to represent BINI-bini Party (noun)? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Andrew (noun) may qualify as nominee.

Legal Basis: Republic Act No. 7941 governs party-list nominees. Atong Paglaum v. COMELEC holds that a nominee of a sectoral party must either belong to the represented sector or possess a track record of advocacy for it.

Application: Andrew (noun) is a bona fide party member and a long-time advocate of women’s rights. His sex alone does not defeat the advocacy-based qualification.

Conclusion: Andrew (noun) is qualified on the stated facts.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Republic Act No. 7941, Section 9; Atong Paglaum, Inc. v. COMELEC, G.R. Nos. 203766 et al., April 2, 2013: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/55861
records.Controlling Doctrine: A sectoral-party nominee need not personally belong to the represented sector when the nominee has the required bona fide advocacy and party membership.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
Fidel (noun), a government official, was convicted of: receiving a gift connected with a government contract under Section 3(b) of Republic Act No. 3019; accepting a gift connected with official functions under Section 7(d) of Republic Act No. 6713; and direct bribery under Article 210 of the Revised Penal Code.

On appeal, Fidel (noun) claimed that the three convictions violated double jeopardy.

Is his contention correct? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The three convictions do not, by themselves, violate double jeopardy.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 21 of the Constitution and Rule 117, Section 7 apply the identity-of-offenses test. Merencillo v. People recognizes that prosecution under different laws is permissible when each offense requires proof of an element the others do not.

Application: The anti-graft offense, the ethical-standards offense, and direct bribery contain distinct statutory elements concerning the transaction, official intervention, and corrupt agreement. None is necessarily identical to or included in every other offense.

Conclusion: Separate convictions for the distinct offenses do not place Fidel (noun) twice in jeopardy for the same offense.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article III, Section 21; Rule 117, Section 7; Merencillo v. People, G.R. Nos. 142369-70, April 13, 2007: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/43394
records.Controlling Doctrine: Double jeopardy bars a second prosecution for the same or an included offense, not cumulative liability for legally distinct offenses with different elements.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Topic: Privacy — Public Officials and Matters of Public Interest
records.Essay Question:
Politico Film Productions (PFP) (noun) planned a mockumentary, “Covidubidapdap” (noun), about the government’s poor pandemic response. The Department of Health Secretary (noun), fearing portrayal as lazy and incompetent, refused consent to the use of his name or image.

PFP (noun) proceeded. The Secretary (noun) sought an injunction based on privacy.

Was his right to privacy violated? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No, not on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: Article III protects privacy, but public officials have a reduced expectation concerning official conduct and matters of legitimate public concern. Labargan v. People discusses the diminished privacy expectations of public figures in matters connected with public life.

Application: The work concerns the government’s pandemic response and the Secretary’s (noun) public performance, not an unrelated intimate matter. Use of his public identity in commentary on official conduct is protected expression absent additional unlawful facts.

Conclusion: The Secretary (noun) cannot enjoin the production solely on the asserted privacy claim.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
The Barangay Council (noun) authorized solicitation of private funds to build a seven-meter statue of Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer (noun) in the plaza before a basilica.

Residents of other barangays challenged the resolution under the constitutional non-establishment clause.

Is the resolution invalid? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The resolution is not invalid on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 5 bars establishment of religion. Peralta v. Philippine Postal Corporation applies the purpose, primary effect, and excessive-entanglement analysis.

Application: A Rudolph (noun) display has a secular holiday purpose; it neither advances nor inhibits a faith, and the facts show no continuing governmental entanglement with the basilica (noun). Its location alone does not convert the display into religious establishment.

Conclusion: The resolution does not violate the non-establishment clause.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article III, Section 5; Peralta v. Philippine Postal Corporation, G.R. No. 223395, December 4, 2018: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/64851
records.Controlling Doctrine: A government act survives establishment-clause review when it has a secular purpose, does not principally advance or inhibit religion, and avoids excessive entanglement.
