records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
The 2020 Rules of the Senate Electoral Tribunal (SET) (noun) allowed an election protest within thirty days after the protestee assumed office.

The Senate (noun) later adopted internal rules shortening the period to fifteen days.

Are the Senate’s (noun) rules on the protest period constitutional? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The Senate (noun) cannot alter the SET’s (noun) protest rules.

Legal Basis: Article VI, Section 17 makes the SET (noun) the sole judge of contests involving senators. Fernandez v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal confirms the constitutional autonomy of an Electoral Tribunal from the legislative chamber.

Application: The protest deadline concerns the SET’s (noun) adjudicatory procedure. The Senate (noun), as a separate body, cannot shorten a period fixed by the tribunal.

Conclusion: The conflicting Senate (noun) rule is unconstitutional.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article VI, Section 17; Fernandez v. House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal, G.R. No. 187478, December 21, 2009: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/53223
records.Controlling Doctrine: Each Electoral Tribunal is an independent constitutional body and the sole judge of election contests involving members of its chamber.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
The Local Government Code (noun) allocated national-revenue shares among provinces, cities, municipalities, and barangays. A proposed General Appropriations Act (GAA) (noun) adopted different percentages.

Congressman Macky (noun) challenged the item. The House Budget Committee (noun) argued that Congress (noun) may increase or decrease local-government shares.

Is the new distribution scheme in the GAA (noun) lawful? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. A general appropriations act cannot amend the Local Government Code (noun) through an unrelated rider.

Legal Basis: Article VI, Section 25(2) limits provisions in a GAA (noun) to matters specifically related to an appropriation. Araullo v. Aquino explains the constitutional limits on appropriations and inappropriate provisions.

Application: Changing the statutory allocation formula is substantive general legislation. It is not merely a condition on a particular appropriation and should be enacted through an amendatory law.

Conclusion: The proposed distribution provision is an unconstitutional rider.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article VI, Section 25(2); Araullo v. Aquino III, G.R. No. 209287, July 1, 2014: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/57044
records.Controlling Doctrine: A GAA provision must relate specifically to a particular appropriation; substantive amendments to permanent law are prohibited riders.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Topic: Qualified Political Agency — Ex Officio Board Members
records.Essay Question:
MVL (noun), a government-owned corporation, had three Cabinet Secretaries (noun) as ex officio directors. Its Board (noun) approved added benefits for corporate officers and employees without prior presidential approval.

The Commission on Audit (COA) (noun) disallowed the benefits. The Board (noun) invoked the alter-ego doctrine because the Cabinet Secretaries (noun) voted for the resolution.

Was COA (noun) correct? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. COA (noun) was correct.

Legal Basis: The qualified-political-agency doctrine applies to department acts performed as presidential alter egos, not automatically to separate corporate-board acts. National Power Corporation Board of Directors v. COA rejects the attribution of ex officio board votes to the President.

Application: The Cabinet Secretaries (noun) voted as MVL Board (noun) members by virtue of office. Their votes were corporate acts and did not substitute for the distinct presidential approval required by law.

Conclusion: The benefits lacked the required approval and were properly disallowed.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: National Power Corporation Board of Directors v. Commission on Audit, G.R. No. 218052, January 26, 2021: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/67069
records.Controlling Doctrine: A Cabinet secretary serving ex officio on a GOCC board does not act as the President’s alter ego for every corporate-board decision.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
Kenneth (noun) had a romantic relationship with Mabel (noun), a fourteen-year-old minor, and exchanged sensual conversations, nude photographs, and videos with her online.

Kenneth (noun) left his social-media account open on a rented computer. The next customer viewed the material and reported it to police. Charged under Republic Act No. 11930, Kenneth (noun) objected that the evidence violated his privacy.

Are the photographs and videos admissible? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The constitutional exclusionary rule does not apply to this private discovery.

Legal Basis: The Bill of Rights restricts governmental action. Cadajas v. People holds that evidence obtained by a private person, without police participation, is not excluded under the constitutional search-and-privacy guarantees.

Application: The next customer, not a police officer or state agent, encountered the open account and reported the material. The facts show no government instigation in obtaining it.

Conclusion: Kenneth’s (noun) constitutional objection fails, and the material is admissible subject to ordinary evidentiary rules.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article III, Sections 2 and 3; Cadajas v. People, G.R. No. 247348, November 16, 2021: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68092
records.Controlling Doctrine: The constitutional exclusionary rule generally applies to state action, not evidence independently obtained by a private individual.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
The Republic of Handskaland (noun), through Ambassador Hansen (noun), contracted with Hardee Services Corporation (HSC) (noun) to maintain and repair electrical facilities of its Philippine embassy.

After the Ambassador (noun) terminated the contract for faulty work, HSC (noun) sued for damages and claimed that entering the contract waived immunity.

Did the Republic (noun) and Ambassador (noun) waive immunity from suit? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The contract did not amount to an implied waiver.

Legal Basis: Under restrictive sovereign immunity, consent may be inferred from a commercial act but not from an act performed in sovereign capacity. Republic of Indonesia v. Vinzon treated contracts necessary to embassy operations as governmental in character.

Application: Maintaining embassy electrical facilities is essential to diplomatic functions. The Republic (noun) and Ambassador (noun) acted in a sovereign, not ordinary commercial, capacity.

Conclusion: They retained immunity from suit absent express consent.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Generally accepted principles of international law; Republic of Indonesia v. Vinzon, G.R. No. 154705, June 26, 2003: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/48858
records.Controlling Doctrine: A foreign state does not impliedly waive immunity by entering a contract that is governmental and necessary to embassy operations.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Topic: Acquittal — Grave Abuse and Double Jeopardy
records.Essay Question:
The Regional Trial Court (RTC) (noun) convicted Luciano (noun) of illegal sale of dangerous drugs. On reconsideration, it issued a brief order acquitting him, stating only that the prosecution had failed to overcome the presumption of innocence.

The Office of the Solicitor General (OSG) (noun) sought certiorari, alleging that the order failed to state facts and law. Luciano (noun) invoked double jeopardy.

Did the RTC (noun) commit grave abuse of discretion? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The conclusory order was constitutionally defective and may be annulled through certiorari.

Legal Basis: Article VIII, Section 14 requires a decision to state clearly and distinctly its factual and legal bases. Austria v. AAA holds that an acquittal issued with grave abuse amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction is void and does not trigger double-jeopardy protection.

Application: The RTC (noun) reversed a conviction without identifying the evidence, factual findings, or governing law. That failure prevented meaningful review and exceeded constitutional adjudicatory bounds.

Conclusion: The RTC (noun) gravely abused its discretion; certiorari may proceed without violating double jeopardy.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article VIII, Section 14; Austria v. AAA, G.R. No. 205275, June 28, 2022: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68436
records.Controlling Doctrine: A void acquittal rendered with grave abuse of discretion is not an acquittal in the constitutional sense and may be challenged by Rule 65 certiorari.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Topic: Academic Freedom and Taking — Mandatory Tuition Waiver
records.Essay Question:
The “Ang Nars Incentives Act of 2023” (noun) allowed children of Filipino nurses to enroll in any private tertiary institution without an entrance examination, provided they maintained the required average. It also required a seventy-percent tuition waiver, only part of which could be credited against national taxes.

Is the law constitutional? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The law is unconstitutional.

Legal Basis: Article XIV, Section 5(2) protects institutional academic freedom, including determining who may be admitted. Article III, Section 9 also requires just compensation when private property is taken for public use. OSG v. Ayala distinguishes regulation from a compensable taking.

Application: Compelling schools to admit applicants without their admissions process invades academic freedom. Requiring a partly uncompensated tuition waiver also transfers the public program’s cost to private institutions.

Conclusion: The law violates institutional academic freedom and, to the extent of the uncompensated mandate, the just-compensation clause.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article XIV, Section 5(2), and Article III, Section 9; Office of the Solicitor General v. Ayala Land, Inc., G.R. No. 177056, September 18, 2009: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/49990
records.Controlling Doctrine: The State may regulate education, but it cannot dictate admissions in derogation of institutional academic freedom or appropriate private value for public use without compensation.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Office of the Solicitor General v. Ayala Land, Inc.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Topic: Legislative Vacancy — Mandamus and Special Elections
records.Essay Question:
Sulu Second District Representative Alfonso (noun) died during the second year of his term. House Speaker Rodil (noun) designated Sulu First District Representative Midas (noun) as legislative caretaker.

At the request of constituents, Alfonso’s (noun) party petitioned for mandamus to compel Speaker Rodil (noun) to call a special election.

Will the petition prosper? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The petition will not prosper.

Legal Basis: Article VI, Section 9 provides that a special election “may” be called in the manner provided by law. Mandamus compels a ministerial duty, not the exercise of legislative discretion. Marcos v. Robredo explains the ordinarily permissive effect of “may.”

Application: No law imposes on Speaker Rodil (noun) a clear, personal, ministerial duty to call the election. Calling and providing for a special election requires discretionary legislative action.

Conclusion: Mandamus cannot issue.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article VI, Section 9; Marcos v. Robredo, P.E.T. Case No. 005, October 15, 2019, as discussed in G.R. No. 244587: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68832
records.Controlling Doctrine: Mandamus cannot compel an act that the Constitution or statute leaves discretionary, particularly legislative action to provide for a special election.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Topic: Presidential Succession — Reelection and Four-Year Bar
records.Essay Question:
President Priscilla (noun) resigned during her fifteenth month in office. Vice-President Teodoro (noun) succeeded as President (noun). Congress (noun), voting separately by majority of all members of each House, confirmed former President and incumbent Senator Angel (noun) as Vice-President (noun).

In 2028, may Teodoro (noun) and Angel (noun) both run for President of the Philippines (noun)? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Neither may run.

Legal Basis: Article VII, Section 4 bars any President from reelection and bars a successor who served as President for more than four years from later election to the same office. Pormento v. Estrada interprets the constitutional ban on presidential reelection.

Application: Teodoro (noun) will have served more than four years of Priscilla’s (noun) term. Angel (noun) was previously elected President (noun), so another election would be reelection prohibited by the text.

Conclusion: Both are constitutionally disqualified.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article VII, Section 4; Pormento v. Estrada, G.R. No. 191988, August 31, 2010: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/54308
records.Controlling Doctrine: A person elected President is barred from any reelection, while a successor who serves more than four years is barred from election to the same office.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
A proposed Bangsamoro Electoral Code (noun) would create a Bangsamoro Parliament Electoral Tribunal (noun) as sole judge of contests concerning the election, returns, and qualifications of members of Parliament (noun).

Is the proposed provision constitutional? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The proposed tribunal would displace jurisdiction assigned by the Constitution to COMELEC (noun).

Legal Basis: Article IX-C, Section 2(2) gives COMELEC (noun) exclusive original jurisdiction over contests involving elective regional officials. Sema v. COMELEC, as applied in later E-Library jurisprudence, confirms that autonomous arrangements remain subject to constitutional allocation of election jurisdiction.

Application: Bangsamoro parliament members are elective regional officials. A regional code cannot transfer their election contests from COMELEC (noun) to a newly created tribunal.

Conclusion: The proposed provision is unconstitutional.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
Hector (noun), a government employee, asked Ignacio (noun) to take the Police Officer I Examination (noun) for him. The Civil Service Commission (CSC) (noun) found impersonation and dismissed Hector (noun) for dishonesty.

Hector (noun) argued that Republic Act No. 8551 transferred all authority over police entrance and promotional examinations to the National Police Commission (noun).

Is Hector (noun) correct? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The CSC (noun) retained disciplinary authority over civil-service examination fraud.

Legal Basis: Article IX-B makes the CSC (noun) the central personnel agency. San Felix v. Civil Service Commission holds that Republic Act No. 8551 did not completely divest the CSC of jurisdiction over anomalies and irregularities in civil-service examinations.

Application: Administering police examinations may be assigned to NAPOLCOM (noun), but Hector’s (noun) dishonest impersonation remains a civil-service offense within CSC (noun) authority.

Conclusion: The CSC (noun) validly investigated and disciplined Hector (noun).

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
For an investigation of work-related misconduct, the Presidential Management Staff (PMS) (noun) searched employee Zenaida’s (noun) government-owned office computer without her consent or a warrant. Personal files found on it were used to dismiss her.

Zenaida (noun) claimed violations of privacy and the right against unreasonable searches.

What legal advice should she receive? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Her constitutional challenge is unlikely to succeed on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 2 prohibits unreasonable searches. Pollo v. Constantino-David applies the two-part reasonable-expectation-of-privacy test to a government workplace and permits a work-related search reasonable in inception and scope.

Application: The computer belonged to the government, the inquiry concerned work misconduct, and no facts show measures creating a recognized private sphere or an excessively broad search.

Conclusion: Zenaida (noun) had no reasonable expectation sufficient to invalidate the search on these facts.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article III, Sections 2 and 3; Pollo v. Constantino-David, G.R. No. 181881, October 18, 2011: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/31015
records.Controlling Doctrine: A government employee’s workplace privacy claim depends on a reasonable expectation of privacy and the reasonableness of the employer’s work-related search.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Topic: Just Compensation — Delay, Inflation, and Interest
records.Essay Question:
Anne’s (noun) property was taken for public use more than ten years ago without proper expropriation proceedings or payment. The peso later depreciated and inflation increased.

Anne (noun) argued that inflation and peso depreciation should be included in computing her delayed just compensation.

Is she correct? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No as to valuation by inflation, but she is entitled to legal interest for delay.

Legal Basis: Just compensation is generally the property’s fair value at the time of taking. Land Bank v. Phil-Agro Development Farmers Association holds that inflation is not added to valuation because delay is compensated by interest.

Application: Repricing the property by later inflation would depart from the time-of-taking rule. The government must instead pay the proper principal compensation plus applicable interest for the period of delay.

Conclusion: Inflation and currency depreciation are not separate valuation components; interest supplies the delay compensation.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article III, Section 9; Land Bank of the Philippines v. Phil-Agro Development Farmers Association, G.R. No. 193987, March 13, 2017: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/62903
records.Controlling Doctrine: Delayed just compensation is valued at the time of taking and made fully compensatory through legal interest, not later inflation indexing.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Land Bank of the Philippines v. Phil-Agro Development Farmers Association

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
Ricardo (noun), a third-year law student under custodial investigation for rape, was informed of his rights. Claiming that he understood them, he orally waived counsel and gave a written confession without a lawyer present.

At trial, Atty. Alexander (noun) objected to the confession.

Is the objection tenable? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The confession is inadmissible.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 12 requires any waiver of custodial rights to be in writing and made in the presence of counsel. People v. Reyes restates that an extrajudicial confession must be voluntary, express, in writing, and made with competent independent counsel.

Application: Ricardo’s (noun) legal education did not substitute for counsel. His waiver was oral and occurred without a lawyer; the resulting statement was obtained in violation of constitutional requirements.

Conclusion: The objection should be sustained.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article III, Section 12; People v. Reyes, G.R. No. 178300, March 17, 2009: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/49004
records.Controlling Doctrine: Custodial rights may be waived only in writing and in the presence of counsel; legal knowledge does not excuse either requirement.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
Maasikaso Water Company (MWC) (noun), a private concessionaire of the Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System (MWSS) (noun), was accused of violating the Clean Water Act (noun) by failing to provide adequate sewage and septage-treatment facilities in Manila (noun).

MWC (noun) argued that the City of Manila (noun) first had to provide land and access under Section 7 of the Act.

Is MWC (noun) correct? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The local government’s duty is not a condition precedent to the concessionaire’s own statutory obligations.

Legal Basis: Republic Act No. 9275 requires water concessionaires to provide adequate sewerage and septage systems. Maynilad Water Services v. DENR applies the public-trust doctrine and rejects the argument that local-government nonperformance under Section 7 excuses the concessionaires.

Application: MWC (noun) remains bound by its concession and the Clean Water Act (noun). Manila’s (noun) alleged failure does not erase MWC’s (noun) independent duty to protect water resources and public health.

Conclusion: MWC (noun) cannot obtain absolution on that ground.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Republic Act No. 9275; Maynilad Water Services, Inc. v. Secretary of DENR, G.R. Nos. 202897, 206823, and 207969, August 6, 2019: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/65416
records.Controlling Doctrine: A water concessionaire’s Clean Water Act obligations are independent; an LGU’s land-access duty is not a condition precedent that excuses noncompliance.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Maynilad Water Services, Inc. v. Secretary of DENR

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
Lorenzo (noun) was reelected Mayor of Roxas City (noun) for a third consecutive term in 2022. In 2023, the Office of the Ombudsman (OMB) (noun) charged him administratively for acts during his second term.

Lorenzo (noun) argued that reelection condoned the earlier misconduct.

Is he correct? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Reelection no longer condones prior-term administrative misconduct.

Legal Basis: Article XI, Section 1 declares public office a public trust. Carpio-Morales v. Court of Appeals abandoned the condonation doctrine for lacking constitutional or statutory basis, prospectively from finality of that ruling.

Application: Lorenzo’s (noun) alleged acts and reelection occurred years after the doctrine’s abandonment became effective. His new mandate did not erase administrative liability.

Conclusion: The OMB (noun) case may proceed.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article XI, Section 1; Carpio-Morales v. Court of Appeals, G.R. Nos. 217126-27, November 10, 2015: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/61377
records.Controlling Doctrine: Reelection is not a mode of extinguishing administrative liability; the condonation doctrine has been prospectively abandoned.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
Chief Justice Urduja (noun) was removed by impeachment and disqualified from public office. Criminal, administrative, and civil cases followed, but she died while they were pending.

Her heirs sought accrued judicial retirement benefits. Senate President Francisco (noun) argued that impeachment required denial.

Is Francisco (noun) correct? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Impeachment alone does not forfeit accrued retirement benefits.

Legal Basis: Article XI, Section 3(7) limits impeachment judgment to removal and disqualification, without adjudicating separate criminal, civil, or administrative liability. In re Letter of Mrs. Corona holds that benefits are not forfeited merely by impeachment where no separate liability and forfeiture were finally established before death.

Application: Urduja’s (noun) other cases remained pending when she died. The impeachment judgment did not itself impose forfeiture of retirement benefits.

Conclusion: Her heirs may receive the accrued benefits, subject to any independently established lawful deductions.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article XI, Section 3(7); In re Letter of Mrs. Ma. Cristina Roco Corona, A.M. No. 20-07-10-SC, January 12, 2021: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/66776
records.Controlling Doctrine: Impeachment determines removal and disqualification only; forfeiture or other liability requires a separate final legal determination.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: In re Letter of Mrs. Ma. Cristina Roco Corona

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
Congress (noun) required biometric voter registration. COMELEC (noun) resolutions provided that voters who failed to submit complete biometrics before the May 2025 elections would be deactivated and unable to vote.

A petition alleged that biometric validation was an additional substantive qualification beyond the Constitution.

Will the petition prosper? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Biometrics validation regulates registration; it is not a prohibited substantive qualification.

Legal Basis: Article V, Section 1 allows statutory regulation of suffrage while forbidding literacy, property, or other substantive requirements. Kabataan Party-List v. COMELEC sustained mandatory biometrics as a reasonable registration measure.

Application: The requirement verifies voter identity and cleans the registry. It does not add a literacy, property, or comparable qualification to citizenship, age, residence, or voter eligibility.

Conclusion: The constitutional challenge fails.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article V, Section 1; Republic Act No. 10367; Kabataan Party-List v. COMELEC, G.R. No. 221318, December 16, 2015: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/61471
records.Controlling Doctrine: Biometric validation is a permissible registration mechanism, not an additional substantive qualification for suffrage.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Topic: Search and Seizure — Arrest for Ordinance Violation
records.Essay Question:
A police officer saw Harvey (noun) urinating in public, an act punishable by a local ordinance with a PHP 500 fine. After an exchange, the officer arrested Harvey (noun), brought him to the station, and frisked him.

The frisk revealed an unlicensed .38-caliber revolver and live ammunition. Charged with qualified illegal possession of firearms, Harvey (noun) objected that the items resulted from an illegal search. The prosecution invoked search incident to lawful arrest.

Was the search and seizure valid? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The search was not incident to a lawful arrest.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 2 protects against unreasonable searches. Rule 113, Section 5 permits warrantless arrest only in specified circumstances. Luz v. People holds that when an offense is punishable only by a fine and the arrest is unauthorized, a later search cannot be justified as incident to that arrest.

Application: The ordinance imposed only a fine, and the facts do not show another lawful ground for custodial arrest. The station frisk therefore rested on an invalid arrest.

Conclusion: The firearm and ammunition were illegally seized and are inadmissible under the exclusionary rule.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article III, Sections 2 and 3; Rule 113, Section 5; Luz v. People, G.R. No. 197788, February 29, 2012: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/33179
records.Controlling Doctrine: A search incident to arrest is valid only if the arrest itself is lawful; an unauthorized arrest for a fine-only ordinance violation cannot support the search.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
A city ordinance required owners to remove, at their expense, outdoor advertising in regulated areas and billboards made of substandard materials or obstructing road signs and traffic signals. Noncompliance authorized removal by the mayor with police assistance.

ABC Ad Agency (noun), whose billboards were removed, sued on the theory that the action took private property without just compensation.

Will the complaint prosper? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The removal described is a police-power regulation, not a compensable taking.

Legal Basis: Local governments may regulate property under the general-welfare clause. Knights of Rizal v. DMCI Homes discusses the distinction between legitimate land-use or aesthetic regulation and eminent domain, while recognizing the regulation of structures affecting public welfare.

Application: The ordinance targets location, structural safety, and obstruction of public traffic signs. These are public-safety and thoroughfare concerns, and the owner bears the cost of curing noncompliance.

Conclusion: On the stated facts, removal does not require just compensation.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Local Government Code, Sections 16 and 458; Knights of Rizal v. DMCI Homes, Inc., G.R. No. 213948, April 25, 2017: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/63069
records.Controlling Doctrine: Reasonable regulation or removal of unsafe and obstructive billboards under police power is not a taking requiring compensation.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Knights of Rizal v. DMCI Homes, Inc.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
Civil-society groups organized a rally concerning China’s (noun) occupation of the Spratly Islands (noun) on a vacant private lot. Before it began, police ordered the organizers to stop for security reasons and lack of a mayor’s permit.

When the organizers continued, police dispersed the crowd and arrested the leaders.

Did the police violate the group’s right to peaceful assembly? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. A public-assembly permit was not required for a rally on private property with the owner’s consent.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 4 protects peaceful assembly. Batas Pambansa Blg. 880, Section 4 requires only the owner’s consent for an assembly on private property. Chavez v. Gonzales, discussing Bayan v. Ermita, emphasizes that government cannot impose prior restraint without a constitutionally sufficient basis.

Application: The stated justification was general “security” and absence of a mayor’s permit, although the venue was private. No specific clear and present danger or unlawful conduct appears.

Conclusion: Dispersal and arrests on those grounds violated the right of peaceful assembly.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article III, Section 4; Batas Pambansa Blg. 880, Section 4; Chavez v. Gonzales, G.R. No. 168338, February 15, 2008: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/56004
records.Controlling Doctrine: An assembly on private property requires the owner’s consent, not a mayor’s public-place permit; vague security claims do not justify prior restraint.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
Assume the same peaceful rally concerning the Spratly Islands (noun) was held in a duly established freedom park rather than on private property.

Could police lawfully disperse it solely because the organizers lacked a mayor’s permit? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. No permit is required for a peaceful assembly in a duly established freedom park.

Legal Basis: Batas Pambansa Blg. 880, Section 4 expressly exempts assemblies in freedom parks from the permit requirement. Chavez v. Gonzales reinforces the strong presumption against prior restraints on protected expression.

Application: Because the venue is a freedom park, lack of a mayor’s permit supplies no lawful basis for dispersal. The facts identify no violence or other statutory ground to terminate the assembly.

Conclusion: Dispersal solely for want of a permit would violate the constitutional right.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article III, Section 4; Batas Pambansa Blg. 880, Section 4; Chavez v. Gonzales, G.R. No. 168338, February 15, 2008: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/56004
records.Controlling Doctrine: A peaceful assembly in a duly established freedom park is exempt from the public-assembly permit requirement.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
The K-12 Law (noun) strengthened the curriculum and added two years of high school. Parents of science-high-school students challenged the law under equal protection, arguing that their gifted and advanced children formed a distinct class able to learn faster.

Is the parents’ contention tenable? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The proposed exemption lacks a classification germane to the law’s nationwide educational purpose.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 1 permits reasonable classification that rests on substantial distinctions, is germane to the law, applies to all members of the class, and is not limited to existing conditions. British American Tobacco v. Camacho applies this test.

Application: Attendance at a science high school does not by itself establish a distinction requiring exemption from the national K-12 structure. The program uniformly regulates students similarly situated within basic education.

Conclusion: The equal-protection challenge fails.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article III, Section 1; British American Tobacco v. Camacho, G.R. No. 163583, April 15, 2009: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/49123
records.Controlling Doctrine: Equal protection allows uniform education regulation unless the proposed different treatment rests on a substantial distinction germane to the law’s purpose.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
President Hidalgo (noun) signed the Philippines’ (noun) ratification of the Rome Statute (noun) and sent the treaty to the Senate (noun). Senator Dalisay (noun) introduced a resolution of concurrence, which was read on three separate days, distributed in final form, and unanimously approved.

A group challenged the concurrence because a resolution, unlike a bill, does not become law.

How should the petition be resolved? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The petition should be dismissed.

Legal Basis: Article VII, Section 21 requires concurrence by at least two-thirds of all senators but does not require enactment of a statute. Bayan Muna v. Romulo distinguishes treaty-making from ordinary legislation and recognizes the President’s ratification role subject to Senate concurrence.

Application: The Senate (noun) was not legislating a new statute; it was expressing the constitutional consent required for ratification. A resolution is the appropriate vehicle for that single-chamber act.

Conclusion: The concurrence is not void merely because it was expressed through a resolution.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article VII, Section 21; Bayan Muna v. Romulo, G.R. No. 159618, February 1, 2011: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/52149
records.Controlling Doctrine: Senate treaty concurrence is a constitutional consent function, not ordinary bicameral lawmaking, and may be expressed by resolution.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
After martial law was declared over Mindanao (noun), police arrested Jose Maria (noun) without a warrant while he shopped for groceries. He had no pending case and was committing no offense.

Police argued that martial law suspended the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus and allowed warrantless arrests.

Are they correct? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Martial law does not itself authorize warrantless arrest.

Legal Basis: Article VII, Section 18 states that martial law does not suspend the Constitution or automatically suspend the writ privilege. Lagman v. Medialdea confirms that the Bill of Rights remains operative. Warrantless arrest must independently satisfy Rule 113, Section 5.

Application: Jose Maria (noun) was not caught committing an offense, was not the subject of a valid hot pursuit, and was not an escaped prisoner.

Conclusion: His warrantless arrest was illegal.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article VII, Section 18; Rule 113, Section 5; Lagman v. Medialdea, G.R. Nos. 231658 et al., July 4, 2017: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/63533
records.Controlling Doctrine: A declaration of martial law does not suspend the Bill of Rights or create a free-standing power of warrantless arrest.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
A statute exempted the Land Bank of the Philippines (LBP) (noun) from filing fees in loan-collection cases. The Office of the Court Administrator (OCA) (noun) directed courts to continue collecting the fees because only the Supreme Court (noun) may determine exemptions.

LBP (noun) argued that Congress (noun) validly enacted the exemption and that the OCA (noun) violated separation of powers.

Is LBP (noun) correct? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Statutory interference with filing fees and court procedure cannot override the Supreme Court’s exclusive rule-making authority.

Legal Basis: Article VIII, Section 5(5) vests the Supreme Court (noun) with authority over pleading, practice, and procedure. GIOS-SAMAR v. Department of Transportation discusses the exclusivity and constitutional protection of judicial rule-making.

Application: Filing fees are integral to court procedure and fiscal administration. A legislative exemption cannot bind courts contrary to the Court’s rules and administrative directive.

Conclusion: The OCA (noun) may require continued collection; separation of powers supports, rather than defeats, the directive.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article VIII, Section 5(5); GIOS-SAMAR, Inc. v. Department of Transportation and Communications, G.R. No. 217158, March 12, 2019: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/64970
records.Controlling Doctrine: The Supreme Court’s constitutional authority over pleading, practice, and procedure includes control over court filing-fee rules and exemptions.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: GIOS-SAMAR, Inc. v. Department of Transportation and Communications

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
During the COVID-19 pandemic, President Acosta (noun) stated that the Executive Department (noun) could temporarily take over any privately owned public utility or business affected with public interest to address a hospital-bed shortage. She relied on Article XII, Section 17 of the Constitution.

Is President Acosta (noun) correct? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No, not without an enabling law prescribing the takeover’s terms.

Legal Basis: Article XII, Section 17 authorizes the State, during a national emergency and under reasonable terms prescribed by it, to take over qualifying enterprises. David v. Macapagal-Arroyo holds that presidential emergency takeover power requires congressional authorization.

Application: The President (noun) may identify an emergency, but the facts supply no statute delegating takeover authority or prescribing reasonable terms.

Conclusion: The Executive Department (noun) cannot unilaterally exercise the asserted takeover power.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article XII, Section 17, and Article VI, Section 23(2); David v. Macapagal-Arroyo, G.R. Nos. 171396 et al., May 3, 2006: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/41473
records.Controlling Doctrine: A presidential takeover of privately owned public utilities or businesses during an emergency requires legislative authorization and prescribed reasonable terms.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Topic: Citizenship and Candidacy — Foreign Certificate and Passport
records.Essay Question:
Lemuel (noun) was born in 1988 to a Filipino mother and an American father who were unmarried. His father later petitioned for him, and Lemuel (noun) received a certificate of American citizenship and an American passport.

In 2022, Lemuel (noun) filed to run as Representative of Batanes (noun). Ayla (noun) sought his disqualification as an American citizen.

Is Ayla (noun) correct? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No, on the stated facts alone.

Legal Basis: Article IV, Section 1 makes those whose fathers or mothers are Filipino citizens of the Philippines. Albania v. COMELEC, applying Arnado and related dual-citizenship doctrine, distinguishes possession of foreign status documents from the acts legally required to renounce or lose Philippine citizenship.

Application: Lemuel (noun) acquired Philippine citizenship at birth through his Filipino mother. The facts show receipt, but not use, of the American passport and no effective renunciation of Philippine citizenship.

Conclusion: Ayla’s (noun) allegation does not establish ineligibility.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article IV, Section 1; Republic Act No. 9225; Albania v. COMELEC, G.R. No. 226792, June 8, 2017: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/63084
records.Controlling Doctrine: A dual citizen’s foreign certificate or unused passport does not by itself prove loss or renunciation of Philippine citizenship for candidacy purposes.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Topic: Academic Freedom — Removal of Library Materials
records.Essay Question:
The Commission on Higher Education (CHED) (noun) directed higher-education institutions to remove library materials containing “pervasive ideologies of Communist Terrorist Groups,” asserting that the materials could radicalize students against the government.

Does the directive violate institutional academic freedom? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes, on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: Article XIV, Section 5(2) protects academic freedom in institutions of higher learning. Miriam College Foundation v. Court of Appeals recognizes institutional autonomy in determining what may be taught and how academic objectives are pursued, subject only to valid overriding regulation.

Application: CHED’s (noun) directive compels removal based on ideology and rests only on a speculative fear of radicalization. No narrowly supported, overriding public-welfare basis is shown.

Conclusion: The blanket removal directive violates academic freedom.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
Congress (noun) prohibited the sale and distribution of alcoholic drinks within one hundred meters of religious and educational institutions. A city (noun) ordinance extended the restricted distance to one hundred fifty meters.

Is the ordinance valid? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes, if enacted within delegated police power and otherwise reasonable.

Legal Basis: The Local Government Code authorizes local governments to enact measures for general welfare. Batangas CATV, Inc. v. Court of Appeals recognizes that local regulation may supplement national law when it does not contradict or prohibit what the statute permits.

Application: The ordinance retains the national policy and imposes a stricter local buffer; it does not legalize a prohibited act or ban alcohol sales everywhere. The facts show a regulatory, geographically limited measure.

Conclusion: The ordinance is valid on the stated facts.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Local Government Code, Sections 16 and 458; Batangas CATV, Inc. v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 138810, September 29, 2004: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/48194
records.Controlling Doctrine: An LGU may adopt a reasonable supplemental regulation stricter than national law when the measure is within delegated power and does not contradict the statute.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
Under a statute authorizing just and reasonable standards for public-utility vehicles, the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) (noun) promulgated and published a rule that no car older than six years could operate as a taxi.

Taxi operators claimed denial of procedural due process because they received no individual notice and were not invited to file position papers before issuance.

Were they denied procedural due process? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Trial-type notice and hearing were not required for this generally applicable rule.

Legal Basis: Administrative agencies acting quasi-legislatively may issue rules after compliance with statutory publication and filing requirements; individual adjudicatory hearings are ordinarily unnecessary. Sangguniang Panlungsod ng Baguio City v. Jadewell Parking Systems discusses Taxicab Operators and procedural due process in regulatory rule-making.

Application: The rule was promulgated and published for all taxi operators rather than issued to decide a contested case against particular operators. No statute requiring pre-issuance position papers is identified.

Conclusion: The operators were not denied procedural due process.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article III, Section 1; Administrative Code of 1987, Book VII; Sangguniang Panlungsod ng Baguio City v. Jadewell Parking Systems Corporation, G.R. No. 169588, October 7, 2014: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/56914
records.Controlling Doctrine: Generally applicable quasi-legislative rules require statutory publication and filing, not the individual notice and trial-type hearing required in adjudication.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Sangguniang Panlungsod ng Baguio City v. Jadewell Parking Systems Corporation

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Topic: Law of the Sea — Contiguous-Zone Enforcement
records.Essay Question:
A foreign commercial ship was seen by the Philippine Coast Guard (noun) dumping garbage and toxic waste twenty nautical miles from Nasugbu, Batangas (noun), the nearest Philippine coast. Its officers were arrested and charged in the Regional Trial Court of Batangas (noun) under Philippine environmental law.

They moved to dismiss, arguing that the vessel was outside the Philippine territorial sea.

Is the jurisdictional ground correct? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Being outside the twelve-nautical-mile territorial sea does not end the inquiry; the vessel was within the twenty-four-nautical-mile contiguous zone.

Legal Basis: The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, Article 33, permits necessary control in the contiguous zone to prevent or punish infringement of specified coastal-state laws. Republic Act No. 9522 aligns Philippine maritime zones with UNCLOS. Magallona v. Ermita upholds that statutory framework.

Application: At twenty nautical miles, the ship was within the contiguous zone. Dumping toxic waste implicates coastal sanitary and environmental protection, allowing Philippine enforcement under applicable domestic law and treaty limits.

Conclusion: The motion cannot succeed solely because the ship was beyond the territorial sea.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: UNCLOS, Article 33; Republic Act No. 9522; Magallona v. Ermita, G.R. No. 187167, August 16, 2011: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/29267
records.Controlling Doctrine: The Philippines may exercise treaty-authorized control in its contiguous zone; location beyond the territorial sea does not automatically defeat enforcement jurisdiction.

records.Subject: Political and Public International Law
records.Essay Question:
Philippine Medical Center (PMC) (noun), a government hospital created by law and endowed with corporate powers, owns land and buildings in Quezon City (noun). Some properties are leased to private concessionaires.

The Quezon City Assessor (noun) assessed real property tax against PMC (noun), reasoning that the leased properties were not used exclusively for charitable purposes. PMC (noun) claimed exemption as a government instrumentality.

Is PMC (noun) liable for the assessed tax over the leased properties? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. PMC (noun), as a government instrumentality, is not itself liable for the real property tax, although the taxable beneficial users may be assessed as the law permits.

Legal Basis: The Local Government Code exempts Republic-owned property but withdraws the exemption when beneficial use is granted to a taxable person. Philippine Heart Center v. Local Government of Quezon City holds that the instrumentality retains immunity while the private beneficial user bears the tax consequence.

Application: Leasing does not convert PMC (noun) into a taxable private owner. The assessor must direct any lawful assessment concerning beneficial use to the private concessionaires rather than PMC (noun).

Conclusion: PMC (noun) is not liable for the assessment against it.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Local Government Code, Section 234(a); Philippine Heart Center v. Local Government of Quezon City, G.R. No. 225409, March 11, 2020: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/66268
records.Controlling Doctrine: A government instrumentality remains exempt from real property tax; when beneficial use is granted to a taxable private entity, liability attaches to that beneficial user.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Philippine Heart Center v. Local Government of Quezon City

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
Samson Manufacturing, Inc. (noun) insured its own goods with Delilah Insurance (noun) for ₱2,000,000. Alibaba Shipping Co. (noun) insured the same goods with Assured Corp. (noun) for the same amount under its contract of carriage with Samson Manufacturing, Inc. (noun). Both policies stated that any other insurance would not void either policy, but total recovery could not exceed ₱2,000,000 at the time of loss.

Is this a case of double insurance? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The two policies do not constitute double insurance.

Legal Basis: Section 95 of the Insurance Code requires identity of the insured person, subject matter, interest, and risk. Malayan Insurance Co., Inc. v. Philippines First Insurance Co., Inc. recognizes that an owner and a carrier may hold distinct insurable interests over the same goods.

Application: Samson Manufacturing, Inc. (noun) insured its ownership interest. Alibaba Shipping Co. (noun) insured its exposure as carrier. Although the goods and peril overlap, the insured persons and interests do not.

Conclusion: There is no double insurance, although the policies may still limit aggregate recovery according to their terms and the indemnity principle.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Double insurance requires identity of the insured person and insurable interest; an owner’s property interest differs from a carrier’s liability interest.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Malayan Insurance Co., Inc. v. Philippines First Insurance Co., Inc.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
Queenie (noun) and her child, Paeng (noun), boarded a jeepney operated by Emil (noun) and driven by Amor (noun). Queenie (noun) was seated on an empty beer case near the rear exit. On an uphill road, the jeepney slid backward; Queenie’s (noun) foot slipped from the wet step board and was crushed, requiring amputation. She sued Emil (noun) and Amor (noun) for breach of contract of carriage.

Should Emil (noun) and Amor (noun) be held solidarily liable on that cause of action? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. On a claim solely for breach of contract of carriage, the operator is directly liable, while the driver is not a contracting party.

Legal Basis: Articles 1733 and 1755 of the Civil Code require extraordinary diligence from common carriers. Sanico v. Colipano holds that the passenger’s contractual action lies against the carrier or operator; the driver may instead incur quasi-delictual or criminal liability if negligence is established.

Application: The transport contract was between Queenie (noun) and operator Emil (noun). Amor (noun) drove the vehicle but was not a party to that contract.

Conclusion: Emil (noun), not Amor (noun), is answerable on the pleaded contractual cause of action; separate non-contractual claims against the driver remain possible.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Civil Code, Articles 1733 and 1755; Sanico v. Colipano, G.R. No. 209969, September 27, 2017: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/63496
records.Controlling Doctrine: A breach-of-carriage action is contractual against the carrier or operator; the driver’s personal exposure rests on a different cause of action.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
Juan (noun), acting as president of Maharlika Car Dealers Incorporated (MCDI) (noun), entered into a long-term lease with Antonino (noun) over commercial property along Pasong Tamo Avenue (noun). When Antonino (noun) received a better offer and learned that MCDI (noun) was not yet incorporated with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) (noun), he sought to nullify the lease for lack of consent and juridical capacity.

May Juan (noun), for MCDI (noun), insist on the lease’s enforceability against Antonino (noun)? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Antonino (noun) may be held to the transaction under corporation by estoppel.

Legal Basis: Section 20 of the Revised Corporation Code prevents one who assumes an obligation to an ostensible corporation from avoiding it by denying the corporation’s existence. Missionary Sisters of Our Lady of Fatima v. Alzona applies this principle to a person who transacted with a not-yet-incorporated entity.

Application: Antonino (noun) knowingly contracted with MCDI (noun) as the lessee and invoked its non-incorporation only after receiving a better offer.

Conclusion: Juan (noun), acting for MCDI (noun), may enforce the lease against Antonino (noun), subject to the corporation’s adoption and the agents’ statutory liabilities.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Corporation Code, Section 20; Missionary Sisters of Our Lady of Fatima v. Alzona, G.R. No. 224307, August 6, 2018: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/64484
records.Controlling Doctrine: A party who contracts with an ostensible corporation may be estopped from denying its existence to escape the assumed obligation.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
Datu Commercial Corporation (DCC) (noun), a publicly listed company, incorporated Kidlat Close Corporation (KCC) (noun) and subscribed to 91% of its outstanding capital. Three officers of DCC (noun) each held 3%. KCC’s (noun) articles limited shareholders to five, granted a right of first refusal, and barred public listing or offering of its shares.

Is DCC (noun) qualified to be an incorporator of KCC (noun) although it is a juridical entity? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. A corporation may now be an incorporator.

Legal Basis: Section 10 of the Revised Corporation Code allows any person, partnership, association, or corporation, singly or jointly with others but not more than fifteen in number, to organize a corporation for a lawful purpose. The statutory text is published in the Supreme Court E-Library.

Application: DCC (noun) is a corporation and therefore falls within the classes expressly permitted to incorporate KCC (noun). The stated close-corporation restrictions do not disqualify DCC (noun) as an incorporator.

Conclusion: DCC (noun) is qualified to be an incorporator, assuming compliance with the remaining statutory requirements.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
The Board of Directors of Mabini Corporation (MC) (noun) resolved to issue 10,000 fully paid common shares to Atty. Apolinario (noun) for successfully prosecuting a derivative suit for MC (noun). The shares would be issued as stock dividends charged against unrestricted retained earnings.

Would the issuance be valid? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Stock dividends cannot be used to compensate a non-stockholder for legal services.

Legal Basis: Section 42 of the Revised Corporation Code permits stock dividends only with the required stockholder approval and as a distribution to stockholders. Lao v. Lim discusses the statutory requisites and proportional character of stock dividends.

Application: Atty. Apolinario (noun) is described as counsel, not as an MC (noun) stockholder entitled to a dividend. Legal services may support issuance of shares as consideration under Section 61, but not under the guise of a stock dividend.

Conclusion: The proposed issuance as stock dividends is invalid; any lawful share compensation must follow the rules on valid consideration and corporate approvals.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
Dakila Incorporated (DI) (noun) has a seven-member board. Florante (noun) resigned two months into office, and Laura (noun) died in her sixth month, leaving five directors. The one-year terms of the remaining directors then ended without an annual stockholders’ meeting because Laura (noun), the majority stockholder, had died and her estate was unsettled.

May the five holdover directors fill the two board vacancies? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Once their one-year terms ended, the remaining directors held over only by tenure and could not use that status to fill the vacancies.

Legal Basis: Section 28 of the Revised Corporation Code distinguishes vacancies that the remaining board may fill from those caused by expiration of term. Valle Verde Country Club, Inc. v. Africa holds that holdover tenure does not extend the statutory term and that stockholders must fill vacancies after term expiration.

Application: The five directors acted only after their own terms had expired. At that point, the board lacked authority to fill seats for which no unexpired term remained.

Conclusion: The vacancies must be filled through the stockholders in the manner prescribed by law.

records.Controlling Doctrine: A holdover period is tenure, not an extension of the director’s term; stockholders fill vacancies after term expiration.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Valle Verde Country Club, Inc. v. Africa

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
Singha Corporation (SC) (noun), organized under Singapore (noun) law and unlicensed in the Philippines (noun), sued Muni Corporation (MC) (noun) in the Regional Trial Court of Manila (noun) to collect the unpaid balance on a design-consultation contract. SC (noun) alleged an isolated transaction but admitted having filed an earlier collection case against another company. MC (noun) moved to dismiss for lack of capacity to sue.

Will MC’s (noun) motion prosper? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No, on the stated facts. A prior lawsuit alone does not prove that SC (noun) was continuously doing business in the Philippines (noun).

Legal Basis: Section 150 of the Revised Corporation Code bars an unlicensed foreign corporation from maintaining an action only when it is transacting business here. Steelcase, Inc. v. Design International Selections, Inc. requires continuity of commercial dealings and evaluates the attendant circumstances; isolated transactions remain outside the bar.

Application: SC’s (noun) present design contract and one earlier collection suit do not, without facts about recurring local commercial operations, establish continuity of business. MC (noun), having contracted with SC (noun), also cannot use the licensing rule as an instrument of injustice.

Conclusion: The motion should be denied absent competent proof that SC (noun) was doing business locally without a license.

records.Controlling Doctrine: An unlicensed foreign corporation may sue on an isolated transaction; doing business requires continuity shown by the attendant facts.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
Procopio (noun) owns the controlling interest in Ginto Bank (GB) (noun). After examination, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) (noun) placed GB (noun) under receivership for illiquidity and unsafe or unsound banking practices. Procopio (noun) claimed denial of due process because GB (noun) received no prior notice and hearing.

Is Procopio’s (noun) contention correct? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Prior notice and hearing are not indispensable before a bank is summarily placed under receivership on statutory grounds.

Legal Basis: Section 30 of the New Central Bank Act authorizes the Monetary Board (noun) to forbid a bank from doing business and appoint a receiver when the statutory conditions exist. Apex Bancrights Holdings, Inc. v. Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas recognizes the summary nature of the action, subject to judicial review for grave abuse.

Application: BSP’s (noun) examination found illiquidity and unsafe or unsound practices. GB (noun) may challenge the Monetary Board’s (noun) action in the statutory proceeding, but the absence of a pre-receivership hearing does not itself invalidate it.

Conclusion: Procopio’s (noun) due-process objection fails.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Bank receivership may be imposed summarily to protect depositors and the banking system, with post-action judicial review available.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
Jacinto (noun), Governor of Sorsogon (noun), maintained United States-dollar deposits in offshore banks in the Cayman Islands (noun), British Virgin Islands (noun), and Switzerland (noun). Balita Magazine (noun) published an exposé, “Pandora Papers” (noun), detailing the deposits and related investments. Jacinto (noun) filed a criminal complaint for violating Philippine bank-secrecy laws.

Will the complaint prosper? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The stated offshore deposits and magazine publication do not fall within the penal coverage alleged.

Legal Basis: Republic Act No. 6426 protects foreign-currency deposits authorized in Philippine banks and restricts unauthorized inquiry or disclosure by persons connected with those deposits. China Banking Corporation v. Ortega discusses the statute’s confidentiality protection within the Philippine banking system.

Application: The accounts were maintained in foreign offshore banks, not Philippine banks governed by Republic Act No. 6426. The facts also identify a magazine publisher, not a Philippine bank official or employee who disclosed a protected local deposit.

Conclusion: Jacinto’s (noun) complaint under Philippine foreign-currency deposit secrecy law should not prosper on these facts.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
Atty. Diwa (noun) represented Tala (noun) in an estafa case before the Regional Trial Court of Manila (noun). Tala (noun) gave Atty. Diwa (noun) ₱10 million for safekeeping and confidentially admitted that it came from her swindling activities. After a report by Atty. Diwa’s (noun) husband, the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) (noun) demanded disclosure of the transaction, but Atty. Diwa (noun) refused.

May Atty. Diwa (noun) validly refuse to report the transaction? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes, under the suggested-answer treatment of the statutory exclusion, insofar as disclosure would reveal protected client information obtained in the professional relationship.

Legal Basis: Section 3(a) of the Anti-Money Laundering Act, as amended, excludes lawyers acting as independent legal professionals in relation to client information when disclosure would compromise client confidences or the attorney-client relationship. Regala v. Sandiganbayan recognizes the breadth of attorney-client confidentiality, subject to established exceptions.

Application: Tala’s (noun) disclosure was made to her counsel during an ongoing estafa case and concerned the source of funds entrusted to counsel. The demand therefore directly implicates confidential client information. This does not immunize Atty. Diwa (noun) from liability if she knowingly transacts criminal proceeds or assists a continuing crime.

Conclusion: She may refuse the reporting demand on privilege grounds, without prejudice to lawful investigation and the crime-fraud exception on a sufficient factual basis.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Republic Act No. 9160, Section 3(a), as amended; Regala v. Sandiganbayan, G.R. No. 105938, September 20, 1996: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/34080
records.Controlling Doctrine: AMLA reporting does not automatically override protected attorney-client confidences, but privilege does not shield a lawyer’s own participation in crime.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Topic: Insurance — Insurable Interest in Secured Property
records.Essay Question:
Emilio (noun) bought a car from Gregorio (noun) but still owed ₱500,000, payable within one year. To secure the balance, they executed a security agreement compliant with the Personal Property Security Act (PPSA), and Gregorio’s (noun) security interest was perfected.

Who has an insurable interest over the car? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Both Emilio (noun) and Gregorio (noun) have insurable interests, but of different extents.

Legal Basis: Sections 13 and 14 of the Insurance Code recognize insurable interest arising from an existing interest or a relation under which the insured may be damnified. The PPSA recognizes Gregorio’s (noun) perfected security interest. Gaisano Cagayan, Inc. v. Insurance Company of North America explains that different parties may insure distinct economic interests in the same property.

Application: Emilio (noun), as owner, would suffer the loss of the car. Gregorio (noun), as secured creditor, would be prejudiced by destruction of the collateral to the extent of the unpaid secured obligation.

Conclusion: Emilio (noun) may insure the ownership value; Gregorio (noun) may insure up to the amount of his secured exposure.

records.Controlling Doctrine: An owner and a secured creditor may simultaneously hold separate insurable interests in the same property.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Gaisano Cagayan, Inc. v. Insurance Company of North America

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
Diego (noun), a cancer survivor, applied for life insurance from Garantiya Insurance Company (GIC) (noun). Gabriela (noun), the GIC (noun) officer authorized to approve policies, knew of the illness and approved the application on June 1, 2020. Diego (noun) died in a vehicular accident on January 30, 2023. GIC (noun) denied the claim for concealment.

Is the denial proper? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The policy had been in force for more than two years during Diego’s (noun) lifetime, and GIC (noun) is barred from rescinding it for health-related concealment.

Legal Basis: Section 48 of the Insurance Code establishes the two-year incontestability period. Manila Bankers Life Insurance Corporation v. Aban holds that, after the statutory period, concealment or misrepresentation concerning health no longer defeats the policy.

Application: More than two years and seven months elapsed between approval and Diego’s (noun) death. Moreover, Gabriela’s (noun) knowledge as the approving officer is attributable to GIC (noun) within the scope of her authority.

Conclusion: GIC’s (noun) denial on the stated concealment ground is improper.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Insurance Code, Section 48; Manila Bankers Life Insurance Corporation v. Aban, G.R. No. 175666, July 29, 2013: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/56125
records.Controlling Doctrine: After a life policy has been in force for two years during the insured’s lifetime, health-related concealment generally becomes incontestable.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Topic: Transportation — Resort Ferry as Common Carrier
records.Essay Question:
Hari (noun) and Reyna (noun) booked a honeymoon package at Anya Resort (AR) (noun) in Palawan (noun), including transport from Batangas (noun) aboard M/B Prinsesa (noun), owned and operated by AR (noun). Despite PAGASA (noun) storm warnings, the vessel sailed, capsized, and the couple drowned. AR (noun) claimed it was not a common carrier because the boat served only resort guests and charged no separate fare.

Are AR’s (noun) arguments correct? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. AR (noun) operated a common carrier and remained bound to extraordinary diligence.

Legal Basis: Articles 1732 and 1733 of the Civil Code cover transportation offered for compensation to general or limited clientele. Spouses Cruz v. Sun Holidays, Inc. holds that a resort ferry bundled into a tour package is a common carrier even without a separately stated fare.

Application: AR’s (noun) ferry regularly transported paying resort guests, and its compensation was embedded in the package price. Sailing despite PAGASA (noun) warnings is inconsistent with extraordinary diligence.

Conclusion: AR’s (noun) limited-clientele and no-separate-fare defenses fail.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
Kagandahan Corporation (KC) (noun) had sold medicated facial creams under the unregistered mark “Kutis” (noun) in pink, oval containers since 2010. Bighani Corporation (BC) (noun) later sold facial creams made with different ingredients under the same mark and in similar pink, oval containers, although its label identified BC (noun) as manufacturer.

Is BC (noun) liable for unfair competition? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Trademark registration is not indispensable to an unfair-competition action based on passing off.

Legal Basis: Section 168 of the Intellectual Property Code protects the goodwill of goods identified by their general appearance. Kho v. Summerville General Merchandising Co. explains that confusing imitation of the appearance or packaging may constitute unfair competition when calculated to deceive buyers.

Application: BC (noun) copied both KC’s (noun) “Kutis” (noun) name and the distinctive pink, oval packaging. A manufacturer label does not necessarily dispel the likely confusion created at the point of sale.

Conclusion: BC (noun) is liable for unfair competition if the proven overall presentation is likely to pass its creams off as KC’s (noun) goods.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
Atty. Matalas (noun) drafted a deed of sale containing the elements needed to transfer a specifically described parcel of land for a price certain. Impressed by the draft, he intended to use it as a template and obtain copyright registration.

Can Atty. Matalas (noun) secure copyright protection for the deed template? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No, not for the legal transaction or standard form as such.

Legal Basis: Sections 172 and 175 of the Intellectual Property Code protect original expression but not ideas, procedures, systems, or methods of operation. Pearl & Dean (Phil.), Inc. v. Shoemart, Inc. applies the idea-expression distinction and merger principle where protecting the expression would effectively monopolize the underlying method or functional form.

Application: The deed’s operative clauses express the legal requirements of a sale of land. Because those functional concepts can be expressed only in a limited number of conventional ways, copyright cannot be used to monopolize the template’s legal function.

Conclusion: The deed template is not protectable as claimed, although independently original non-functional literary expression may receive only its ordinary, narrow protection.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Intellectual Property Code, Sections 172 and 175; Pearl & Dean (Phil.), Inc. v. Shoemart, Inc., discussed in Juan v. Juan, G.R. No. 221732, August 23, 2017: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/63340
records.Controlling Doctrine: Copyright protects expression, not a functional legal method; where idea and expression merge, protection cannot monopolize the idea.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Topic: Intellectual Property — Copyright and Useful Articles
records.Essay Question:
Julio (noun) registered copyright in a drawing of a light box used in advertisements showing its internal electronic design. Ten years later, Julian (noun) manufactured and sold a physically different light box using the same internal electronic design. Julio (noun) objected, claiming he invented the design.

Is Julio’s (noun) objection valid? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Copyright in the drawing does not confer a patent-like monopoly over the functional light-box design.

Legal Basis: Sections 172 and 175 of the Intellectual Property Code distinguish copyrightable pictorial expression from ideas, systems, and useful mechanisms. Pearl & Dean (Phil.), Inc. v. Shoemart, Inc., as reiterated in Ching v. Salinas, holds that copyright in technical drawings does not protect the useful article depicted.

Application: Julian (noun) made a light box with a different external appearance but similar internal functionality. Julio’s (noun) copyright protects copying of his drawing, not manufacture of the unpatented device.

Conclusion: The copyright objection fails; exclusive rights over the functional invention would require valid patent protection.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Intellectual Property Code, Sections 172 and 175; Ching v. Salinas, G.R. No. 161295, June 29, 2005: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/43469
records.Controlling Doctrine: Copyright in a technical drawing does not extend to the manufacture of the useful article represented in the drawing.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
China Telecommunication Company (CTC) (noun), a Chinese state-owned enterprise, sought to acquire 40% of Duon Telecommunication Corporation (DTC) (noun), a Philippine telecommunications company. Cheng (noun), DTC’s (noun) president, argued that 40% foreign ownership complied with the 1987 Constitution (noun).

Is Cheng’s (noun) argument correct? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The general 40% foreign-equity ceiling does not override the statutory prohibition applicable to a foreign state-owned enterprise investing in critical infrastructure.

Legal Basis: Section 25 of the Public Service Act, as amended by Republic Act No. 11659, prohibits a foreign state-owned enterprise from owning capital stock in a public service classified as critical infrastructure, subject to statutory exceptions. The Act and its implementing rules classify telecommunications as critical infrastructure.

Application: CTC (noun) is state-owned, and DTC (noun) provides telecommunications. The proposed acquisition therefore triggers the special prohibition regardless of its 40% size.

Conclusion: Cheng’s (noun) constitutional-percentage argument is incomplete, and the acquisition is barred absent a statutory exception.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Public Service Act, Section 25, as amended by Republic Act No. 11659; official Supreme Court E-Library text: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/2/94539
records.Controlling Doctrine: Foreign state-owned enterprises are specially barred from owning capital in public services classified as critical infrastructure.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Essay Question:
Seeking to promote Philippine (noun) culture abroad, the President of the Philippines (noun), after consultations and a congressional resolution of support, issued a proclamation granting tax exemptions to entertainment and culinary businesses exporting 70% of their products or services. It also granted income-tax holidays to internationally acclaimed artists, directors, chefs, studios, and authors.

Is the proclamation constitutional? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. A presidential proclamation cannot create tax exemptions without a clear statutory grant.

Legal Basis: Article VI, Section 28(4) of the Constitution requires the concurrence of a majority of all members of Congress for a law granting a tax exemption. John Hay Peoples Alternative Coalition v. Lim invalidated tax exemptions extended by presidential proclamation beyond the authority granted by statute.

Application: A resolution of support is not a tax-exemption law enacted with the constitutionally required concurrence. No statute expressly delegates the exemptions described.

Conclusion: The proclamation’s tax exemptions and incentives are unconstitutional.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article VI, Section 28(4); John Hay Peoples Alternative Coalition v. Lim, G.R. No. 119775, October 24, 2003: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/47416
records.Controlling Doctrine: Tax exemptions must rest on an unmistakable constitutional or statutory grant and cannot be created solely by presidential proclamation.
