records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Essay Question:
Pedro (noun) operated an illegal gambling den called Apolaki (noun) in Intramuros, Manila (noun), earning millions from onsite and online betting. He did not file an income-tax return. Charged under Section 255 of the National Internal Revenue Code (NIRC), Pedro (noun) argued that illegal gambling profits are not income and that reporting them would violate his right against self-incrimination.

Is Pedro’s (noun) argument tenable? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Illegal gains are taxable income, and the privilege against self-incrimination does not create a blanket exemption from filing a return.

Legal Basis: Sections 23, 32, and 255 of the NIRC tax income from whatever source and penalize willful failure to file. People v. Mendez explains the independent legal obligation to pay tax and the elements of a Section 255 prosecution.

Application: Pedro (noun) realized economic gain from gambling operations. He could comply with the tax law without supplying unnecessary incriminating detail and invoke the privilege only against specific compelled disclosures presenting a real danger of prosecution.

Conclusion: His illegal profits are taxable, and his asserted blanket excuse for non-filing is untenable.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: NIRC, Sections 23, 32, and 255; People v. Mendez, G.R. Nos. 208310-11 and 208662, March 28, 2023: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69095
records.Controlling Doctrine: Illegality of the income source does not remove the tax obligation; self-incrimination is not a blanket defense to filing.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Essay Question:
Marites (noun), chief executive officer and sole shareholder of Tsismis Ngayon OPC (TNO) (noun), employed her daughter Laya (noun) as a two-month intern performing simple press-room tasks. TNO (noun) then granted Laya (noun) a ₱2 million bonus, which she used to buy a car.

May TNO (noun) deduct the ₱2 million bonus? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The amount is not shown to be reasonable compensation or an ordinary and necessary business expense.

Legal Basis: Section 34(A)(1) of the NIRC allows ordinary and necessary expenses, including reasonable compensation for services actually rendered. ING Bank N.V. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue emphasizes that deductions are strictly construed and must be substantiated, while compensation must be reasonable in relation to the services.

Application: Laya’s (noun) brief internship and routine tasks bear no reasonable relationship to a ₱2 million bonus. Her close relationship to the sole shareholder further requires careful proof that the payment was genuine compensation rather than a personal benefit.

Conclusion: TNO (noun) cannot deduct the bonus on the stated facts.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: NIRC, Section 34(A)(1); ING Bank N.V. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 167679, July 22, 2015: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/60762
records.Controlling Doctrine: Deductible compensation must be for services actually rendered, reasonable in amount, ordinary and necessary, and properly substantiated.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: ING Bank N.V. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Essay Question:
Ikapati Corporation (IC) (noun), a value-added-tax-registered seller of instant noodles, credited its success partly to tax counsel Atty. Mahal (noun). To show appreciation, IC (noun) transferred 1,000 boxes of spicy bulalo noodles to Atty. Mahal (noun).

Is the transfer subject to value-added tax (VAT)? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The gratuitous transfer is a transaction deemed sale.

Legal Basis: Section 106(B)(1) of the NIRC treats as a sale the transfer, use, or consumption, outside the ordinary course of business, of goods originally intended for sale or business use. Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Magsaysay Lines, Inc. discusses the statutory deemed-sale rule.

Application: The noodles were inventory held for sale. IC (noun) withdrew and transferred them to its lawyer as a gratuitous benefit rather than selling them in the regular course.

Conclusion: The transfer is subject to VAT as a deemed sale, measured under the applicable valuation rules.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: NIRC, Section 106(B)(1); Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Magsaysay Lines, Inc., G.R. No. 146984, July 28, 2006: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/41526
records.Controlling Doctrine: Business goods withdrawn and transferred outside the ordinary course are subject to VAT as transactions deemed sale.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Magsaysay Lines, Inc.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Essay Question:
Quezon City (noun) assessed real-property taxes on lands, buildings, machinery, and terminal stations registered to the Light Rail Transit Authority (LRTA) (noun). After nonpayment, the city issued a notice of delinquency and warrants of levy. LRTA (noun) asserted that it operates the national rail system and that the Republic of the Philippines (noun) is the true owner.

Is LRTA (noun) exempt from real-property tax? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes, for property owned by the Republic of the Philippines (noun) and devoted to public use, subject to the beneficial-use exception.

Legal Basis: Section 234(a) of the Local Government Code exempts real property owned by the Republic, unless beneficial use is granted to a taxable person. Light Rail Transit Authority v. Quezon City holds that LRTA (noun) is a government instrumentality and that its public-use properties belong to the Republic.

Application: The assessed rail lands, stations, and machinery are held for the national light-rail system. No taxable private beneficial user is identified in the facts.

Conclusion: LRTA (noun) is exempt from the assessment as stated.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Local Government Code, Section 234(a); Light Rail Transit Authority v. Quezon City, G.R. No. 221626, October 9, 2019: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/66014
records.Controlling Doctrine: Real property of a government instrumentality owned by the Republic and used for public purposes is exempt, unless beneficial use is granted to a taxable person.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
Nympha (noun), a famous author, collaborated with Tobias (noun), a novice illustrator, on a children’s book. Nympha (noun) supplied the manuscript, inspiration, specifications, and instructions; Tobias (noun) rendered the characters without charge. Nympha (noun) published the book and claimed sole copyright because Tobias (noun) followed her ideas.

Is Nympha (noun) the copyright owner of the images or drawings? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Tobias (noun), not Nympha (noun), is the author of the illustrations.

Legal Basis: Section 175 of the Intellectual Property Code excludes ideas and concepts from copyright protection. Republic v. Heirs of Tupaz IV holds that authorship belongs to the person who uses skill and labor to give concrete expression to an idea.

Application: Nympha (noun) supplied concepts and directions, but Tobias (noun) created the visual expression. His gratuitous service does not transfer authorship or copyright absent a valid legal basis for transfer.

Conclusion: Nympha (noun) owns the text, while Tobias (noun) owns the copyright in the drawings, subject to any proven agreement.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Intellectual Property Code, Sections 171.1 and 175; Republic v. Heirs of Tupaz IV, G.R. No. 197335, September 7, 2020: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/23/69955
records.Controlling Doctrine: Copyright protects concrete expression, and authorship belongs to the person who creates that expression rather than merely supplies the underlying idea.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
The Nova Family (noun) organized North Nova, Inc. (NNI) (noun) in 1984 with a forty-year corporate term ending August 31, 2024. The board did not renew the term, but the family continued NNI’s (noun) operations. Rival South Moon, Inc. (SMI) (noun) argued that NNI (noun) first had to revive its corporate existence.

Are NNI’s (noun) continued operations valid? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. NNI’s (noun) term was converted to perpetual existence by operation of law.

Legal Basis: Section 11 of the Revised Corporation Code provides perpetual existence and deems corporations existing before its effectivity to have perpetual terms unless they timely elect to retain a specific term. The official statute is published in the Supreme Court E-Library.

Application: Nothing indicates that NNI’s (noun) stockholders elected to retain the forty-year term within the statutory transition period. No articles amendment was needed for the automatic conversion.

Conclusion: NNI (noun) continued to exist beyond August 31, 2024, and its operations were valid.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Corporation Code, Section 11; Republic Act No. 11232: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/2/86463
records.Controlling Doctrine: Pre-existing corporations acquired perpetual existence automatically unless they timely elected to retain their fixed term.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
Ernest Bicycle Corporation (EBC) (noun) and Max Speed Corporation (MSC) (noun) sold leading electric-bicycle models at ₱25,000. Gryffin Pedals, Inc. (GPI) (noun) entered in 2023, sold comparable models online for ₱20,000 without physical stores, and reached a 75% market share in one year. EBC (noun) and MSC (noun) complained to the Philippine Competition Commission (PCC) (noun) that GPI (noun) was monopolizing the market.

Will the complaint prosper on those facts? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Dominance by itself is not unlawful; abuse must be proved.

Legal Basis: Section 15 of the Philippine Competition Act prohibits abuse of dominant position, not the legitimate acquisition of market share through superior efficiency or business acumen. Philippine Contractors Accreditation Board v. Manila Water Company, Inc. distinguishes market power from unlawful exclusionary conduct.

Application: GPI’s (noun) lower overhead, digital distribution, and lower price explain its market share. The facts do not establish below-cost predatory pricing, exclusionary contracts, or another prohibited abuse.

Conclusion: The complaint cannot prosper solely from GPI’s (noun) 75% share and lower price.

records.Controlling Doctrine: A dominant position is not illegal unless maintained or exercised through conduct that substantially prevents, restricts, or lessens competition.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
Audrey (noun) joined a twenty-four-hour sale on Easy Shopping (noun) offering free shipping and 50% cash back for purchases of at least ₱10,000. Easy Shopping (noun) accepted her orders and marked them “pending payment,” but her digital wallet lacked funds until the next day, after the promotion ended. Audrey (noun) demanded the promotional terms and presented a screenshot; Easy Shopping (noun) argued there was no written contract.

Is the transaction enforceable on the basis of the screenshot? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The electronic transaction and its terms may be proved by an authenticated screenshot, but Audrey (noun) cannot compel benefits conditioned on timely payment that she failed to make.

Legal Basis: Sections 7 and 16 of the Electronic Commerce Act give electronic documents legal effect and allow offer, acceptance, and contract formation to be proved electronically. MCC Industrial Sales Corporation v. Ssangyong Corporation recognizes the evidentiary and contractual effect of electronic communications.

Application: The screenshot may establish the order and acceptance subject to “pending payment.” Audrey’s (noun) insufficient funds prevented performance of the payment condition during the sale period.

Conclusion: The screenshot defeats the no-writing objection, but it does not entitle Audrey (noun) to expired promotional benefits after her nonpayment.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Electronic Commerce Act, Sections 7 and 16; MCC Industrial Sales Corporation v. Ssangyong Corporation, G.R. No. 170633, October 17, 2007: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/45248
records.Controlling Doctrine: Electronic records can prove a contract, but their enforceability remains subject to the parties’ conditions and performance.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Topic: Corporation by Estoppel — Donation Before Incorporation
records.Essay Question:
Annie (noun), Brenda (noun), Clara (noun), Donna (noun), and Enola (noun) formed Nurturing Family Organization (NFO) (noun) to assist single parents. Before SEC (noun) registration, Gregory (noun) donated land to NFO (noun) in a public instrument, and Clara (noun) accepted in that instrument. NFO (noun) was incorporated in 2023. After Clara’s (noun) death, her heirs included the land in her estate, arguing that NFO (noun) lacked personality when the donation was accepted.

Is the donation to NFO (noun) valid? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The donor is estopped from denying the donee’s existence, and NFO’s (noun) later incorporation and affirmation cured the pre-incorporation defect.

Legal Basis: Section 20 of the Revised Corporation Code embodies corporation by estoppel. Missionary Sisters of Our Lady of Fatima v. Alzona holds that one who assumes an obligation in favor of an ostensible corporation cannot evade it by denying the corporation’s existence after later incorporation and ratification.

Application: Gregory (noun) executed a public donation expressly in NFO’s (noun) favor. NFO (noun) later acquired juridical personality and accepted the benefit through the authority previously exercised for it.

Conclusion: The donation is enforceable for NFO (noun), and Clara’s (noun) heirs cannot treat the land as her personal property.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Corporation Code, Section 20; Missionary Sisters of Our Lady of Fatima v. Alzona, G.R. No. 224307, August 6, 2018: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/64484
records.Controlling Doctrine: Later incorporation and ratification, together with corporation by estoppel, can sustain an obligation undertaken for an ostensible corporation.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
Pierre (noun) and Fonzi (noun) earned ₱2 million each month from illegal Philippine (noun) wildlife trading and delivered the money to Phoebe (noun), an art collector. Phoebe (noun) bought high-value paintings with the funds and auctioned them through galleries. Charged with money laundering, she argued that she did not participate in the wildlife trafficking.

Is Phoebe (noun) criminally liable for money laundering? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Not on the facts as stated, because her knowledge that the funds were criminal proceeds is not established.

Legal Basis: Section 4 of the Anti-Money Laundering Act requires that the accused know that the monetary instrument or property represents, involves, or relates to proceeds of unlawful activity. Lingad v. People applies the statutory elements of money laundering and the required proof of knowledge.

Application: Phoebe (noun) transacted the money by converting it into paintings, but the question supplies no fact showing that she knew its wildlife-trafficking source. Participation in the predicate offense is unnecessary, yet knowledge of the proceeds remains essential.

Conclusion: Absent proof of knowledge beyond reasonable doubt, Phoebe (noun) cannot be convicted.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Anti-Money Laundering Act, Section 4; Lingad v. People, G.R. No. 224945, October 11, 2022: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68639
records.Controlling Doctrine: Money laundering does not require participation in the predicate crime, but it requires knowledge that the property is connected to unlawful activity.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
Nina (noun) and Roxanne (noun) were shareholders of insolvent Essean & Essaiah Corporation (EEC) (noun). Despite three years of insolvency, EEC’s (noun) board distributed dividends and released unpaid stock subscriptions. In 2024, directors and shareholders dissolved EEC (noun) and divided its assets. Creditors sued Nina (noun) and Roxanne (noun), who invoked EEC’s (noun) separate personality and lack of privity.

May the creditors pursue them? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes, to recover unpaid subscriptions and improperly distributed corporate assets within the limits of what they received or owe.

Legal Basis: The trust fund doctrine treats subscribed capital and corporate assets as a fund for creditors, especially upon insolvency or dissolution. Enano-Bote v. Alvarez recognizes a creditor’s direct action against unpaid subscribers when the corporation is insolvent, dissolved, or has condoned subscriptions.

Application: EEC (noun) condoned unpaid subscriptions, distributed dividends while insolvent, and transferred assets on dissolution. Nina (noun) and Roxanne (noun) cannot use separate personality to retain value belonging to the creditor fund.

Conclusion: The creditors may proceed against them for unpaid subscriptions and recoverable distributions.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Corporation Code, Sections 42, 66, and 139; Enano-Bote v. Alvarez, G.R. No. 223572, November 10, 2020: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/66972
records.Controlling Doctrine: Under the trust fund doctrine, corporate creditors may reach unpaid subscriptions and assets improperly distributed during insolvency or dissolution.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
Felix (noun), Ivan (noun), and Ruth (noun) formed a partnership to operate a coffee shop. Felix (noun) and Ivan (noun) contributed capital; Ruth (noun) contributed industry. Felix (noun) opened a plant kiosk inside the shop, Ruth (noun) opened a souvenir shop there, and Ivan (noun) set up a coffee stall two blocks away.

May the partners lawfully engage in those separate businesses? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Felix (noun) may operate the non-competing plant kiosk; Ruth (noun) and Ivan (noun) may not operate their stated businesses without the required permission or contrary stipulation.

Legal Basis: Article 1789 of the Civil Code bars an industrial partner from engaging in business for herself without express partnership permission. Article 1808 bars a capitalist partner from engaging for his own account in the same kind of business, absent a stipulation to the contrary. The Civil Code is published in the Supreme Court E-Library.

Application: Felix’s (noun) plant kiosk does not compete with coffee sales. Ruth (noun), as industrial partner, opened another business without permission. Ivan’s (noun) coffee stall directly competes with the partnership.

Conclusion: Only Felix’s (noun) separate business is lawful on the stated facts.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Civil Code, Articles 1789 and 1808; official Supreme Court E-Library text: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/2/53360
records.Controlling Doctrine: Industrial partners need express permission for a separate business; capitalist partners may not compete in the partnership’s line absent a contrary stipulation.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
Express Innovation Corporation (EIC) (noun) submitted proposed articles of incorporation to the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) (noun). The articles placed EIC’s (noun) principal office in Sakurajima, Konohana Ward, Osaka, Japan (noun), and named Haru Nikko (noun), a resident of Japan (noun), as treasurer.

Should the SEC examiner approve the articles? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The proposed articles contain statutory defects.

Legal Basis: Sections 14 and 24 of the Revised Corporation Code require the principal office to be located in the Philippines (noun) and the treasurer to be a resident. The official statute is published in the Supreme Court E-Library.

Application: EIC’s (noun) stated principal office is in Japan (noun), and its proposed treasurer is also a Japanese resident. Both provisions conflict with mandatory corporate requirements.

Conclusion: The examiner should withhold approval until the articles are corrected.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Corporation Code, Sections 14 and 24; Republic Act No. 11232: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/2/86463
records.Controlling Doctrine: A domestic corporation’s principal office must be in the Philippines, and its treasurer must be a resident.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
Blaine Builders Corporation (BBC) (noun) had 200,000 outstanding voting shares, including 10,000 shares under dispute in pending litigation. Harold (noun) and Joaquin (noun) called a meeting at which 98,400 shares were represented and directors were elected. Joaquin (noun) protested for lack of quorum; Harold (noun) argued that the disputed shares should be excluded.

Was there a quorum? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The disputed shares remained outstanding and counted in the quorum base.

Legal Basis: Sections 6 and 51 of the Revised Corporation Code base quorum on a majority of outstanding capital stock unless law or the bylaws provide otherwise. Villongco v. Yabut holds that shares do not cease to be outstanding merely because their ownership is litigated.

Application: A majority of 200,000 is more than 100,000 shares. Only 98,400 were represented. Excluding the disputed 10,000 shares has no statutory basis.

Conclusion: The meeting lacked quorum, so the director election was invalid.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Corporation Code, Sections 6 and 51; Villongco v. Yabut, G.R. No. 225022, February 5, 2018, discussed in Gamboa v. Finance Secretary: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69360
records.Controlling Doctrine: Shares under ownership dispute remain outstanding and are included in computing the stockholders’ quorum.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
Justin (noun) discovered that an impostor had used forged withdrawal slips to take ₱3 million from his Ozzy Pay Bank (OPB) (noun) account and deposit the proceeds into a conspirator’s OPB (noun) account. In Justin’s (noun) negligence suit against OPB (noun), the court ordered production of the conspirator’s bank records. OPB (noun) refused, arguing that the conspirator’s account was not the subject of litigation.

Was OPB’s (noun) refusal valid? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No, where the pleaded and traced money deposited in the conspirator’s account is itself the subject matter of the action.

Legal Basis: Section 2 of Republic Act No. 1405 permits inquiry pursuant to a court order when the money deposited or invested is the subject matter of litigation. Republic v. Rabusa applies the exception where allegedly illegally acquired money is placed in the account sought to be examined.

Application: The investigation traced Justin’s (noun) specific unauthorized withdrawals into the conspirator’s newly opened account. The order seeks the whereabouts and recovery of that money, not a general examination of unrelated deposits.

Conclusion: OPB (noun) may not invoke bank secrecy to refuse the narrowly directed court order.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Republic Act No. 1405, Section 2; Republic v. Rabusa, G.R. No. 208183, August 31, 2022: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68812
records.Controlling Doctrine: Bank secrecy yields to a court-ordered inquiry when the deposited money itself is the subject matter of litigation.

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Topic: Insurance — Premium Paid to Authorized Agent
records.Essay Question:
Safe Assurance Corporation (SAC) (noun), through agent Laureen (noun), issued Flavio (noun) a one-year fire policy beginning August 25, 2024. Flavio (noun) delivered the premium check to Laureen (noun) on August 26 and received an acknowledgment. His house burned on August 27. Laureen (noun), unaware of the fire, deposited the check on August 28, when SAC’s (noun) account was credited. SAC (noun) denied the claim for nonpayment before the loss.

Was there a valid and binding policy when the fire occurred? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Payment to SAC’s (noun) authorized agent before the loss bound the insurer.

Legal Basis: Sections 77, 79, and 315 of the Insurance Code govern premium payment and deem an insurer’s agent authorized to receive premiums when the policy is delivered through that agent. South Sea Surety and Insurance Co., Inc. v. Court of Appeals recognizes the effect of payment through the insurer’s authorized representative.

Application: Flavio (noun) delivered the check and received Laureen’s (noun) acknowledgment one day before the fire. Laureen’s (noun) later deposit was an internal act that did not postpone receipt by SAC (noun).

Conclusion: The policy was valid and binding when the loss occurred.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Insurance Code, Sections 77, 79, and 315; South Sea Surety and Insurance Co., Inc. v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 102253, June 2, 1995: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/33779
records.Controlling Doctrine: Premium paid to an insurer’s authorized agent before loss is payment to the insurer despite the agent’s later deposit of the check.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: South Sea Surety and Insurance Co., Inc. v. Court of Appeals

records.Subject: Commercial Law
records.Essay Question:
Sierra Electronics, Inc. (SEI) (noun) had 100 voting common shares owned by Filipino citizens and 100 non-voting preferred shares owned by foreigners. SEI (noun) planned to buy land for a manufacturing plant in the Philippines (noun).

May SEI (noun) own land in the Philippines (noun)? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Filipino ownership covers only 50% of SEI’s (noun) total outstanding capital stock.

Legal Basis: Article XII, Section 7, in relation to Section 2, of the Constitution permits land acquisition by corporations at least 60% Filipino-owned. Roy v. Herbosa requires 60% Filipino ownership both of voting shares and of total outstanding capital stock with full beneficial ownership.

Application: Filipinos own all voting common shares but only 100 of the 200 total outstanding shares. The foreign-held preferred shares remain part of outstanding capital despite being non-voting.

Conclusion: SEI (noun) does not meet the 60% total-capital requirement and may not acquire the land.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: 1987 Constitution, Article XII, Sections 2 and 7; Roy v. Herbosa, G.R. No. 207246, April 18, 2017: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/63014
records.Controlling Doctrine: For constitutionally restricted ownership, Filipino nationals must hold at least 60% of voting shares and 60% of total outstanding capital stock.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Essay Question:
The City Treasurer (noun) assessed Luminous Star Corporation (LSC) (noun) ₱900,000 in local business taxes, excluding interest and penalties. After its protest was denied, LSC (noun) appealed to the Metropolitan Trial Court (MeTC) (noun) and sought a preliminary injunction against collection. The City Treasurer (noun) argued that courts cannot enjoin tax collection.

May the MeTC (noun) issue injunctive relief? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes, if the requisites for injunction are proved.

Legal Basis: The Local Government Code contains no counterpart to the National Internal Revenue Code’s express anti-injunction rule for national taxes. Angeles City v. Angeles Electric Corporation holds that courts may issue preliminary injunctions in local-tax cases when ordinary equitable requisites are satisfied.

Application: The assessment concerns local business tax. The City Treasurer’s (noun) categorical claim of an absolute statutory prohibition is therefore incorrect, although LSC (noun) must still establish a clear right, urgency, and irreparable injury.

Conclusion: The MeTC (noun) may issue injunction upon proof of the procedural and substantive requisites.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Local Government Code; Rule 58 of the Rules of Court; Angeles City v. Angeles Electric Corporation, G.R. No. 166134, June 29, 2010: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/53986
records.Controlling Doctrine: Collection of local taxes is not subject to the NIRC’s absolute anti-injunction provision; ordinary injunction rules apply.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Essay Question:
On August 23, 2024, Topaz Gems Industries (TGI) (noun) filed an administrative claim with the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) (noun) for refund of overpaid final withholding tax on 2023 dividends. Five days later, it filed a judicial refund claim in the Court of Tax Appeals (CTA) (noun). The BIR (noun) argued that the CTA (noun) lacked jurisdiction because the judicial claim was premature.

Does the CTA (noun) have jurisdiction? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The judicial claim was prematurely filed under the Ease of Paying Taxes Act rules already effective in August 2024.

Legal Basis: Section 229 of the NIRC, as amended by Republic Act No. 11976, gives the Commissioner of Internal Revenue 180 days to act on a refund claim; appeal lies within 30 days after denial or expiration of that period. Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Carrier Air Conditioning Philippines, Inc. treats compliance with statutory refund waiting periods as jurisdictional.

Application: TGI (noun) went to the CTA (noun) only five days after its administrative filing, before denial and before expiration of 180 days.

Conclusion: The CTA (noun) lacks jurisdiction over the premature judicial claim.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: NIRC, Section 229, as amended by Republic Act No. 11976; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Carrier Air Conditioning Philippines, Inc., G.R. No. 226592, July 27, 2021: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/67901
records.Controlling Doctrine: A judicial refund appeal filed before the statutory administrative period expires, and before denial, is premature.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Carrier Air Conditioning Philippines, Inc.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Essay Question:
Fritzie Presley, Inc. (FPI) (noun), a VAT-registered corporation engaged in zero-rated transactions, claimed a refund of ₱9,811,152.02 in attributable input VAT for the second quarter of 2022. A final ₱8,501,355.53 deficiency-output-VAT assessment existed for the same quarter. The Court of Tax Appeals (CTA) (noun) offset the deficiency and refunded only the difference, although FPI (noun) had elected a full refund rather than crediting input VAT against output VAT.

May the CTA (noun) make the offset without FPI’s (noun) election? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The option to credit attributable input VAT or claim it for refund belongs to the taxpayer.

Legal Basis: Section 112(A) of the NIRC provides the alternative remedies for input VAT attributable to zero-rated sales. Chevron Holdings, Inc. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue holds that the choice is vested in the taxpayer and that the CTA may not impose an offset the taxpayer did not elect.

Application: FPI (noun) chose to claim the qualifying input VAT for refund in its entirety. The CTA (noun) substituted a different remedy by crediting the amount against a separate final deficiency assessment.

Conclusion: The involuntary offset was improper, without prejudice to lawful collection of the final deficiency.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: NIRC, Section 112(A); Chevron Holdings, Inc. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 215159, July 5, 2022: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68508
records.Controlling Doctrine: The election to credit or refund input VAT attributable to zero-rated sales belongs to the taxpayer, not the CTA.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Chevron Holdings, Inc. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Topic: Tax Prosecution — Civil Tax Liability After Acquittal
records.Essay Question:
The Court of Tax Appeals (CTA) (noun) acquitted Stephen (noun) of willful failure to file an annual income-tax return under Section 255 of the National Internal Revenue Code (NIRC), but ordered him to pay the resulting deficiency income tax. Stephen (noun) argued that acquittal extinguished all civil liability arising from the offense.

May the CTA (noun) impose the unpaid tax despite acquittal? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The obligation to pay the tax arises from law and is not extinguished by failure to prove criminal guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

Legal Basis: Sections 205 and 255 of the NIRC allow tax collection and criminal prosecution. People v. Mendez holds that the civil action for tax recovery is jointly instituted and that unpaid tax is a statutory obligation, not merely civil liability ex delicto.

Application: Stephen’s (noun) acquittal means only that the prosecution failed to prove the criminal offense beyond reasonable doubt. It does not negate the tax assessment or the lower evidentiary basis for the collection component.

Conclusion: The CTA (noun) may order payment of the established deficiency tax despite acquittal.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: NIRC, Sections 205 and 255; People v. Mendez, G.R. Nos. 208310-11 and 208662, March 28, 2023: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69095
records.Controlling Doctrine: Unpaid tax is an obligation created by law and may be recovered in the criminal tax case even when criminal guilt is not established.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Essay Question:
The Commissioner of Internal Revenue (CIR) (noun) issued a Letter of Authority (LOA) to Revenue Officer Arjun (noun) and Group Supervisor Simone (noun) to audit Waldorf Weston Corporation (WWC) (noun) for taxable year 2021. After their reassignment, Revenue District Officer Desmond (noun) issued a Memorandum-Referral authorizing Revenue Officer Valerie (noun) and Group Supervisor Warren (noun) to continue. Their recommendation led to a final assessment.

Was the Memorandum-Referral valid authority to examine WWC’s (noun) records? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. An internal referral cannot substitute for a new or amended LOA issued by an authorized official.

Legal Basis: Sections 6 and 13 of the NIRC require a valid LOA identifying the revenue officers empowered to examine the taxpayer. Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. McDonald’s Philippines Realty Corp. and Medicard Philippines, Inc. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue hold that memoranda of assignment or referral do not confer audit authority.

Application: The original LOA named Arjun (noun) and Simone (noun), not Valerie (noun) and Warren (noun). Desmond’s (noun) internal memorandum neither amended the LOA through the proper authority nor independently supplied statutory power.

Conclusion: The continued examination and resulting assessment were unauthorized and void.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Condition Precedent — Earnest Efforts Between Family Members
records.Essay Question:
Gomez (noun) died leaving a will that named his wife, Morticia (noun), as sole heir. Their daughter, Wednesday (noun), opposed probate without first alleging earnest efforts toward a family compromise. Morticia (noun) moved to dismiss for failure to satisfy Article 151 of the Family Code.

Should the probate opposition be dismissed?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The earnest-efforts requirement is inapplicable when a suit among family members concerns a matter that cannot lawfully be compromised.

Legal Basis: Article 151 of the Family Code requires earnest efforts only for suits between specified family members and excludes matters that may not be compromised. Moreno v. Kahn explains the statutory requirement and its exceptions.

Application: Probate determines whether the instrument is the decedent’s valid will. The probate court cannot validate or reject a will merely through the parties’ compromise.

Conclusion: The opposition should not be dismissed for failure to allege earnest efforts.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Earnest efforts toward compromise are not a condition precedent where the controversy is legally incapable of compromise.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Res Judicata — Successive Unlawful Detainer Actions
records.Essay Question:
Myrna (noun) filed an unlawful-detainer action against Geybin (noun), but it was dismissed because the demand to vacate was defective. After serving a valid new demand, Myrna (noun) filed another unlawful-detainer action involving the same property. Geybin (noun) invoked res judicata.

Is the second action barred?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The first dismissal did not adjudicate the parties’ possessory rights on the merits, and the second case arose from a new valid demand.

Legal Basis: Rule 39, Section 47 governs res judicata. Diaz, Jr. v. Valenciano holds that dismissal of an ejectment case for a deficient demand does not bar a later action founded on a proper demand.

Application: The first court resolved only the procedural defect. The later valid demand supplied a new jurisdictional fact and cause of action.

Conclusion: The second unlawful-detainer action is not barred.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Rules of Court, Rule 39, Section 47; Diaz, Jr. v. Valenciano: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/63625
records.Controlling Doctrine: A dismissal for a defective demand is not a judgment on the merits and does not bar a new ejectment action after a valid demand.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Essay Question:
The Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA) (noun) applied before a Regional Trial Court in Manila (noun) for a warrant to search Aidan’s (noun) residence in Quezon Province (noun). The application did not show that the place of application was among the venues specially permitted by the Rules of Criminal Procedure.

May the Manila court validly issue the warrant?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. A search warrant must be sought from a court territorially authorized under Rule 126, subject only to its stated exceptions.

Legal Basis: Rule 126, Section 2 identifies the courts where an application may be filed. Alagaban v. People treats compliance with those venue rules as essential to a valid warrant.

Application: The premises were in Quezon Province (noun), while the application was made in Manila (noun), and the facts establish no qualifying exception.

Conclusion: The warrant is invalid for want of territorial authority.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Essay Question:
Ivanka (noun) appealed her theft conviction to the Court of Appeals (CA) (noun). She failed to file an appellant’s brief within the period fixed by the Rules. The prosecution moved to dismiss the appeal.

Should the CA (noun) dismiss the criminal appeal automatically?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Dismissal for failure to file a brief is discretionary in a criminal appeal and must be exercised with special regard for the accused’s right to liberty and review.

Legal Basis: Rule 124, Section 8 authorizes, but does not compel, dismissal. Sanico v. Colipano emphasizes that procedural rules should not defeat substantial justice through an automatic sanction.

Application: Ivanka’s (noun) omission permits the CA (noun) to consider dismissal, but the court must evaluate the explanation, prejudice, and the interests of justice.

Conclusion: The appeal should not be dismissed automatically; the CA (noun) must exercise sound discretion.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Essay Question:
Karter (noun), a child, told Hermie (noun) that Vincent (noun) had abused him. At trial, the prosecution offered Hermie’s (noun) testimony about Karter’s (noun) statement without first establishing the requirements under the Rule on Examination of a Child Witness.

Is the testimony admissible?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Not on the stated foundation. The statement is hearsay unless the prosecution establishes the child-witness rule’s special requisites.

Legal Basis: Section 28 of the Rule on Examination of a Child Witness permits a child’s hearsay statement describing abuse only after notice, a reliability hearing, and either the child’s testimony or a legally recognized unavailability supported by corroboration. People v. XXX applies these safeguards.

Application: Hermie’s (noun) proposed testimony repeats Karter’s (noun) out-of-court assertion for its truth, while the required reliability and availability findings were not shown.

Conclusion: The testimony should be excluded unless the prosecution first satisfies every applicable Section 28 requirement.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Rule on Examination of a Child Witness, Section 28; People v. XXX, G.R. No. 258054: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69604
records.Controlling Doctrine: A child’s out-of-court abuse statement is admissible only upon strict compliance with the special hearsay exception.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Death of a Party — Survival and Attachment
records.Essay Question:
Esnyr (noun) sued Fonzie (noun) to collect money under a contract and obtained a preliminary attachment over Fonzie’s (noun) property. Fonzie (noun) died while the action was pending. His heirs sought dismissal and dissolution of the attachment so the estate could dispose of the property.

Do the action and attachment terminate upon Fonzie’s (noun) death?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. A contractual money claim survives the defendant’s death, and a prior attachment is not automatically dissolved.

Legal Basis: Rule 3, Section 20 directs continuation of a contractual money action after the defendant’s death, followed by enforcement as a claim against the estate. Alipio v. Court of Appeals recognizes this procedure and the preservation of liens acquired before death.

Application: Esnyr’s (noun) action is contractual, and the attachment was obtained while Fonzie (noun) lived. The heirs’ desire to dispose of estate property is not itself a ground to dissolve the writ.

Conclusion: The action should continue through the proper legal representative, and the attachment remains unless dissolved on a ground provided by Rule 57.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Rules of Court, Rule 3, Section 20 and Rule 57; Alipio v. Court of Appeals: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/36251
records.Controlling Doctrine: A contractual money action survives death, and a lien acquired by attachment before death is preserved.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Electronic Evidence — Text Messages and Screenshots
records.Essay Question:
Virgil (noun) offered screenshots of text messages exchanged with Atty. Flores (noun). Virgil (noun) personally received the messages and could identify the number, participants, and circumstances of the exchange, but Atty. Flores (noun) objected that only the device or a digital-forensics witness could authenticate them.

May Virgil (noun) authenticate the screenshots?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. A party with personal knowledge of an ephemeral electronic communication may authenticate it by testimony explaining its identity and integrity.

Legal Basis: Rules on Electronic Evidence, Rule 11, Section 2 permits proof by a party to the communication or a person with personal knowledge. Mabanag v. Mabanag applies the rule to electronic messages and screenshots.

Application: Virgil (noun) was a participant and personally received the messages. His testimony about the sender, number, context, and accurate capture can supply the required foundation, subject to contrary evidence.

Conclusion: The screenshots may be admitted after Virgil (noun) gives adequate authenticating testimony.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Ephemeral electronic communications may be authenticated by a participant or another witness with personal knowledge.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Prejudicial Question — Criminal and Administrative Cases
records.Essay Question:
Atty. Perez (noun) faced a disbarment complaint filed by Eunice (noun) arising from alleged sham trading. A related criminal case was pending, and Atty. Perez (noun) asked that the disciplinary case be suspended because the criminal action supposedly presented a prejudicial question.

Should the disciplinary proceeding be suspended?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. A prejudicial question exists only in the relationship between a previously filed civil action and a later criminal action, not between a criminal prosecution and a lawyer-disciplinary case.

Legal Basis: Rule 111, Section 7 states the elements of a prejudicial question. Wilson Po Cham v. Spouses Lim explains that an administrative disciplinary proceeding is independent and is not the civil action contemplated by the rule.

Application: The disbarment case concerns professional fitness under its own evidentiary standard and may proceed independently of criminal guilt.

Conclusion: The request to suspend the disciplinary proceeding should be denied.

records.Controlling Doctrine: A criminal case does not create a prejudicial question that suspends an independent lawyer-disciplinary proceeding.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Essay Question:
Colin (noun), a government employee, used a petition for a writ of habeas data to challenge his transfer and to seek restoration of his former position, alleging that personnel records had been used against him.

Is habeas data the proper remedy?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Habeas data protects informational privacy connected with life, liberty, or security; it is not a remedy for security of tenure or ordinary personnel disputes.

Legal Basis: Section 1 of the Rule on the Writ of Habeas Data defines its limited reach. Gamboa v. Chan holds that the writ does not issue without a concrete nexus between data gathering and a threat to life, liberty, or security.

Application: Colin’s (noun) complaint seeks reversal of a transfer and restoration to office. The facts show no qualifying threat to life, liberty, or security from unlawful data processing.

Conclusion: The petition should be dismissed without prejudice to the appropriate administrative or civil remedy.

records.Subject: Legal and Judicial Ethics
records.Essay Question:
Cassandra (noun), a lawyer, instructed Sandro (noun), her nonlawyer employee, to prepare, sign in her name, and file an appellate brief while she was away. Cassandra (noun) intended to review the document only after filing.

Was the delegation proper?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. A lawyer may delegate clerical work but may not permit a nonlawyer to exercise professional judgment, sign counsel’s name, or file a pleading without the lawyer’s prior review and responsibility.

Legal Basis: The Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability requires competence, diligence, supervision, and personal accountability for legal work. Rebarter v. Villa disciplines conduct that enables unauthorized practice or misuse of a lawyer’s professional identity.

Application: Preparing the legal arguments and signing and filing the brief are professional acts. Cassandra’s (noun) promised post-filing review cannot cure the absence of prior supervision.

Conclusion: The delegation violates the lawyer’s ethical duties and may constitute assistance in unauthorized practice.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability, Canons II and IV; Rebarter v. Villa, A.C. No. 12516: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/23/70033
records.Controlling Doctrine: A lawyer remains personally responsible for legal work and may not delegate professional functions to a nonlawyer.

records.Subject: Legal and Judicial Ethics
records.Topic: Legal Ethics — Communication with Represented Adverse Party
records.Essay Question:
Francis (noun), counsel for Kyle (noun), directly contacted Madam Toyoh (noun), who was represented by Caleb (noun), and negotiated settlement terms without Caleb’s (noun) knowledge or consent.

Did Francis (noun) violate the Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. A lawyer may not communicate or negotiate about the subject of the representation directly with a represented adverse party without that party’s counsel’s consent or legal authorization.

Legal Basis: The Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability bars improper direct communication with a represented person. Vera Law v. Spouses Edang applies the no-contact principle and protects the integrity of counselled dealings.

Application: Francis (noun) knew that Caleb (noun) represented Madam Toyoh (noun), yet bypassed him to negotiate the dispute.

Conclusion: Francis (noun) committed an ethical violation unless a recognized exception or Caleb’s (noun) consent is proven.

records.Subject: Legal and Judicial Ethics
records.Topic: Legal Ethics — Online Misconduct During Suspension
records.Essay Question:
While suspended from law practice, Diwata (noun) operated fictitious social-media accounts to circulate knowingly false and abusive claims against judges and lawyers. Diwata (noun) argued that suspension placed the conduct beyond professional discipline and that the Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability could not apply.

May Diwata (noun) be disciplined?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Suspension does not end a lawyer’s membership in the Bar or duty to maintain the profession’s standards, and the current disciplinary code applies to pending and future proceedings when fair and practicable.

Legal Basis: The Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability governs responsible social-media use and permits its procedural application under its general provisions. Supreme Court rulings on disturbing social-media posts recognize that online falsehoods and abuse may demonstrate unfitness to remain a lawyer.

Application: Diwata (noun) remained a lawyer while suspended and allegedly used deception to attack the justice system. The conduct bears directly on honesty and fitness.

Conclusion: Diwata (noun) may receive additional discipline after due process.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Essay Question:
Pauline (noun) sued Regine (noun) for partition and included another claim involving a transaction that did not arise from the same occurrence or present a common controlling question. Regine (noun) moved to dismiss the entire complaint for misjoinder.

Should the complaint be dismissed?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Misjoinder is not a ground to dismiss the action.

Legal Basis: Rule 3, Section 11 directs the court to drop or add parties, or sever claims, on just terms. Ada v. Baylon holds that procedural misjoinder should be corrected rather than used to defeat the entire suit.

Application: The unrelated party or claim may be dropped or separately tried without extinguishing Pauline’s (noun) properly joined partition claim.

Conclusion: The motion to dismiss the whole complaint should be denied, with severance or dropping of the misjoined matter as appropriate.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Rules of Court, Rule 3, Section 11; Ada v. Baylon, G.R. No. 182435, August 13, 2012: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/55115

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Essay Question:
In the criminal prosecution involving Clarisse (noun), the prosecution sought to take the deposition of Myra (noun), who was imprisoned abroad, through written interrogatories before a foreign consular officer. Gaita (noun) objected on confrontation and criminal-procedure grounds.

May the prosecution take the deposition in that manner?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The prosecution cannot substitute a foreign deposition on written interrogatories for the personal examination required in a Philippine criminal case.

Legal Basis: Rule 119, Section 15 permits conditional examination of a prosecution witness only before the court where the case is pending. Go v. People, discussing People v. Sergio, distinguishes this from the accused’s conditional examination and protects confrontation.

Application: Myra (noun) would be examined abroad, outside the trial court’s supervision, and by written questions that prevent effective contemporaneous cross-examination.

Conclusion: The proposed prosecution deposition should be denied.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Essay Question:
After William (noun) was arraigned, the prosecution discovered that the accused’s complete name was Carding Cruz III (noun), not Carding Cruz (noun), as stated in the information. It moved to add the suffix “III” without changing any alleged act or element.

Is the amendment permissible without re-arraignment?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Adding the suffix is a formal amendment that neither changes the offense nor prejudices the accused’s defense.

Legal Basis: Rule 110, Section 14 allows a formal amendment after plea with leave of court when it does not prejudice the accused. Bartolome v. People, discussing Villarba v. Court of Appeals, treats correction of a name that preserves identity as formal.

Application: The suffix merely completes Carding Cruz III’s (noun) name. The same person, transaction, and charge remain, so no new plea is required.

Conclusion: The court may allow the amendment without re-arraignment.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Essay Question:
Angel (noun) was convicted by the Regional Trial Court (RTC) (noun) of murder. On appeal, the Court of Appeals (CA) (noun) found him guilty only of homicide. Before the CA (noun) judgment became final, Angel (noun) applied for bail in the RTC (noun).

Which court may act on the application?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Only the appellate court may act on bail once the records have been transmitted and the case is pending on appeal.

Legal Basis: Rule 114, Section 5 provides that an application for bail pending appeal may be filed and acted upon by the trial court only before transmission of the original record; thereafter it belongs to the appellate court. Leviste v. Court of Appeals applies this allocation.

Application: Angel’s (noun) case was already before the CA (noun), which had modified the conviction. The RTC (noun) no longer possessed the record or authority over appellate bail.

Conclusion: Angel (noun) must apply for discretionary bail in the CA (noun), subject to Rule 114.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Essay Question:
A warrant for Erica’s (noun) arrest remained unserved for more than ten days after receipt by the implementing officer. Erica (noun) argued that the warrant had become stale and could no longer be executed.

Is Erica’s (noun) argument correct?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The ten-day period governs the officer’s duty to report, not the warrant’s validity.

Legal Basis: Rule 113, Section 4 requires the officer to execute the warrant within ten days from receipt and report the result, but an arrest warrant remains effective until executed, recalled, or quashed. Manangan v. Cudia confirms that it does not become stale merely through lapse of time.

Application: The officer’s failure to serve or report within ten days may call for explanation or sanction, but it does not cancel the judicial command.

Conclusion: The warrant may still be executed unless the issuing court recalls or quashes it.

records.Controlling Doctrine: An arrest warrant does not expire after ten days; that period concerns execution reporting.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Essay Question:
The information charging Bel (noun) and Chi (noun), prepared by Assistant Prosecutor Jill (noun), lacked the written approval and signature of the city prosecutor. The accused entered pleas and proceeded to trial without timely objection, then challenged the defect.

Does the omission invalidate the proceedings?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The lack of the chief prosecutor’s written approval is a formal defect that may be waived by failure to object before plea.

Legal Basis: Rule 110, Sections 4 and 5 govern prosecution of criminal actions and the authority to file informations. Villagomez v. People holds that absence of the required approval does not deprive the court of subject-matter jurisdiction and is waivable.

Application: Bel (noun) and Chi (noun) pleaded and participated in trial without timely raising the defect.

Conclusion: Their belated challenge should be denied, absent proof that Jill (noun) had no authority at all to prosecute.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Child Witnesses — Competency and Filial Privilege
records.Essay Question:
Raisa (noun), a minor, was called to testify against her parent, Ton (noun), concerning an offense against Rox (noun). Ton (noun) objected that Raisa (noun) was too young and invoked the parent-child testimonial privilege.

Are the objections automatically valid?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. A child is presumed qualified to testify, and the filial privilege belongs to the child-witness, not to the parent.

Legal Basis: Rule 130, Section 25 states the parental and filial privilege, while the Rule on Examination of a Child Witness presumes competency subject to examination when substantial doubt exists. Esugon v. People explains that age alone does not establish incompetence.

Application: Ton (noun) cannot personally suppress Raisa’s (noun) testimony by invoking a privilege held by her. The court must assess Raisa’s (noun) ability to perceive, remember, communicate, and appreciate truth.

Conclusion: The court should not exclude Raisa (noun) automatically; it must apply the competency rule and determine whether the statutory privilege and any exception actually apply.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Evidence — Corpus Delicti and Circumstantial Proof
records.Essay Question:
Erika (noun) was prosecuted for killing Chelle (noun). The body and weapon were not recovered, and no paraffin test linked Erika (noun) to a firearm. Ly (noun) and Ted (noun), however, testified to a chain of circumstances identifying Erika (noun) as the perpetrator.

Do the missing body, weapon, and paraffin result necessarily require acquittal?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Those omissions are not automatically fatal if the corpus delicti and guilt are established beyond reasonable doubt by competent circumstantial evidence.

Legal Basis: Rule 133, Section 4 permits conviction on circumstantial evidence when multiple proven circumstances form an unbroken chain excluding other reasonable conclusions. Zabala v. People recognizes that neither recovery of the body nor production of the weapon is invariably indispensable.

Application: The prosecution must still prove death, criminal agency, and Erika’s (noun) identity. If Ly’s (noun) and Ted’s (noun) credible testimony supplies a complete chain, the physical omissions do not defeat the case.

Conclusion: Acquittal is required only if the remaining evidence fails the beyond-reasonable-doubt standard.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Corpus delicti and identity may be established by a complete chain of circumstantial evidence even without the body or weapon.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Essay Question:
Vangie (noun) offered Jay’s (noun) birth certificate and family letters to prove pedigree. She did not establish that the declarants were dead or unavailable, that they were related to the family, or that the declarations preceded the controversy.

Are the documents admissible under the pedigree exception?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No, not on the stated foundation.

Legal Basis: Rule 130, Sections 39 and 40 require the declarant’s unavailability, qualifying family relationship or intimate association, and a declaration made before the controversy. Jison v. Court of Appeals enforces these prerequisites for pedigree evidence.

Application: Vangie (noun) did not prove the declarants’ unavailability, relationship, or ante litem motam character. A document’s existence does not itself satisfy the hearsay exception.

Conclusion: The birth certificate and letters cannot be admitted under the asserted pedigree exception unless the missing foundation is supplied or another rule independently permits admission.

records.Subject: Legal and Judicial Ethics
records.Essay Question:
While suspended from law practice, Atty. Irish (noun) acted as Janet’s (noun) attorney-in-fact in an execution sale. She communicated with court personnel, asserted legal positions, and performed acts ordinarily undertaken by counsel, but argued that a special power of attorney made the conduct private agency rather than law practice.

Did she violate her suspension?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. A suspended lawyer cannot evade the prohibition on practice by labeling professional legal services as acts of an attorney-in-fact.

Legal Basis: The Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability requires obedience to disciplinary orders. Bonifacio v. Era holds that practice of law includes activities requiring legal knowledge and representation before legal bodies, not merely courtroom appearance.

Application: Atty. Irish’s (noun) dealings in the execution proceeding required legal judgment and advanced Janet’s (noun) legal interests before court personnel.

Conclusion: Her conduct constitutes unauthorized practice during suspension and supports further discipline.

records.Controlling Doctrine: A suspended lawyer may not perform professional legal services under the guise of acting as an attorney-in-fact.

records.Subject: Legal and Judicial Ethics
records.Essay Question:
The Office of the Ombudsman (noun) investigated Judge Ferdie (noun) for conduct directly connected with the performance of judicial duties and ordered his dismissal. Romy (noun) defended the order as part of the Ombudsman’s (noun) general disciplinary authority over public officials.

May the Ombudsman (noun) dismiss the judge?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Administrative supervision and discipline of judges belong exclusively to the Supreme Court (noun).

Legal Basis: Article VIII, Section 6 of the Constitution vests administrative supervision over all courts and personnel in the Supreme Court (noun). Maceda v. Vasquez and Office of the Ombudsman v. Judge Dolalas require complaints implicating judicial duties to be referred to the Court.

Application: The charge against Judge Ferdie (noun) concerns judicial conduct. The Ombudsman (noun) cannot impose removal without intruding on the Court’s exclusive constitutional authority.

Conclusion: The dismissal order is void; the matter must be referred to the Supreme Court (noun), without prejudice to any distinct criminal investigation within lawful bounds.

records.Subject: Legal and Judicial Ethics
records.Topic: Practical Exercise — Deed of Absolute Sale
records.Essay Question:
Edsel Flores (noun) agreed to sell a specifically described parcel of land to Joel Vargas (noun) for a stated price. Prepare the essential clauses of a notarizable deed of absolute sale that identifies the parties, records the consideration and conveyance, and provides for execution and acknowledgment.

What provisions should the instrument contain?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The deed should contain verified party identities and capacity, a complete property description, the price and receipt, an unequivocal present conveyance, warranties and tax or expense allocations, signatures, witnesses, and a proper notarial acknowledgment.

Legal Basis: Civil Code Articles 1458, 1475, and 1358 govern sale, perfection, and the public-document requirement for real rights over immovable property. Requina v. Magno explains that a deed must be read as a whole to determine a perfected sale and the parties’ intent.

Application: The instrument should state that Edsel Flores (noun), for the acknowledged consideration, absolutely sells and transfers the described property to Joel Vargas (noun), with title details, boundaries, encumbrances, possession, warranties, and agreed obligations accurately disclosed.

Conclusion: The final deed must truthfully reflect the transaction and be personally acknowledged before a duly commissioned notary after competent proof of identity.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Essay Question:
Asya (noun) sued Kobe (noun), who was temporarily staying at Makati Hotel (noun). The sheriff left the summons with a hotel receptionist without first showing diligent attempts at personal service or that the receptionist was a competent person in charge of Kobe’s (noun) residence or regular place of business.

Was substituted service valid?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Substituted service is exceptional and requires strict proof of prior diligent personal-service attempts and delivery at a place and to a person authorized by the rule.

Legal Basis: Rule 14, Section 6 requires personal service whenever practicable; substituted service under Section 7 is allowed only for justifiable causes and prescribed recipients. Manotoc v. Court of Appeals demands a detailed sheriff’s return showing compliance.

Application: A temporary hotel and its receptionist were not shown to be Kobe’s (noun) residence, regular business, or authorized recipient, and the return did not establish diligent prior attempts.

Conclusion: The substituted service was invalid.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Essay Question:
Kay (noun) received allegedly defective summons and filed a stand-alone motion to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction over her person after the 2019 amendments to the Rules of Civil Procedure.

How should the court treat the objection?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The court should not grant a prohibited stand-alone motion to dismiss, but Kay (noun) may preserve lack of jurisdiction over her person as an affirmative defense in the answer.

Legal Basis: Rule 15, Section 12 generally prohibits motions to dismiss except for specified grounds, while Rule 8, Section 12 requires affirmative defenses, including lack of personal jurisdiction, to be pleaded and resolved early. United Coconut Planters Bank v. Ongpin explains that voluntary appearance may confer personal jurisdiction except when made solely to object.

Application: Kay’s (noun) objection remains potentially valid, but the amended procedure requires it to be asserted through the answer unless it falls within an express motion exception.

Conclusion: The stand-alone motion should be denied without treating the jurisdictional objection as waived if Kay (noun) timely pleads it as an affirmative defense.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Essay Question:
Attorney Woo (noun) served a pleading on Attorney Han (noun) through an accredited private courier although personal service was practicable. No written explanation for not using personal service accompanied the pleading.

Is service valid under the amended rules?

Legal Basis: Rule 13, Sections 5 and 6 expressly permit service and filing through accredited courier. IP E-Game Ventures, Inc. v. Tan discusses the governing modes and the effect of the amended procedural framework.

Application: Attorney Woo (noun) used a mode expressly authorized by the current rule. The former written-explanation requirement cannot be reintroduced when the amended text does not require it.

Conclusion: The courier service is valid upon compliance with the rule’s addressing and proof requirements.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Filing and Service — Proof by Accredited Courier
records.Essay Question:
Samurai (noun) asks what proof must accompany or later establish service of a pleading sent through an accredited private courier.

What documents constitute sufficient proof?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Proof consists of the sender’s affidavit of service together with the courier’s official receipt and tracking or delivery record, as required by Rule 13.

Legal Basis: Rule 13, Section 17 prescribes proof for service by accredited courier. Heirs of Deloy v. Court of Appeals illustrates the need for competent documentary proof of the chosen service mode.

Application: The affidavit should identify the pleading, addressee, date, place, and manner of deposit, while the courier records independently show acceptance and delivery tracking.

Conclusion: Samurai (noun) should retain and submit the affidavit, official receipt, and available tracking or delivery confirmation.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Essay Question:
Jimuel (noun) filed a second petition to declare his marriage to Jewel (noun) void, relying on a ground or supporting theory different from one that had already been finally rejected between the same parties. The validity of the marriage had been directly adjudicated in the first case.

Is the second petition barred?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes, to the extent the second petition seeks to relitigate the same finally determined marital-status issue.

Legal Basis: Rule 39, Section 47 embodies bar by prior judgment and conclusiveness of judgment. Dy v. Bibat-Palamos holds that a final adjudication binds the parties on matters directly resolved and cannot be evaded by changing theories.

Application: Jimuel (noun) and Jewel (noun) are the same parties, and the first final judgment determined the validity issue. A new label for substantially the same asserted defect does not reopen that adjudication.

Conclusion: The second petition should be dismissed under res judicata or conclusiveness of judgment, as the identity of causes and issues warrants.

records.Controlling Doctrine: A final judgment binds the parties on issues actually and directly resolved, notwithstanding a later change in legal theory.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Essay Question:
Isol (noun) sought a writ of preliminary injunction to prevent Rona (noun) from removing or altering a kitchen while ownership and possession were disputed. Isol (noun) alleged imminent destruction but had not yet established a clear legal right to the kitchen.

Should the writ issue?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No, unless Isol (noun) proves a clear and unmistakable right, an urgent necessity, and irreparable injury that cannot be adequately compensated.

Legal Basis: Rule 58, Section 3 governs preliminary injunction. Cahambing v. Espinosa states that the remedy protects an existing right and cannot create one while title or entitlement remains doubtful.

Application: Isol’s (noun) asserted right to control the kitchen is itself disputed. Imminent alteration may show urgency, but urgency cannot replace proof of a clear right.

Conclusion: The application should be denied on the stated facts, without prejudice to renewed relief upon sufficient proof.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Preliminary injunction requires a clear existing right and urgent irreparable injury; it cannot establish a disputed right.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Succession — Action by Heirs Without Prior Declaration
records.Essay Question:
The acknowledged heirs of a decedent filed an ordinary civil action to recover estate property. No probate or intestate proceeding was pending, and no prior judicial declaration of heirship had been obtained.

May the heirs maintain the action?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. When no special proceeding is pending and the action’s purpose is not primarily to establish heirship, heirs may sue to protect inherited rights without a prior separate declaration.

Legal Basis: Civil Code Article 777 transmits successional rights at death. Treyes v. Antonio abandons the inflexible prior-declaration rule and permits heirship to be determined in an ordinary action when necessary and no special proceeding is pending.

Application: The plaintiffs invoke inheritance as the basis for recovering property, and there is no competing estate proceeding in which heirship should first be settled.

Conclusion: The civil action may proceed, with heirship proved as an incident of the case.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Special Proceedings — Recognition of Foreign Divorce
records.Essay Question:
Namjoon (noun), a Korean national (noun), obtained a divorce from Regine (noun), a Filipino citizen (noun), in Korea (noun). Regine (noun) sought judicial recognition in the Philippines (noun) and correction of the civil-registry entry under Rule 108.

Is Rule 108 an available procedure, and where should the petition be filed?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. A foreign divorce may be recognized in a Rule 108 proceeding, filed in the Regional Trial Court of the province where the corresponding civil registry is located.

Legal Basis: Rule 108, Sections 1 and 2 govern cancellation or correction of civil-registry entries. Fujiki v. Marinay holds that recognition of a foreign judgment affecting civil status may be joined with correction proceedings, subject to proof of the judgment and foreign law.

Application: Regine (noun) seeks to annotate the marriage record based on Namjoon’s (noun) Korean divorce. She must prove the authentic divorce decree and applicable Korean law and implead the required parties.

Conclusion: The petition is procedurally proper in the RTC (noun) where the relevant civil registry is situated.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Essay Question:
Notting Hill (noun) obtained an ejectment judgment against lessee Hugh (noun). Julia (noun), who occupied the premises as Hugh’s (noun) sublessee or transferee during the litigation, resisted the writ of execution because she was not named as a defendant.

Is Julia (noun) bound by the judgment?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes, if she entered under Hugh (noun) or derived possession from him after commencement of the action.

Legal Basis: Rule 39, Section 47 and the ejectment rules bind successors-in-interest and persons holding under the defendant. Heirs of Mariano v. City of Naga explains that a judgment may be enforced against privies whose possessory right is subordinate to the adjudged party.

Application: Julia’s (noun) occupation came through Hugh (noun), so she has no independent possession superior to the judgment and cannot defeat execution by nonjoinder.

Conclusion: The writ may be enforced against Julia (noun), subject to proof that she is in fact Hugh’s (noun) privy.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Essay Question:
Cain (noun) pleaded guilty to an offense then punishable by a capital penalty. The trial court immediately relied on the plea and imposed judgment without requiring the prosecution to present evidence of guilt and degree of culpability.

Was the procedure valid?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. For a capital offense, the court must conduct a searching inquiry, require prosecution evidence, and allow the accused to present evidence despite the guilty plea.

Legal Basis: Rule 116, Section 3 makes these safeguards mandatory. People v. Pagal reiterates that a guilty plea does not relieve the prosecution of proving guilt and the precise degree of culpability.

Application: The court skipped the prosecution-evidence stage and based judgment solely on Cain’s (noun) plea.

Conclusion: The judgment is procedurally defective and must be set aside for compliance with Rule 116.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Essay Question:
Identify and briefly describe three judicial warrants available under the Rule on Cybercrime Warrants for obtaining, intercepting, or examining computer data.

What are the three warrants?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Three are the Warrant to Disclose Computer Data (WDCD), Warrant to Intercept Computer Data (WICD), and Warrant to Search, Seize, and Examine Computer Data (WSSECD).

Legal Basis: A.M. No. 17-11-03-SC defines the WDCD as compelling disclosure from a service provider; the WICD as authorizing real-time interception; and the WSSECD as authorizing search, seizure, and forensic examination of computer data. Nicolas v. Romulo documents judicial use of a WDCD and reinforces that these powers require the particular warrant prescribed by the Rule.

Application: Investigators must select the warrant matching the intended act: provider disclosure, real-time interception, or physical or remote search and examination.

Conclusion: The three requested warrants are WDCD, WICD, and WSSECD, each subject to probable cause, particularity, and the Rule’s safeguards.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Cybercrime investigation requires the specific judicial warrant corresponding to disclosure, interception, or search and examination of computer data.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Evidence — Offer of Compromise in Quasi-Offense
records.Essay Question:
Ricky (noun), charged with reckless imprudence after a collision involving Dante’s (noun) Maserati (noun), offered to pay for the damage to avoid litigation. The prosecution offered the compromise as an implied admission of guilt.

Is the offer admissible for that purpose?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. An offer to compromise a quasi-offense or criminal-negligence charge is excluded from the implied-admission rule.

Legal Basis: Rule 130, Section 28 provides that an accused’s compromise offer may imply guilt except in quasi-offenses or offenses legally allowed to be compromised. People v. XXX states and applies the distinction between ordinary crimes and quasi-offenses.

Application: Reckless imprudence is a quasi-offense. Ricky’s (noun) willingness to pay for the Maserati’s (noun) damage may reflect a desire to settle civil consequences, not an admission of criminal negligence.

Conclusion: The offer is inadmissible as an implied admission of guilt.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Rules of Court, Rule 130, Section 28; People v. XXX, G.R. Nos. 136870-72, January 28, 2003: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/48029
records.Controlling Doctrine: An offer to compromise a quasi-offense is not admissible as an implied admission of criminal guilt.
